text:
A figure that earns its place

11:22



w10-labelled-figure.R



Same data as Pitfall 2 later in this deck. Point at each element in turn — axis names, units, the “so what” in the subtitle, the source — so students recognize the stripped version when it reappears.
The subtitle percentages are computed by the script, not typed. Say so: a number written by hand into a caption is a number that can drift out of step with the figure above it.

title: Bringing it together
text:
Every line equally loud

11:24



w10-annotation-before.R · idea after Heiss (2026)



This is Week 4’s “after” standard: axes, units, title, source, legend ordered by size. Nothing here is wrong. Ask: what is this figure about? Expect several answers — that is the problem.
Watch the room shuttle between legend and lines. Then ask which line is bioenergy: gas and bioenergy are two near-identical dark colours. Six series is more than a legend can carry.
Numbers for narration, from the script (shares of total generation, 2025): gas 31.7 %, wind 29.4 %, bioenergy 14.0 %, nuclear 12.2 %, solar 6.8 %, coal 0.0 %.

title: Bringing it together
text:
One story, labelled directly

11:27



w10-annotation-after.R · idea after Heiss (2026)



Same data, same scales. Three decisions, and each is one you can make in your report:

Label the lines directly. The legend is gone; the eye never leaves the data.
Highlight the story, grey the rest. The grey lines stay: they answer “compared to what?” without competing.
Annotate the point that matters. 2017 is the first year bioenergy generated more than coal (9.4 % vs 6.7 %; in 2016 coal was still just ahead, 9.1 % vs 8.9 %). The script finds the year; nobody typed it.

The title now states the finding. Carbon Brief does exactly this — it is on the next slide.
Tie back to Phase 1: this is the chart the biomass briefing was about. Much of that bioenergy is imported wood pellets burned at Drax, a former coal station — which is why “carbon-neutral?” was a real question.
The labels are placed without an add-on package: the script nudges them apart just far enough not to overlap. Students can open it.
For more on labels: Cara Thompson, Level up your labels (useR! 2022).

title: Bringing it together
text:
Good figures in the wild

11:30

Each makes one decision well. Look at the figure, then ask what it chose not to show.

Carbon Brief — UK’s electricity was cleanest ever in 2024: every title states the finding; the fuel chart labels its lines and greys out nuclear.
Our World in Data — Share of electricity by source: sources and downloadable data sit beneath the chart, and the reader can add a country — compared to what? built in.
Financial Times — Visual Vocabulary: choose the chart by the relationship you want to show, not by habit.
Ed Hawkins — Show your stripes: drops axes and numbers entirely for one unmissable message. Right for a poster; would it survive a policy report?
The Pudding — Women’s pockets are inferior: measures real jeans, draws the pockets to scale, and asks what actually fits.



[1 min, within 11:10–11:33] Show the slide and open none: one sentence on Carbon Brief (closest to their reports), the rest are homework before they finalize figures. This minute pays for the risk-perception slide in block 3.
The stripes are a deliberate contrast: a brilliant public-engagement graphic that would lose marks in a report, because a reader cannot check a single number. Decisions depend on the audience.
The deck has preview-links: auto, so a click opens the page inside the slide. If a site refuses to be framed and the preview is blank, ctrl/cmd-click to open it in a new tab.

Quick-fire: spot the problem

12:03


Six excerpts from fictional reports. Two minutes each; one you’ve already seen. What went wrong, and at which PPDAC stage?



[12:03–12:15] These are cumulative — each pitfall connects to a specific week’s content. Students should recognize most of them.
The stage is revealed with each problem. Plan: 5. Analysis: 3. Conclusion: 1, 2, 4, 6. Most go wrong at Conclusion, the “communication gap”: the analysis may be fine, the report isn’t.

title: Bringing it together
text:
Pitfall 1

12:05


“The data clearly demonstrate that offshore wind is the most cost-effective energy source.”


Conclusion. Not supported by the data shown. The report only compared three sources and used levelized cost from 2019.

title: Bringing it together
text:
Pitfall 2

12:06



w10-unlabelled-figure.R


Conclusion. The reader can’t interpret it. A figure that isn’t discussed is decoration, not evidence.


[30 s] The labelled twin was in block 1. Ask “what’s missing?”, take one answer, move on: this saving pays for the risk-perception slide.

title: Bringing it together
text:
Pitfall 3

12:08


“p = 0.04, therefore the effect is significant and the policy should be adopted.”


Analysis. No effect size, no CI, no discussion of practical significance. “Is that a big number?”

title: Bringing it together
text:

12:10


“The results prove that solar power will eliminate fossil fuel use by 2040.”


Conclusion. Overstatement. “Prove” is almost never appropriate. Extrapolation without caveats.

12:12

12:13

Conclusion. Every analysis has limitations. Omitting them doesn’t make them disappear — it makes the reader distrust you.

title: Bringing it together
section: Shape the message, not the data
text:
Shape the message, not the data

12:28

A figure for a reader is built around one message:

Write the headline first: what should the reader take away?
Cut or aggregate detail that doesn’t advance the story; mute axes and gridlines.
Connect the numbers to your readers’ interests and lives.



Choosing what to emphasize is editing. Changing the evidence to fit the story is HolmesCo.



[3 min, within 12:15–12:40] The pull-idea from Krzywinski & Cairo, “Storytelling”, Nature Methods 10, 687 (2013), https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.2571. Its standfirst: “Relate your data to the world around them using the age-old custom of telling a story.” Their test for the message is the newspaper headline your study would get; then shape the figure (aggregate, emphasize, sequence the panels) so the headline is what the reader sees. Paraphrase; don’t read it out.
Two more points of theirs worth saying aloud: leaving readers to draw their own conclusions is risky, and “always be accurate”. A story that bends the evidence is the traitor briefing.
Link back to the coal/bioenergy pair: greying four lines was editing. Deleting gas and wind, so that bioenergy looked like the thing that replaced coal, would have been advocacy: wind grew far more. That is the Week 4 traitor line, and the difference between analysis and advocacy this block is about.
Suggested reading before submission: Krzywinski & Cairo (one page; paywalled, so via the library) and the free chapter Wilke, Telling a story and making a point.
Idea sequence after Heiss (2026), session 15.

title: Bringing it together
text:
Your reader has feelings too

12:30

People weigh a risk by how it feels, not only by how often it happens:

Dreaded, unfamiliar, imposed risks loom large
Familiar, chosen risks shrink



Which feels riskier: a fracking tremor you can barely feel, or an old mine working under your street? Which is likelier to crack your walls?




Give the reader counts, not percentages: “about 1 house in 1000”, not “0.1 %” or “risk doubled”. And say what the risk is compared to.



[5 min, within 12:15–12:40] One minute on the prompt; take two answers, then the key point.
Tremor: in August 2019 a magnitude 2.9 event at Preston New Road, Lancashire, led to the moratorium on fracking in England that November. Mine workings: County Durham is old coalfield; the Coal Authority deals with subsidence and collapsed shafts as a matter of routine. Don’t argue which is riskier: the point is how differently they feel.
Slovic (1987), “Perception of risk”, Science 236: 280–285: dread and unknown risk are the two factors that predict public concern.
Counts are Week 6’s natural frequencies: the medical test worked out of 100 000 people because counts are how readers think. “Risk doubled” with no baseline is a pitfall: doubled from what?
It cuts both ways. A report on flood or landslide risk is read by people who feel it; writing as though they don’t is a failure of communication, and inflaming it is the traitor briefing.
Your own feelings count too: the analyst who dreads a hazard is readier to believe the evidence for it.

title: AI, reproducibility, and integrity
text:
Live demo (if possible)

11:18


🖥️ Give an AI the HolmesCo gold assay scenario
“We tested 1000 soil samples with a 95 %-accurate assay. 54 tested positive. What’s the probability of a true gold deposit?”


Watch what it does with the base rate.


The AI will likely either get it wrong (ignoring the base rate) or give a generically correct but vague answer without applying it to the specific numbers.
The point: fluent ≠ thoughtful.
This is the Week 6 press release: same assay, same 54 of 1000. They have already worked it out by hand — the test is whether the AI can.
Whatever number it offers, the next slide is the answer, and it is not a number.

title: AI, reproducibility, and integrity
section: The discovery is no bigger than the false-positive rate
text:
The discovery is no bigger than the false-positive rate

11:22



w09-assay-floor.R



Week 6 did this arithmetic in a 2×2 table. Same numbers, same press release — keep the two in step if either is ever edited.
A 95 %-specific assay calls 5 % of barren ground positive: 50 samples out of 1000, before any gold is involved. HolmesCo found 54, well within chance (binomial SD about 7, as in Week 6).
So the honest answer is not a percentage at all. It is “you have no more hits than your own assay produces from nothing, and you never told me how common deposits are here, so a probability was never available.”
That is what to check the AI’s answer against. A fluent one will give a confident number — which means it invented the base rate.

title: AI, reproducibility, and integrity
text:
The key distinction

11:26


AI is fluent but not thoughtful.
It can write a convincing paragraph about any result — including a wrong one.

title: AI, reproducibility, and integrity

11:30


Think about a time in this module when you used AI (or were tempted to). What did it help with? Where did you have to override it?


Common patterns:

Useful: debugging code, plot templates, explaining errors
Unreliable: interpreting results, choosing methods

title: AI, reproducibility, and integrity
text:
The replication crisis

11:45

Many published findings don’t hold up when others try to reproduce them.


w09-replication-rates.R



[11:45–12:10] Reproducibility as a practical skill.
“Many” is exactly the kind of word this course spends ten weeks training them to challenge, so it should not survive on our own slide.
The three definitions of success differ, and that is the second lesson here: “replicated” is not one thing. Psychology counted a significant replication; economics required the same direction too; cancer biology used three of five criteria. Comparing the bars directly is the mistake to point at.
All three numbers come from the papers’ own abstracts, cited under the chart.

title: AI, reproducibility, and integrity
text:
Why?

11:49


p-hacking — trying many analyses, reporting the one that “works”
Underpowered studies — too few observations to detect real effects
Selective reporting — filing away null results
Data not shared — no one can check your work

title: AI, reproducibility, and integrity
section: One number, or the shape it came from
text:
One number, or the shape it came from

11:57

A bootstrap interval — like the one you’ll build this afternoon in exercise w9_1, from uk_electricity.csv — is not a fact about the world. It is a range read off a distribution of 1000 resampled means.


w09-bootstrap-distribution.R



Idea adapted from Andrew Heiss, Data Visualization with R, session 6 “Uncertainty” — show uncertainty as a distribution, not just an interval.
Same statistic as exercise w9_1: the mean of late (UK wind generation, 2015–2025), bootstrapped 1000 times.
The top panel is what goes in a report sentence: “65.6 TWh [55.2, 75.1]”. The bottom panel is what that sentence compresses — the shaded band is the same interval, cut out of the same shape.
Point to ask: the histogram is not symmetric around 65.6 in the way a textbook normal curve would be. That is real information the single-number interval throws away.

title: AI, reproducibility, and integrity
text:
Rerun it without the seed

12:02

This afternoon’s bootstrap draws random resamples. Run the same code twice with no set.seed() and the 95 % interval moves both times:



Run
95 % interval (TWh)




No seed, run 1
55.8 to 74.8


No seed, run 2
55.7 to 76.1


set.seed(2847), any run
55.2 to 75.1, always





Which of these three rows would you want printed in your report?



Numbers are from three actual runs of this afternoon’s replicate() code against uk_electricity.csv (two unseeded, one with set.seed(2847)), not estimated.
The point is not that the seeded number is “more correct” — all three intervals are equally valid draws from the same procedure. It is the only one a reader, a marker, or you in six months can check against what you wrote down.
This is the same distinction as reproducibility generally: a seed does not fix an answer, it fixes which answer you get, so it can be checked.

title: AI, reproducibility, and integrity
text:
Practical reproducibility habits

12:06


Script everything — no “I typed this in the console”
Document your decisions — why this test, why you excluded those data points
Record software versions — sessionInfo() in R
Seed anything random — set.seed() before sample() or replicate(), once, not inside the loop
Share data and code — within ethical limits



Connection to the policy report: a policy-maker should be able to trace your conclusion back to your data.
Item 4 connects straight to this afternoon’s exercise w9_1, whose fourth fault is exactly a missing seed.

Run your analysis script from scratch.

Hardcoded file paths
Missing libraries
Steps done in the console but not saved



Fix what you can. 10 minutes.

title: Models and their limits
text:
How did you do?
The Economist, 23 September 2026: “Many surgical interventions are little better than placebo”.

Hands up: a row? Two rows? Full house?


Which square was hardest to fill?


[20 min; clock time TBC: Week 8 plan not yet rebalanced] Recap of Weeks 3–7 through the bias-bingo homework (materials/bias-bingo.md). Answer key with paragraph numbers: staff/bias-bingo-key.qmd.
Quick show of hands, then ask for the hardest square. Expect base rate neglect or multiple comparisons. Multiple comparisons has no clean example; reward anyone who argued “not here”.
Don’t read the article out; students have it. Quote only the phrases on the slides.

title: Models and their limits
section: Why did surgeons think it worked?
text:
Why did surgeons think it worked?
Patients felt better after surgery. Three stories fit that:

The operation fixed the problem
The body healed on its own
Being cared for made them feel better (placebo)


Pooling 100 surgical trials: about two-thirds of the improvement was stories 2 and 3.


Squares: confounding, placebo, effect size.
Recovery and ritual always travel with the operation, so an uncontrolled before/after comparison credits the scalpel with all three. That is confounding in its purest form.
“Is that a big number?” One-third of the benefit is still a benefit; the question is whether it justifies the risk and cost.
Ask: which square did you put this under? Several answers are right.

title: Models and their limits
text:
How do you separate them?



Compare
Isolates




Surgery vs sham surgery
the operation itself


Sham surgery vs no treatment
the placebo


No treatment, before vs after
natural recovery




One 2002 trial splashed water into a dish so the sham sounded right.


Squares: control group, randomization, blinding, “Compared to what?”.
Each row is a control group answering a different question. Most of the benefit in the sham arm turned out to be natural recovery, not placebo.
Moseley’s knee trial (165 patients): the team matched even sounds a patient under general anaesthetic might register. Blinding taken seriously.
A 2020 review: only about 1 % of trials for chronic musculoskeletal pain compared surgery with doing nothing at all.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Why were surgeons so sure?

Patients who come back for check-ups are mostly the ones who got better
Those who come back don’t want to disappoint their surgeon
Surgeons’ predictions of who will improve: no better than a coin toss



Squares: survivorship bias, reporting bias, confirmation bias.
The surgeon’s evidence is their own follow-up clinic. The failures have gone elsewhere; the successes are polite. Years of experience build confidence on a biased sample.
“Confidently be unconfident” (Blazeby) is a good line to leave on the screen verbally.

title: Models and their limits
text:
The square most people missed
Scans find tears and “abnormalities” in knees, backs and shoulders.

The same abnormalities are common in people with no pain at all.


How plausible was this before we tested?


Square: base rate neglect (Week 6).
We want P(abnormality causes pain | abnormality seen). If most pain-free people of the same age have it too, finding it in a patient tells you very little. Same structure as HolmesCo’s gold assay.
Also worth a minute: the paid-per-operation vs salaried contrast (UK shoulder operations fell by about four-fifths after the trials; US numbers did not). Is that a fair comparison? Countries differ in far more than how surgeons are paid: confounding again.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Now make it geological
What does each of these look like in a geological investigation?




Surgery
Geology




Only recovered patients return
Dry holes and failed slopes never get written up


Patients heal anyway
Groundwater recovers once pumping stops. Did the remediation work?


Abnormal scans in painless knees
Faults are everywhere. Is this one why the ground subsided?


Surgeons have no uncertainty
Experts disagree on the same seismic section





In geology nobody says the word “placebo”. Would you spot these?


Ask for the geological versions students wrote at home first; reveal the table only as backup.
Seismic interpretation: Bond et al. (2007, GSA Today) gave the same synthetic section to hundreds of geoscientists; most did not reach the right interpretation.
Remediation is rarely compared with an untreated control site. The answer is the Week 5 before–after–control–impact design.
Link forward: a model is a claim about causes. Today’s question, “What is the model not capturing?”, is another way of asking which of these we’ve missed.

title: Models and their limits
text:
What is a model?
A deliberate simplification that captures some features of reality and ignores others.

Every statistical test you’ve run contains an implicit model.
The t-test models the data as two normal distributions, one per group.
Now we make the model explicit.


[20 min block; clock time TBC: Week 8 plan not yet rebalanced] Linear regression — concept and live demo.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Linear regression
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon\]

“y increases by β₁ for every one-unit increase in x, plus noise.”


That’s the whole model. It’s powerful — and limited.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Live demo










Type this, don’t paste it. The students have elec on their own page; tell them to beat you to the R² and start typing a minute in.
Anticipated code:
elec <- read.csv("data/uk_electricity.csv")

ggplot(elec, aes(x = year, y = bioenergy_twh)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

model <- lm(bioenergy_twh ~ year, data = elec)
summary(model)
The slide previously showed lm(output ~ windspeed, data = turbine_df) and claimed R² ≈ 0.6. No such dataset exists in this repo, so no one could ever have run it. Biomass over time is real data the students already know from Week 1.
Numbers: slope 1.693 TWh per year, R² = 0.926, p = 4.4e-15, residual SE 3.73 on 24 df. “Biomass generation has risen about 1.7 TWh a year, and a straight line accounts for 93 % of the variation.”
Deliberately not the solar data — that is Exercise 1 in a few slides’ time, and its negative slope should surprise them.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Reading the output



Element
Meaning




Intercept (β₀)
Predicted y when x = 0


Slope (β₁)
Change in y per unit change in x


R²
Proportion of variance explained


p-value (slope)
Is the slope distinguishable from zero?





Read it off the demo: “R² = 0.93 means 93 % of the variation is explained. 7 % is something else.”
The intercept is −3387 TWh: the line’s prediction for the year 0. Ask what it means. Nothing: it is where the line happens to cross x = 0, far outside the data.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Solar panels and temperature
Solar panel output against panel temperature.
Before you plot: do hotter panels produce more power, or less?


Make a scatter plot
Fit lm()
Interpret the slope and R²
Plot the fit




Is the relationship linear? Does the model capture the pattern?

title: Models and their limits
text:
The four assumptions

Linearity — the relationship is actually linear
Independence — residuals don’t influence each other
Homoscedasticity — constant variance of residuals
Normality of residuals (for inference)

title: Models and their limits
text:
Diagnostic plots








Four plots, two that matter most:



Plot
What to look for




Residuals vs Fitted
Pattern = non-linearity or heteroscedasticity


QQ plot
Departures from the line = non-normal residuals





Anticipated code — one line, and model is still in the session from the live demo a few slides back:
plot(model)
If the session has been reset, re-run the demo cell first.
Walk through each plot. “No pattern in residuals vs fitted = good. Points on the QQ line = good.”
Biomass over time is a useful case here: R² is 0.93 and the residuals-vs-fitted panel still curves, because growth was flat then steep. High R², wrong shape — which is the point of the whole session.

title: Models and their limits
text:
The scenario


⚒️ HolmesCo
Geological Consultants Since 2019
“Our Trends Hold Water”™

Groundwater Analysis Report
Linear model: groundwater level ~ rainfall. R² = 0.49.
“Rainfall is the dominant control on groundwater levels.”


Exercise 3 on your page: reproduce their model, then plot what it left behind.


[15 min; clock time TBC: Week 8 plan not yet rebalanced] Students plot the residuals against month (Exercise 3). Don’t move on to the next slide until they have drawn it themselves: it is the debrief.
plot(model) will not show the cycle: its panels don’t know the order of the observations. The pattern only appears against month.

title: Models and their limits
text:
What’s wrong?


w08-residuals.R


The residuals show a seasonal pattern — the model is missing a time-dependent structure
R² = 0.49 means 51 % of the variation is unexplained
“Dominant” is a stretch when your model misses more than it captures



Debrief, after Exercise 3. Ask what they found before revealing.
Key question: what is the model not capturing? (Seasonal recharge, time lag between rainfall and groundwater response, temperature effects on evapotranspiration.)

title: Models and their limits
text:
Failure 1: Overfitting
A model that fits the training data perfectly but fails on new data.
It’s memorized the noise.


[25 min block; clock time TBC: Week 8 plan not yet rebalanced] Three failures — each a different form of hubris. Demo the polynomial overfitting live.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Demo: polynomial degree 15








The polynomial passes close to almost every point, and swings wildly between them. The straight line fits worse, but predicts better.


More complex ≠ more useful.



Type this, don’t paste it. Anticipated code (the same simulation as the next slide’s figure):
set.seed(2801)
pts <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(20, 0, 10)))
pts$y <- 3 + 1.4 * pts$x + rnorm(20, 0, 2.5)

ggplot(pts, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 15), se = FALSE,
              colour = "red", n = 400) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-5, 25))
The visual contrast is striking. coord_cartesian() keeps the data on screen when the polynomial leaves it.
The next slide is the same contrast, pre-rendered — use it as the fallback if WebR misbehaves, and leave it up while they discuss.

title: Models and their limits
text:
What that looks like


w08-overfitting.R



Both R² values are read off the fitted models, so “fits worse” is arithmetic. “Predicts better” is not measured on this figure: make it concrete with the question below.
Ask for a prediction at x = 11 from each model. One of them has an answer; the other has left the building.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Failure 2: Extrapolation
A model that works within the observed range but breaks down outside it.

Example: UK solar generation has grown roughly exponentially since 2010. Extrapolate the curve, and by 2035 solar alone exceeds all UK generation.










w08-extrapolation.R



What’s the model not capturing?


Take answers before offering any: planning constraints, grid limits, diminishing suitable sites.

title: Models and their limits
text:
HolmesCo’s extrapolation


⚒️ HolmesCo
Geological Consultants Since 2019
“Our Trends Hold Water”™

“Our linear trend in groundwater decline predicts the aquifer will be empty by 2028.”


What would you need to know before believing this?


Take answers first. The two that matter: seasonal recharge (a short record that ends in a dry spell exaggerates the decline), and whether the decline was caused by temporary pumping that will stop.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Failure 3: Blind spots
Things the model structurally cannot represent.


A single-turbine power curve has no term for wake interference → overpredicts wind farm output by 10–20 %
A carbon accounting model that counts biomass as zero structurally cannot see the emissions it ignores




You can only fix a blind spot if you know it’s there.

title: Models and their limits
text:
The new refrain

“What is the model not capturing?”

Overfitting: too much faith in your data.
Extrapolation: too much faith in your model.
Blind spots: too much faith in your framework.


These are three forms of the same mistake: confusing the map for the territory. Each is a different flavour of hubris.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Write one sentence

“In my project, the biggest thing my analysis might be missing is…”



[5 min; clock time TBC: Week 8 plan not yet rebalanced] Quick written reflection. Students keep this for their reports.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Key points

A model is a simplification — powerful, but limited
Always check the diagnostics: residuals don’t lie
Three failures: overfitting, extrapolation, blind spots
Always ask: “What is my model not capturing?”

title: Comparing groups
text:
The problem

11:10

Three groups (e.g., wind farms in three regions).
You could run three pairwise t-tests: A vs B, A vs C, B vs C.

Each test, on its own, has a 5 % chance of a false positive.

Run 20 tests where nothing is going on. How often do you “find” something?



[11:10–11:30] Multiple comparisons. Take guesses before the next slide; most of the room will say 5 % or “once”.

title: Comparing groups
text:
Chance in action

11:15











Type this, don’t paste it. Same move as Week 6’s null world: build a world where nothing is going on, then watch what the test does there.
Anticipated code:
t.test(rnorm(25), rnorm(25))$p.value

survey <- replicate(20, t.test(rnorm(25), rnorm(25))$p.value)
sum(survey < 0.05)

set.seed(7)
hits <- replicate(1000, {
  survey <- replicate(20, t.test(rnorm(25), rnorm(25))$p.value)
  sum(survey < 0.05)
})
mean(hits >= 1)
table(hits)
Run steps 1 and 2 unseeded, three or four times each: the room sees p bounce around, and some surveys turn up one or two “discoveries”.
Step 3, from a real run with set.seed(7) just before replicate(): 67 % of surveys find at least one; 76 of 1000 (about 1 in 13) find three or more. Theory says 64 %; the difference is simulation noise.
Then the shortcut, exactly as the t-test was a shortcut for the shuffle: 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.64. Put the formula on the board; it reappears in Exercise 1.

title: Comparing groups
text:
HolmesCo’s mineral survey

11:20



⚒️ HolmesCo
Geological Consultants Since 2019
“Leave No Stone Untested”™

Press Release — Multi-Element Anomaly Discovered!
“We tested soil samples from 20 sites for enrichment in 20 elements. We found statistically significant enrichment (p < 0.05) for three elements at one site!”



If there’s truly nothing there, how many significant results would you expect by chance?



Their survey is 20 of our simulated surveys, one per site. Students can reason from the last slide: 20 expected false positives, about one per site.

title: Comparing groups
text:
The answer

11:25

20 × 20 = 400 tests at α = 0.05
Expected false positives: 20, about one per site.

With nothing there at all, some site scores three or more four times in five.
The “discovery” is what noise looks like.


Each site’s hits are binomial(20, 0.05): one site reaches three with probability 0.075; across 20 sites, 1 − 0.925²⁰ ≈ 0.79.
In the simulation, about 1 survey in 13 found three or more by itself. With 20 sites, one of them doing so is the expected outcome.
Ask what the press release leaves out: the total number of significant results across all 400 tests, and which site HolmesCo would have predicted before looking. They picked the site after seeing which came out best.

title: Comparing groups
text:
Your project

11:30


How many comparisons are you planning to make?


If you run all of them at α = 0.05, what’s your family-wise false positive rate?


Formula: 1 − (1 − α)k where k = number of tests


[11:30–11:37] Students calculate for their own projects. Then discuss: “If you’re testing more than one thing, you need to account for it.”

title: Comparing groups
text:
One test for multiple groups

11:37

ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) asks:

“Does any group differ from the others?”

Without specifying which.


[11:37–12:02] “Same data, four ways” (~5 min), from δ to F, the null world for F (live), corrections.

title: Comparing groups
text:
Same data, four ways

11:37

Before any test: how you show a comparison changes what you see.
Four regions, same 100 sites, same order (low mean to high) — shown four different ways.


[11:37–11:42, inside concept block 2] A quick sequence, no discussion prompts needed on each panel — let the four builds speak for themselves, then land the takeaway on the last one.
Idea adapted from Andrew Heiss, Data Visualization with R, session 6 (“Uncertainty”) and session 8 (“Comparisons”) — After Heiss (2026).

title: Comparing groups
section: Same data, four ways: the bar
text:
Same data, four ways: the bar

11:38



w07-groups-bar.R



The “dynamite plot.” Ask: would you trust this? What would change your mind?
What it hides: the spread within each region, the sample size, and whether the gap between any two bars is bigger than the noise.
Region order here is by group mean. The exercise page’s Exercise 1 orders its violins by median, which swaps Wales and Southern England — worth a one-line heads-up if a student notices the mismatch.

title: Comparing groups
section: Same data, four ways: the box plot
text:
Same data, four ways: the box plot

11:39



w07-groups-box.R



Better: the spread is visible, and the two-cluster pattern starts to show. Still hides the individual sites and the sample size per box.
If someone asks “why not just use this” — flag Nick Desbarats’ Nightingale piece, linked on the exercise page: box plots take longer to teach than most students realize, and a good fraction of any room cannot read one confidently.

title: Comparing groups
section: Same data, four ways: the raw points
text:
Same data, four ways: the raw points

11:40



w07-groups-points.R

Takeaway: a bar of means can hide a bad idea; the points behind it usually don’t.


This is the picture ANOVA reasons about: a mean, its uncertainty, and the scatter behind it. Compare it to the F-ratio figure three slides later — same encoding, cyan points and an ink summary.
Point out that individual sites overlap heavily between regions even though the means and CIs are cleanly separated. Both things are true at once.

title: Comparing groups
section: Same data, four ways: the raincloud
text:
Same data, four ways: the raincloud

11:41



w07-groups-raincloud.R · after Heiss (2026)



Optional coda, after the takeaway on the previous slide: shape, sites and interval on one axis. If the block is running long, cut this slide and move straight to “From δ to F”.
Ask what this shows that panel 3 didn’t. Northern England’s cloud has two bumps: two kinds of site? Let students argue, then tell them that every region was drawn from a single normal distribution (data/generate-teaching-data.R). Twenty-five points through a smoother make bumps. Before believing a sub-group, ask whether the points alone would show it.
The cloud is drawn with ggdist; the interval is the same hand-computed mean ± 95 % CI as the previous slide.
Further reading (Nick Desbarats, “I’ve Stopped Using Box Plots. Should You?”, Nightingale, and Claus Wilke’s “Visualizing uncertainty”) is linked on the exercise page — don’t read it out.

title: Comparing groups
text:
From δ to F

11:42

Week 6: two groups, one number. δ = difference between the means.

Four groups: six differences. Testing each is the problem we just met.


One number instead:
\[F = \frac{\text{how far the group means spread}}{\text{how far sites spread within their group}}\]


δ was “how far apart are the means?”, judged against the null world’s spread. F asks the same of four means at once: how spread out are they, compared with the noise inside each group?
The bottom line is the same yardstick δ used. In Week 6 we judged δ against the spread of the null world (the SE), which came from the scatter of the boreholes.
With exactly two groups, F = t²: same test (Exercise 2’s extension has students check this).

title: Comparing groups
text:
“Relative to within”

11:47



w07-f-ratio.R



Left is our data, the same sites as the last four slides. Right: the same four means, each site moved twice as far from its region’s mean.
Ask which panel you would be willing to call a real regional difference, before reading the F values.
Doubling the scatter divides F by four: the spread enters squared.
Both F values come from aov() on the panel’s own points.
Is 14.2 big? Compared to what? The next slide builds the comparison.

title: Comparing groups
text:
The null world for F

11:52











Type this, don’t paste it. It is Week 6’s shuffle, line for line, with F where δ was. Students have the data; race them.
Anticipated code:
wind <- read.csv("data/wind_output.csv")
f_of <- function(region) {
  summary(aov(wind$capacity_pct ~ region))[[1]][["F value"]][1]
}
f_obs <- f_of(wind$region)
f_obs

f_of(sample(wind$region))

set.seed(7)
null_f <- replicate(1000, f_of(sample(wind$region)))

ggplot(data.frame(null_f), aes(x = null_f)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = f_obs, colour = "red")

mean(null_f >= f_obs)
Numbers from a real run: F = 14.21. Shuffled F values huddle near 1; the largest of 1000 is 8.8, and the 95th percentile 2.8. None reaches 14.2, so the simulated p is below 1/1000.
One tail only: F can’t be negative, and only a big F is surprising.
The shortcut: summary(aov(capacity_pct ~ region, data = wind)) gives F(3, 96) = 14.21, p = 9.8 × 10⁻⁸. Say it, don’t type it: that line is Exercise 2.
“This is an ANOVA”, just as last week’s shuffle was a t-test.

title: Comparing groups
text:
Corrections for multiple comparisons

11:57




Method
How
When




Tukey’s HSD
All pairwise, designed for ANOVA
After a significant ANOVA


Bonferroni
Divide α by number of tests
Simple, conservative, any context




Both reduce the false positive rate by being stricter about what counts as significant.


Don’t go deep into the math. The key idea: when you test multiple things, you raise the bar for each individual test.

title: Comparing groups
text:
“Significant” ≠ “important”

12:15


A p-value tells you whether an effect is detectable.


It does not tell you whether it’s big enough to matter.



[12:15–12:35] Effect sizes — the statistical formalization of “Is that a big number?”
Don’t explain it: ask. Week 6’s application page had them grow n until the same 0.5 °C difference became “highly significant”. What happened to the p-value, and what happened to the difference?

title: Comparing groups
text:
Cohen’s d

12:20

A standardized measure of how far apart two groups are:
\[d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_\text{pooled}}\]



d
Interpretation




0.2
Small


0.5
Medium


0.8
Large





It answers “how many standard deviations apart are the groups?”

title: Comparing groups
text:
What those numbers look like

12:25



w07-cohens-d.R



The point is the right-hand panel. “Large” still leaves two groups overlapping across most of their range — so a significant result with d = 0.8 does not mean you can tell an individual’s group from their measurement.
The shared percentage is integrated from the curves, not asserted.

title: Comparing groups
text:
For ANOVA: η² (eta-squared)

12:30

Proportion of variance explained by the grouping variable.



η²
Interpretation




0.01
Small


0.06
Medium


0.14
Large





Always report both the p-value and an effect size.
A policy-maker needs to know “how big?” — not just “is it real?”



Link to “Is that a big number?” from Week 2. Same habit, formalized.

text:
Is the difference real?

11:10





The Whin Sill at Holwick Scars, Teesdale. Gordon Hatton / Geograph, CC BY-SA 2.0


Boreholes in the Stainmore Formation run hotter, on average, than boreholes in the Whin Sill.

“Is this difference larger than we’d expect by chance?”




[11:10–11:42] The null world by simulation, then the t-test as its shortcut, each with a live demo.
Don’t say “t-test” yet. The whole block builds one idea, the null world, and only names the formula once students own the idea. The reveal is “This is a t-test”, after the null-world demo.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Five steps, every test

11:13


Measure δ — the one number you care about. Here: Stainmore’s mean temperature minus Whin Sill’s.
Build a null world — a world where δ really is zero. Simulate it: shuffle the formation labels, recompute δ, repeat.
Drop your δ into it. Does it look at home?
Count how often the null world makes a δ at least as extreme. That fraction is the p-value.
Decide, against a standard you set before you looked.



Steps 2–4 are the heart of it. Today we do them by brute force, by shuffling; the named tests come later and only replace those steps with a formula.
The idea that every test is this one test is Allen Downey’s (“There is only one test”); the five-step framing and the interactive version are Andrew Heiss’s Null worlds, https://nullworlds.andrewheiss.com/. Point students there — the sliders make the intuition stick.
The whole method rests on one question: how surprising would this be if nothing were going on? Plant a flag here. In block 3 we will meet its partner — how plausible was this before we tested? — and the gap between the two is the base-rate fallacy. A null world only ever answers the first question.

title: Testing hypotheses
section: A world where formation doesn’t matter
text:
A world where formation doesn’t matter

11:16



w06-null-world.R · After Heiss (2026), Null worlds



Left is step 1: the data as sampled. δ = 8.4 °C.
Right is step 2: keep every temperature exactly as measured, but deal the formation labels out again at random, 1000 times. In every one of those worlds formation cannot matter — the labels are noise — so the spread of δ is what chance alone produces with these boreholes.
Step 3: the dashed lines are our real δ, both signs, because the question is “this extreme”, not “this large”.
Step 4: count the red. 26 of 1000, so p = 0.026.
Hold on to this picture: after the reveal, “What ‘how often’ means” shows a smooth curve with shaded tails. That curve is the formula’s version of this histogram.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Build the null world

11:20











Type this, don’t paste it. Students have the same data; invite them to beat you to the p-value.
Anticipated code:
borehole <- read.csv("data/borehole_temp.csv")
temp <- borehole$temperature_c

delta <- mean(temp[borehole$formation == "Stainmore"]) -
  mean(temp[borehole$formation == "Whin Sill"])
delta

shuffled <- sample(borehole$formation)
mean(temp[shuffled == "Stainmore"]) - mean(temp[shuffled == "Whin Sill"])

set.seed(6)
null_deltas <- replicate(1000, {
  shuffled <- sample(borehole$formation)
  mean(temp[shuffled == "Stainmore"]) - mean(temp[shuffled == "Whin Sill"])
})

ggplot(data.frame(null_deltas), aes(x = null_deltas)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-delta, delta), colour = "red")

mean(abs(null_deltas) >= abs(delta))

sd(null_deltas)
Numbers from a real run: δ = 8.417; p = 0.026 (26 of 1000 shuffles). The null deltas run from about −11.4 to +11.1.
Step 3 is unseeded on purpose: run it two or three times so the room sees each shuffle give a different δ, near zero. Then set.seed(6) immediately before replicate() — that is what the figure on the previous slide used, so the p-value matches it exactly. Put the seed anywhere else and the third decimal moves; that wobble is itself worth a sentence: a simulated p-value is an estimate, and 1000 shuffles is plenty to tell 0.03 from 0.3.
abs() twice makes it two-sided: “this extreme”, either way.
Step 7 gives about 3.9 °C (the exact value depends on the seed). Don’t explain it yet: it is the hook for the next slide.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
SD or SE?

11:23



w06-sd-or-se.R

SD: spread of the boreholes. SE: spread of δ between samples.


[2 min] Students met SD in Weeks 1 and 2; SE is new. Every later week leans on it (Week 7’s ± 1.96 SE, Week 8’s slope SE).
Left column: “more points keep the same scatter”: SD 20 and 9 °C in both rows. Right column: “but with more points, a shuffle is less likely to put the means far apart by chance”, so the null world narrows from about 7.5 °C to 3.9 °C.
The SD describes the data; the SE describes a statistic (here δ) across the samples we might have drawn. The null-world histogram is exactly that picture: the bottom right is the null world the room just built, and its SE is the sd(null_deltas) they just saw.
Formula, if asked: SE of δ = √(SD₁²/n₁ + SD₂²/n₂), which gives 3.75 °C at n = 35 per formation, close to the shuffle’s 3.94 °C. The n under the root is why more data narrows the SE while leaving the SD where it is.
The 8-per-formation subset is real boreholes, drawn at random. Numbers: sd() gives 20.26 °C (Stainmore) and 9.10 °C (Whin Sill).

title: Testing hypotheses
section: What would the null world be?
text:
What would the null world be?

11:26

For each claim: what would you shuffle, simulate, or hold fixed?

The same 15 boreholes, logged in 2005 and again in 2025, read warmer now.
HolmesCo struck water in 8 of its 10 boreholes, beating the regional rate of 50 %.
Downstream wells have more sulphate than upstream ones. The wells were sampled in upstream–downstream pairs, one pair per site.



[3 min, within 11:10–11:42] Desks, one minute per claim. Ask for the null world, not a test name. Each claim needs a different step 2.
1: paired. Within each borehole, swap the two readings at random (equivalently, flip the sign of each 2025 − 2005 difference). Shuffling across boreholes would mix in the differences between sites, which is not what the claim is about. Aside: even a clear result answers “chance?”, not “why?” (newer probes? Week 5’s confounders).
2: simulate from a model. There are no labels to shuffle. Flip a fair coin 10 times, count the heads, repeat 1000 times; how often do we get 8 or more?
3: constrained shuffle. A free shuffle breaks the pairing: sites differ in geology, so sulphate varies more between sites than within them. Swap the labels only within each site. Good place to plant the word “assumption” for block 2: every null world assumes something about which values could have traded places.
The point to drill: the same five steps every time, but step 2 is where the thinking is.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
This is a t-test

11:29

A t-test asks the same question with a formula, instead of a shuffle:

Assume no difference: the null world (the null hypothesis)
Calculate how far apart the means are, relative to the variability (→ t-statistic)
Ask: if there were really no difference, how often would we see a t this extreme? (→ p-value)



The reveal. Map each line back to the five steps: line 1 is step 2, lines 2–3 are steps 3–4.
The payoff line: “Everything t.test() does is a shortcut for what we just did by hand.” Shuffling needs no normality assumption — but it still compares means, and Stainmore’s long tail drags its mean. Block 2 comes back to that, and it is not the test’s fault.
The formula buys speed and a smooth curve; it costs assumptions about the shape of the data. Next demo: does it agree with our 0.026?

Every test rests on assumptions

11:50

For the t-test:

Independence — observations don’t influence each other
Normality — data within each group are roughly normal
Equal variance — groups have similar spread (Student’s t; Welch’s t relaxes this)



[11:50–12:05] Assumptions, how to check, what to do when violated. Keep “How to check” to a quick pass: name Levene’s test but don’t demo it. The skew figure is where the time should go.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
When assumptions are violated

11:58

A skewed variable can produce misleading p-values.


w06-skew-and-logs.R



This is the dataset from the live demo. The test they just ran is the one that breaks: p = 0.030 raw, p = 0.22 logged. Both p-values are computed by the script.
Nothing was removed and no outlier was excluded. The only change is the scale the test was run on.
Someone may ask: the shuffle test assumed nothing about normality and still gave 0.03 — so was the t-test really broken? Shuffle the log temperatures and you get p ≈ 0.23, close to the logged t-test’s 0.22. Both machines agree on whichever δ you hand them; the transform changes the question (typical ratio, not mean difference in °C), and with a tail like Stainmore’s the mean is the wrong question.

title: Testing hypotheses
section: HolmesCo stopped at the first test
text:
HolmesCo stopped at the first test

12:01



⚒️ HolmesCo
Geological Consultants Since 2019
“Our Results Are Never Skewed”™

Borehole Temperature Survey — Statistical Analysis
t-test on raw values: p = 0.03 → “Significant! Drill the Stainmore.”
t-test on log-transformed values: p = 0.22 → not in the report.
The “significant” result was an artefact of skewness.



Same data as the live demo and the figure on the last slide. HolmesCo ran the raw test, got 0.03, and wrote it up; the report is at the top of the Week 6 exercise page, which the students are about to open. They never looked at the histograms, so never took logs.
Temperature at depth, like permeability and grain size, is often roughly log-normal, so “check the shape first” is a habit, not a one-off.

Expected: about 51 hits, 1 of them real. HolmesCo found 54.


Is 54 different from 51? Is it different from 50 hits and no gold?


True positives: 1 × 0.95 ≈ 1. False positives: 999 × 0.05 ≈ 50. P(gold | positive) ≈ 1 / 51 ≈ 2 %.
Let desks argue about 54 vs 51. By chance alone the false-positive count varies by about ±7 (binomial SD, √(999 × 0.05 × 0.95) ≈ 6.9), so 54 is unremarkable: it is what the assay produces if there is almost no gold at all. The press release is nonsense.
This is the Week 6 equivalent of the traitor reveal.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Connection to p-values

12:34

A p-value tells you: P(data | H₀)
How surprising is this data if the null is true?

What you actually want: P(H₀ | data)
How likely is the null to be true given this data?



These are not the same thing. The difference depends on the base rate.



Call back to the null world: every p-value today answered “how surprising would this be if nothing were going on?” The refrain on the next slide is the question the null world cannot answer.
Key sentence: “If you’re testing an implausible hypothesis, a significant p-value is probably a false positive. If you’re testing something well-supported, a significant result is more convincing.”

title: Testing hypotheses
section: “How plausible was this before we tested?”
text:
“How plausible was this before we tested?”

12:37




Russell’s Teapot: a claim no telescope can refute Alex Zak, CC BY-SA 4.0




This is the Bayesian insight without the formula. The habit of asking about prior plausibility is what matters.
This also sets up Week 7: if you run 20 tests, the base rate for any individual hypothesis being true is low → false positives accumulate.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
HolmesCo double-checks

12:40



⚒️ HolmesCo
Geological Consultants Since 2019
“Where There’s a Test, There’s Gold”™

Update — Gold Discovery Confirmed!
“We re-assayed all 54 hits, and 49 were positive again. The chance of a false positive passing both tests is 0.05 × 0.05 = 1 in 400.”



When is it fair to multiply the two probabilities?




Only when the two tests’ false positives are independent. Same samples, same lab, same method: whatever fooled the first assay fools the second.



[12:40–12:45] Desks, one minute on the prompt, then reveal.
Arithmetic for quick desks: about 50 of the 54 hits are false. If the second assay’s false positives were independent of the first’s, 5 % of those would pass again: 2 or 3. HolmesCo got 49. The re-test has shown that the false positives are not independent, not that the gold is real.
What would make them independent? A different method (fire assay), a different lab, fresh samples from the same spot.
Geoscience versions: Fukushima Daiichi’s grid connection and its backup generators both failed in one event (earthquake, then tsunami); storm surge and river flood arrive in the same storm; two “independent” barriers on a tailings dam overtopped by one rainfall. If each barrier fails one year in 100, multiplying says both fail one year in 10 000; if the same storm overtops both, it is nearer one year in 100.
Same assumption as the t-test’s first: independence.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Controls

11:20

What you hold constant so you can isolate the variable of interest.

Example: How does latitude affect wind farm output?


What else differs between wind farms at different latitudes, apart from latitude?


Here I’m thinking on the scale of the UK. But could think more broadly too.





Control for
Why




Turbine model
Different models have different capacities


Terrain
Ridgetop/valley/offshore: affects wind speed


Grid curtailment
Grid operator tells certain farms to stop generating







Harder to control: Weather; maintenance schedules; …



Geoscience angle: in field sciences we rarely get true experiments. We observe natural variation and try to isolate factors. This makes design more important, not less.
Maintenance schedules: more efficient after a service? Lack the data to be able to control for this - operators won’t tell you.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Treatment vs control groups

11:25



Lab sciences
Treatment group gets the intervention.
Control group doesn’t.
Random assignment.


Field sciences
“Treatment” is often a natural condition.
“Control” is a comparison group.
You can’t randomize geology.




Because we can’t randomize, we need to think harder about what might confound our comparisons. That’s next.

Work with the rest of your desk for 5 minutes.



Students read the full report from the link on this slide or on the exercise page.
[11:30–11:45] Expected problems: (a) boreholes are in the valley, turbines are on ridgetops; (b) 3 is tiny; (c) convenience sampling; (d) no context for whether “competent sandstone” = “suitable for foundation”. Requires comparison to safe & unsafe wind farm geology; presence of mine workings?

36 specimens from 3 holes is n = 3 for “what is the site like?”: the narrow CI is pseudoreplication. Name it only if a desk raises it; the sampling block comes back to it.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Attendance

11:30


Show the QR from https://attendance.durham.ac.uk/mytimetable, then ← back to the task.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
The problems

11:38


Tiny sample: 3 boreholes for a multi-km² site; 36 specimens don’t change that
Wrong location: boreholes in the valley, turbines on the ridgetops
Selection bias: sampled where it was convenient, not representative
No comparison: how do we know this is unusually good (or bad)?
Is this the right question? e.g. presence of mine workings?

title: Designing your investigation
text:
What is a confounder?

11:45

A variable that is correlated with both the treatment and the outcome.
You can’t tell which caused the effect.


[11:45–12:15] Confounders are the hidden trap in observational studies.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Confounding examples

11:47





Ice cream by the sea: Hatice Baran / Pexels





Observation
Apparent cause
Real cause (confounder)




Ice cream sales ↑, drowning ↑
Ice cream causes drowning?
Hot weather


More solar panels → higher GDP
Solar causes wealth?
Latitude, governance, investment


Wind farms → fewer bird species
Turbines harm birds?
???





Confounders, contra causation, can cause correlation.


The third row is real data, and the next four slides unpack it. Leave the “real cause” column for now; come back to it.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Wind farms and birds

11:50



w05-wind-map.R



Real data, and a real question: do wind farms harm birds? Every square of Great Britain that is mostly land. Wind farm = 8 or more turbines, from the government’s Renewable Energy Planning Database.
Birds: every species recorded in each square in 2006–15, from the British Trust for Ornithology’s volunteer records (Garden BirdWatch, BirdTrack and surveys), via the NBN Atlas.
Ask where the wind farms are: exposed, windy, away from towns. Park that.

title: Designing your investigation
section: Wind farm squares have fewer species
text:
Wind farm squares have fewer species

11:52










Polished version: w05-birds-raw.R


Turbines harm birds?





# Wind farm by 2015, or not
squares$farm <- squares$largest_farm_by_2015 >= 8

# What am I measuring? Bird species recorded, 2006–15
ggplot(squares, aes(x = farm, y = species)) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se,            # mean and
               fun.args = list(mult = 1.96))  # 95 % CI
Then hone:
# At top:
theme_set(theme_grey(base_size = 18))

# Replace sq$farm:
ifelse(squares$largest_farm_by_2015 >= 8,
                       "Wind farm", "None")

Output: no wind farm 134.5 species (95 % CI 132.8–136.2, 2100 squares); wind farm 126.3 (120.8–131.8, 139 squares). About 8 fewer.
The next five boxes each rebuild squares in a hidden setup block, so any of them runs on its own: you can jump in mid-deck.
mean_se(mult = 1.96) is a normal-approximation CI; the polished script uses the t quantile. Same numbers to one decimal place.
Let the room agree that turbines harm birds. It is the story they expect, and the confidence intervals do not overlap.
Then ask: where do birdwatchers live? Who submits these records?

title: Designing your investigation
text:
A possible confounder: recording effort

11:54














A confounder must be tied to both sides. Check the diagnosis before treating it. This slide: the outcome. Next slide: the exposure.
cor(): One number for how closely two columns rise together: 1 in lockstep, 0 no relation, −1 one falls as the other rises.
Anticipated code:
cor(squares$records, squares$species) # Pearson coefficient = 0.71
# What have I done wrong?
# ALWAYS LOOK AT THE DATA FIRST!
ggplot(squares, aes(x = records, y = species)) + geom_point()
cor(squares$records, squares$species, method = "spearman") # 0.82
Outputs: Pearson 0.71, Spearman 0.82. The scatter curves: species climb fast, then level off. Spearman uses ranks, so it doesn’t need a straight line. Busier squares list more species: tied to the outcome.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
A possible confounder: recording effort

11:57














tapply(): Do it the long way first, one group at a time, then: “But there’s a shortcut!” tapply(x, group, f) splits x by group and applies f to each piece. (In Python: groupby().agg().)
Anticipated code:
ggplot(squares, aes(x = farm, y = records)) + geom_violin()
median(squares$records[squares$farm == "Wind farm"])
median(squares$records[squares$farm == "None"])

# the shortcut
tapply(squares$records, squares$farm, median)
The violins are squashed flat by a few city squares with hundreds of thousands of records. + scale_y_log10() shows the shapes, if wanted. That skew is also why median, not mean.
Median records: wind farm 5130, no wind farm 11 456. Wind farm squares are looked at half as hard. Tied to both: a confounder.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Allowing for recording effort: Stratification

11:59














The method is stratification: put squares into ten bands by number of records; compare each square with its own band.
New in R: quantile(x, 0:10 / 10) gives the cut points that split x into ten equal-sized groups; cut() puts each square in its band. ave(x, group) is tapply()’s cousin: the group average, repeated for every row, so it lines up with x.
Anticipated code:
# 1.
squares$band <- cut(squares$records,
                    quantile(squares$records, 0:10 / 10),
                    include.lowest = TRUE, dig.lab = 6)
table(squares$band)  # about 224 squares in each

# 2.
squares$vs_band <- squares$species -
  ave(squares$species, squares$band)
dig.lab = 6 prints the band edges as plain numbers (1176, not 1.18e+03). Leave it out first if you want to show why it’s there.
Bands run from 158–1176 records to 52 207–311 015: about 224 squares in each.
A square with ten thousand garden-feeder records will list more species than a moor that three people visited. Records stand in for effort.

title: Designing your investigation
section: Allowing for recording effort: the result
text:
Allowing for recording effort: the result

12:01













Polished version: w05-birds-effort.R


Turbines help birds?



Anticipated code: the first slide’s plot, with vs_band for species.
ggplot(squares, aes(x = farm, y = vs_band)) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se,
               fun.args = list(mult = 1.96))
Plot: no wind farm −0.3 (−1.3 to 0.7); wind farm +4.5 (1.1 to 7.9). A gap of about +5.
The answer has reversed. A wind farm developer would print this one.
The implicit message is that wind farms are responsible for the increase. Are we reading correlation the right way?

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Before the turbines

12:03













Polished version: w05-birds-before.R


The “benefit” was there before any turbine. Something else chose those squares.



Narrate the logic first: if turbines caused the gap, it cannot predate them.
Anticipated code:
# 1.
untouched <- squares[!squares$any_wind_by_2015, ]

# 2.
untouched$later <- ifelse(untouched$largest_farm_later >= 8,
                          "Wind farm later", "Never")

# 3.
ggplot(untouched, aes(x = later, y = vs_band)) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se,
               fun.args = list(mult = 1.96))
The effort bands were set on all squares on the last slide, before this subset: the measure is the same one. Worth saying if asked.
Output: never 1711 squares, −1.4 (−2.5 to −0.3); wind farm later 238 squares, +3.7 (1.2 to 6.2). A gap of about +5, before any turbine.
These squares had no turbines while the birds were being recorded, so turbines cannot have caused the gap. Developers pick sites that were already better for birds: windy, open, unenclosed, away from people.
“Later” includes refused applications: they still show where developers chose to go.
Correcting for one confounder changed the answer; it did not make the answer right. Back to the table: the “real cause” for row three is both recording effort and site selection.

title: Designing your investigation
section: What would a controlled experiment look like?
text:
What would a controlled experiment look like?

12:06


You fund wildlife research. Design the study that would tell you what wind farms do to birds.



[5 min, desks, within 11:45–12:15] Hoped-for answers: count birds at the same site before and after; compare with similar sites where nothing was built; count the same way every time.
You cannot randomize where wind farms go — so this is the best that field science can do.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Same sites, before and after

12:08





Curlew: Odd Rune Falch / Pexels


Pearce-Higgins et al. (2012) J. Appl. Ecol. 49: 386–394




Design

18 upland wind farms, UK
Breeding birds counted before, during and after construction
Same counts on nearby reference sites with no turbines



Findings

Snipe −53 % during construction
Curlew about −40 %, with no recovery
No such declines on reference sites





Each wind farm is compared with itself, which removes site selection; the reference sites catch changes that would have happened anyway. This is a before–after–control–impact design.
Skylark and stonechat increased: “may be spurious” (differences between wind farm and reference sites). But is this confirmation bias? Even a good design has to watch for confounders.
Most of the damage was during construction, not operation. A snapshot map lacks that granularity.
doi:10.1111/j.1365-2664.2012.02110.x

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Why the reference sites?

12:10



⚒️ HolmesCo
Geological Consultants Since 2019
“Results Well Above Average”™

Remediation Results
Last summer we treated the five wells with the highest nitrate in the catchment. This summer, all five are lower. Treatment works.



What would those five wells have done without treatment?




Regression to the mean: pick sites because they were extreme, and they look better next time anyway. An extreme reading is partly bad luck, and luck doesn’t repeat.



[4 min, within 11:45–12:15] Desks, one minute, then reveal.
Hoped-for answer: fallen anyway. Last summer’s top five were partly high because of that summer: a dry spell, a fertilizer application, a sampling day after rain. Next year’s draw is ordinary.
Not a confounder, but the same cure: a comparison group selected the same way. Five equally bad wells, left untreated, show how much improvement comes for free. That is what Pearce-Higgins’s reference sites do.
It runs the other way too: the best sites slip back. The top of any league table (wettest catchment, windiest turbine, best borehole) is partly luck.
Geoscience versions: rockfall netting after the worst year on record; flood defences after a record flood; “our intervention” credited with a return to normal.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
How to handle confounders

12:13


Randomization — when possible (rare in geoscience)
Stratification — compare within subgroups
Matching — pair similar observations
Acknowledgement — when all else fails, be honest about what you can’t control



1: e.g. “Choose at random which requested turbine sites we’ll build on”
2: e.g. stratify by n bird observations, earlier
3: Compare sites where confounders happen to have the same values
4: most common in geoscience and policy analysis. Honesty about confounders is itself a research skill.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
How to choose your sample

12:15





Shap Granite. Sample a grain: which one? jtweedie1976 / Flickr, CC BY 2.0





Strategy
How
When




Random
Every unit has equal probability
Gold standard; often impractical


Stratified
Sample within each subgroup
Ensures representation


Systematic
Every nth unit
Regular grids, monitoring stations


Convenience
Whatever’s easiest
HolmesCo’s default






[12:15–12:40] Practical sampling. The key message: your sampling strategy is a decision you must justify.
Characterizing a magma body. Could: sample grains at random. Have to be careful: if we just point at a sample, we’re more likely to hit a big grain. That might be good if we want to characterize the composition - or bad if we want to characterize grain size!
Stratified: Sample all plag grains, all qz, all micas…
Systematic: A grid?

title: Designing your investigation
text:
The same site, four ways

12:23











w05-sampling-strategies.R




High Hedley Hope wind farm, County Durham. Where on this site would you sample? Oliver Dixon / Geograph, CC BY-SA 2.0




Random and systematic are the pair the table cannot separate: both are “unbiased”, and they look nothing alike. Note the gaps in the random panel — that is what stratification exists to prevent.
Systematic: Regular spacing is a shorthand for “pick the samples that are most different from one another” – R package Coreset. Difference may not be “distance in XY”.
The convenience panel is HolmesCo’s default: “we sampled these because they were there”. Honest, but weak. Ask what question that sample can answer, and about what area.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
One sample, or many?

12:32

HolmesCo tested 36 core specimens from 3 boreholes.
Is that n = 36, or n = 3?

A replicate is one independent sample of the thing you are asking about. For “what is the site like?”, that thing is the ground, and specimens from one hole share its ground: n = 3.


Count them as 36 and the confidence interval shrinks for free. That is pseudoreplication.



Your sampling strategy, and your unit of replication, are decisions you must justify in your report.



[5 min, within 12:15–12:40] Ask the room before revealing. Some will say “it depends on the question”, which is the right answer: for “how variable is the rock within BH-01?”, 12 specimens are 12 replicates.
Geoscience versions: 100 grains from one thin section; hourly output from one turbine as evidence about turbines in a region; ten readings from one gauge on one day.
Sets up Week 6: “independence” is the first assumption of the t-test.
Research plan question 4 now asks each group for its unit of replication. Students will need to explain why they chose their data sources and whether their sample is representative.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Choose your topic

12:40


Browse the available project topics.


Form provisional groups (3–4 people).


Pick a candidate topic. Then sketch:

Question — what are you investigating?
Data — what would you need?
Comparison — what’s your control?
Confounders — what should you worry about?



[12:40–12:50] Groups form and discuss. Each group shares one sentence. Topics don’t need to be final — that happens in the app session.

text:
Key points

12:43


Good design = clear comparison + controlled confounders
Extremes drift back: compare with sites that were left alone
Sampling, and what counts as a replicate, are choices you must justify
HolmesCo’s mistakes are easy to make — watch for them in your own work

title: Making the case
text:
Who is your reader?

11:10

Policy-makers are busy non-specialists who need to make a decision they can stand by.

What they need:

A clear bottom line
Evidence that bears the weight of the conclusion
Clarity on what’s uncertain



[11:10–11:20] Writing for non-specialists. This is the communication strand coming to a head.
Uncertainty: Which “fact”’s gonna turn around and bite them on the ass?

title: Making the case
text:
Structure of a policy briefing

11:15




Section
Purpose




Summary
The answer. Reader could stop here.


Evidence
Figures, data, analysis


Caveats
Uncertainty, assumptions: what’s a journalist going to hurl at me?


Conclusions
Considered recommendation




An academic paper / dissertation / PPDAC cycle goes the other way round: progressively build up to an answer.


Key principle: “Your reader should be able to stop after the summary and still know the main message.”
Evidence: How big is the problem being solved? Why is this the solution?
Caveats: Prepare for scrutiny by the opposition / Lords / public / Today
“Considered” recommendation → How strongly should the policy-maker argue?

title: Making the case
text:
Inspect the text

11:20

Handout: §Solar biomass, from David MacKay, Sustainable Energy – without the hot air (2008), pp. 42–44.


Use three different colours to highlight:

Claim: what MacKay wants the reader to take away
Evidence: what the claim is based on
Caveat: what limits the claim (e.g. assumptions)



Text: withouthotair.com, CC BY-NC-SA 2.0 UK.



About the book: Mackay was sick of greenwash: vague but unsubstantiated claims of how we could live sustainably. His one desideratum: Numbers that add up! The book asks the question: What would a sustainably-powered UK look like?
Nine months after it came out he was Chief Scientific Adviser at DECC. The numbers, well communicated, drove policy.
Converts the numbers to kWh per person and works through one source/sink of energy at a time. Here we’ve reached biomass.
NOTE: The numbers are from 2008. The approach is timeless. “Do the numbers add up?”. “Is that a big number? Compared to what?”
[11:20–11:26] Hand out pp. 42–44, and highlighters. Students read alone, then highlight on paper.
Anticipated highlights:

Claim: biofuels “can’t add up”, in Britain at least, and not as a replacement for all transport fuels; at most 24 kWh/d per person, and he thinks that’s an over-estimate.
Evidence: sunlight 100 W/m²; best European crops 0.5 W/m²; 75 % of the country = 3000 m² per person; 0.5 × 3000 → 36 kWh/d per person; lose at least a third in processing → 24.
Caveats: 75 % of the country is “outrageously generous”; the figure ignores growing, harvesting and processing; food competes for the land; farming inputs can cancel the delivered energy; no one predicts better than 1 W/m², even with genetic engineering; Fig. 6.11’s caption: wood manages only 0.095–0.254 W/m².

title: Making the case
text:
Discuss with your desk:

11:26



What is MacKay’s main claim?
What evidence supports it?
What does it assume or omit?
What real-world decisions might be influenced by this perspective? (How?)




Where on the page was the claim? The caveats?



[11:26–11:32] Easy to hard: the first three are in the text; the fourth is an inference. MacKay doesn’t name a decision-maker.
Reflection: the answer is the last paragraph, after a page and a half of arithmetic. Caveats are everywhere: in the figure caption, mid-sentence asides, a closing aside about food. That is the right order for a textbook, which builds the case for a reader with time. A briefing reverses it (Concept block 1).
Q4 answers vary: a transport minister weighing biofuel mandates is the reader MacKay’s conclusion fits best. Hold that thought.

title: Making the case
text:
Briefing the minister

11:32

The UK imports 9.3 million tonnes of pellets annually, equivalent to 1.7 kWh/d per person of fuel.
The Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero is looking for ways to reduce our reliance on imported pellets to improve our energy security and cut transport emissions.


Discuss with your neighbour: what would you tell the minister about the feasibility of replacing imported wood pellets with home-grown biomass?



[11:32–11:35] The sum: 1.7 / 36 × 75 % ≈ 3.6 % of the UK, at best-crop yields.
Pellets are wood. At Fig. 6.11’s 0.095–0.254 W/m² it is about 20 000–53 000 km²: 8–22 % of the UK. The UK’s woodland is about 13 %. County Durham is about 2200 km²: 4–5 County Durhams at best, 9–24 as forest.
1.7 kWh/d per person (and MacKay’s 36) is chemical energy, before conversion to electricity.
Source: data/pellet_imports.csv (2024 sums to 9317 kt); 17 GJ/t from data/README.md. Population 69.3 million (ONS mid-2024).

title: Making the case
text:
Writing a summary

11:34


If your reader stops after the first paragraph, do they know:

What you investigated?
What you found?
What you recommend?




This is the standard for a good summary. If any of the three are missing, the summary needs work.
Keep the three questions live for the rest of the session. The two exemplar reports are built so that this test separates them: the faithful summary answers all three, the traitor’s answers only the middle one — loudly. Students who apply the test catch it; students who read for tone do not.

title: Making the case
text:
Write the summary

11:35


Write a 3–4 sentence summary of a briefing on the feasibility of replacing imported wood pellets with home-grown biomass


Pass your summary paragraph to your left. Read your neighbour’s:


Is the message clear?
Is ambiguity acknowledged?
Would the Minister know what to do?




At home: Rewrite the summary in your drax briefing the same way.


[11:35–11:45] Seven minutes writing, three sharing. Push for the number in the first sentence, with a comparator: “4 % of the UK”, “four County Durhams”. Compared to what?
A summary that would pass: “Growing Drax’s fuel in the UK would take at least 10 000 km², about 4 % of the country, even with the best energy crops, and two to five times that as forest. Most of it would have to come from farmland, competing with food. Home-grown supply would cut shipping and import dependence, but at a land cost the UK is unlikely to bear. We recommend [their call].”

11:40




Section
Purpose

✔️ 😃

title: Making the case
text:
A real parliamentary briefing

11:45

Supply chains for low carbon electricity infrastructure — POSTnote 782, Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology.
https://post.parliament.uk/research-briefings/post-pn-0782/ · DOI 10.58248/PN782


Read it (5 minutes), then discuss with your neighbours:

How does it map onto summary → evidence → caveats → conclusions?
What is the effect of a more fluid structure?
Is a standard template helpful, or overly restrictive?




[11:45–11:55] Students have just forced MacKay into the template. Now: how far does a real briefing bend it?
Students read the briefing themselves rather than being given the mapping. Open it live — preview-links: auto opens it in-frame.
Likely observations. The opening paragraph is the summary, and it stands alone. The body is a run of questions as headings (“What are the main supply chain risks?”), so the reader can jump to the question they have. Caveats are not a section: they are woven through (e.g. “the exact mapping of the supply chain constraints … is yet to be published”; “gaps in the analysis”). The closing section lists options, not a single recommendation — POST is neutral by remit. Contributors are listed at the end; that is “evidence they can trust” in practice.
Fluid structure: reads naturally and fits the topic, but caveats can be missed or buried, and the reader must work to find the uncertainty. Template: guarantees the uncertainty gets its own place and helps novices, but can force a recommendation the evidence doesn’t support, or split a caveat from the claim it qualifies.
Steer towards: the template is scaffolding for people learning to write briefings, and experts adapt it to the audience. Ask what the minister’s office would lose if caveats appeared only inline.

title: Making the case
text:
AI and the environment

11:55

You have two reports that use the same data to reach opposite conclusions.

Read each report, then discuss as a desk:

What makes each report feel trustworthy?
Where is it misleading?



[11:55–12:20] Uses the faithful and traitor AI environmental impact reports.
Links: Pro-AI | Anti-AI

title: Making the case
text:
Spotting the traitor

11:59





Ardross Castle, where The Traitors is filmed. Derek Spence / Geograph, CC BY-SA 2.0



Faithful report
Balanced evidence
Open about caveats
Acknowledges uncertainty


Traitor report
Selective evidence
Misleading framing
Unduly confident




Traitors: here’s your toolkit. Faithful: Don’t do these by mistake, lest you be suspected!

title: Making the case
text:
Cherry-picking

12:03

Choose the number that tells your story.

Example: energy per AI query — 0.3 Wh (Epoch AI’s estimate for a typical query) or 18.9 Wh (one lab’s estimate for a newer model). A handy 63× difference can stack a comparison in your favour!


Antidote?


The traitor report cites 18.9 Wh as the cost of “a single query”, with no hint that it is one of the highest published estimates, and sets it beside a 0.3 Wh Google search. The faithful report gives the range: 0.3–3 Wh for typical use, up to 20 Wh for reasoning models.
Ask students for the antidote: Cite a range? Acknowledge the context?

title: Making the case
text:
Invalid chart type

12:07



A pie chart of things that don’t form a whole.










w02-double-counted-pie.R



Or a bar chart where the y-axis doesn’t start at zero.










w02-truncated-axis.R





This is a recap: We saw these in Week 2’s “spot the lie” charts.

title: Making the case
text:
Cross-scale conflation

12:12

Compare a small thing to a big thing without adjusting the scale.


“By 2030, AI alone could be consuming more electricity than every home, factory, office, and railway in Britain combined.”

Numbers are legit (347 TWh for AI > 319 TWh for the UK)
Comparison is not (Whole world, projected for 2030 > one country, measured in 2024)


From the traitor report’s second figure: two bars of nearly equal height, with a dashed line to show AI “overtaking” the UK.
Ask: compared to what? Global AI against global electricity demand (about 35 000 TWh by 2030) is about 1 %.

title: Making the case
text:
Omission

12:16

What you don’t show matters as much as what you do.
Never neglect the counterfactual.


What would have happened otherwise?

An AI query costs 0.3 Wh.
Counterfactual: a task takes a minute longer
One minute of laptop time costs 0.45 Wh


One minute of human time (at 75 kWh/day) costs 52 Wh


27 000 kWh/year is UK primary energy per person: DUKES 2026 gives 162.5 Mtoe for 2025 (× 11.63 MWh/toe ≈ 1890 TWh), over about 69 million people. That is about 75 kWh/day; MacKay’s Without the Hot Air puts it at 125 kWh/day once imported goods are counted.
27 000 000 Wh ÷ 525 960 min/year ≈ 52 Wh, about 170 AI queries.
