title: How confident should we be?
text:
An uncertain world

11:10


All measurements are uncertain. But some are less certain than others.


Error = difference between measurement and truth.

Exactly quantifiable – if you know the true value

Uncertainty = how good we believe our measurement to be

How well can our experiment answer our research question?




[11:10–11:25] Two types of error, then precision vs accuracy.
What’s important is how far we can trust our numbers.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Error: Two categories

11:13



Random error (noise)
Measurements vary each time.
Example: repeat readings from a chimney CO₂ monitor scatter around the true value.


Systematic error (bias)
Your instrument is consistently wrong.
Example: Some CO₂ leaks from the chimney before reaching the monitor.




Systematic error is the sneaky one — you can’t detect it by repeating the measurement. You need an independent check.
Random error averages out with enough data. Systematic error doesn’t.
Random error is scatter in the measurement, not real change in the thing measured: generation that rises and falls with the weather is variability, and a perfect meter would still record it.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Precision vs. accuracy

11:15





Always on target, or always into your own goal? Dominic Nelson, CC BY-SA 4.0



Example: Footballer hoofing in a long-range shot.

Precise, accurate: always on target
Equally precise, inaccurate: Always hoofs ball into own goal
Imprecise, accurate: Always gets it to right end of the pitch.
Imprecise, inaccurate [me]: Could end up anywhere

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Precision vs. accuracy

11:18



Precise but inaccurate
Measurements cluster tightly around the wrong value.
e.g., a miscalibrated thermometer


Accurate but imprecise
Measurements scatter widely around the true value.
e.g., noisy field readings






Always on target, or always into your own goal? Dominic Nelson, CC BY-SA 4.0


Which is worse? It depends on whether you can correct the bias.



Geoscience examples: radiometric dating is precise but relies on assumptions about initial conditions (accuracy). A borehole thermometer read to the nearest degree is accurate but imprecise.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Precision vs. accuracy

11:20



w03-precision-accuracy.R



The dashed line is a real formation mean from borehole_temp.csv.
Culminating in the precise-but-inaccurate panel: repeating the measurement increases your confidence in the wrong value. If we don’t know about the bias, we might underestimate our uncertainty.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Communicating uncertainty

11:23



Uncertainty – The extent to which an estimate addresses the relevant user questions. The extent of uncertainty is influenced by randomness and inherent variability, as well as the context in which the statistics are used.






Code of Practice for Statistics 3.0: © Crown copyright



“Be rigorous”: Quantify statistical error, including bias, and produce measures of confidence, where possible




“Be open about quality”: […] prominently explain the quality of the statistics, including strengths and limitations, and communicate the uncertainty in estimates



Definition: reflects our understanding of error, as well as framing.
We’ll talk about how to do this quantification later. Understand first, measure later.
Source: https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/Code-of-Practice-for-Statistics-3.0.pdf

title: How confident should we be?
text:
The courtroom analogy

11:40





The Jury (1861), John Morgan — Buckinghamshire County Museum, public domain



In a trial

Start with “innocent”
Look at the evidence
Decide: enough to convict?



In statistics

Start with “no effect” (null hypothesis)
Look at the data
Decide: enough to reject the null?





[11:40–11:55] This is conceptual — no formulae yet. The goal is to build intuition for why we need formal testing.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Two types of mistake

11:45





Null is true
Null is false




Reject null
✘ Type I error(false positive)
✔ Correct


Don’t reject
✔ Correct
✘ Type II error(false negative)






Type I: Convicting an innocent person.
Claiming a biomass plant emits more CO2 than a coal plant when they’re really the same.


Type II: Acquitting a guilty one.
Missing a real difference because your sample was too small.




Type I: Null = innocence; rejection = convict
Type II: Null = innocence; failing to reject = release (not “accepting” the null: acquittal is not proof of innocence)
We choose our tolerance for each type of error:

The significance level (α, usually 0.05) is our threshold for Type I error: how much surprise we require.
Type II error depends on sample size, effect size, and variability.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Distinguishing two populations

11:50



w03-overlap.R


Connect the concepts of ‘spread’ (last time) and ‘precision’.



At-chimney emissions: CO₂ measured as it leaves the plant. Same means in each panel (Coal: 910; Biomass: 1000 kg CO₂/MWh).



What the figure shows. At-chimney emission factors from combustion only. Equivalent to stack monitor readings at the point of combustion — the CO₂ physically leaving the plant per MWh generated.
The spread is invented.
Biomass is higher than coal at the chimney(!): wood holds less energy per unit of carbon than coal, so a MWh from pellets sends more CO₂ up the stack. Nothing about the chimney makes biomass cleaner; the case for biomass rests on regrowth.




The question: is this difference bigger than we’d expect by chance?


“Would you bet these are different?” Ask it of each panel in turn. The gap between the centres is identical — only the spread changes.
The shaded band is where a single measurement tells you nothing: it could have come from either kind of plant. Verbal example: in the wide panel, a biomass plant reading 900 and a coal plant reading 1000 would surprise no one, reversing the true order of the means.
Just visual intuition for now: we’ll formalize this mathematically in Week 6.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Population vs. sample

12:08





One power station, standing in for a whole fuel. © Drax


In 2025, a third of UK bioenergy electricity was generated by one power station (Drax).

If we want to understand bioenergy electricity more generally, is Drax’s outsize contribuition a help or a hindrance?




Drax generated 14.6 TWh of biomass electricity in 2024 (Drax full-year results, Feb 2025), against 40.1 TWh of bioenergy in uk_electricity.csv: 36 %. Of the plant-biomass part (about 66 % of bioenergy, data/README.md) it is over half.
So Drax dominates wood-pellet power, but “bioenergy” also covers energy from waste, landfill gas and anaerobic digestion: a different population altogether. Which one is “biomass electricity”?
And Drax is unusual: massive, converted from coal, with a specific supply chain. Other biomass plants may behave very differently.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Selection bias

12:12


If you only measure the biggest, best-known facility, your results may not generalize.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Survivorship bias

12:15


“The fishermen prayed to Zeus and survived”.





The prayer of the drowned fishermen. Royal Navy / MOD, OGL v1.0



Diagoras of Melos
Bonus tidbit: Diagoras once chopped up a wooden statue of Heracles to use as firewood, casually telling the god to perform a “thirteenth labour” by boiling his turnips.



Diagoras of Melos:

“Where are those who prayed, then drowned?”

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Survivorship bias

12:18




Where should you fit the armour?




Location of recorded bullet-holes on bombers (hypothetical). Martin Grandjean, McGeddon, US Air Force / Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0




Second World War: the US military examined returning bombers.
Abraham Wald (Statistical Research Group, Columbia) pointed out that these were the planes that came back. Holes in the wings and fuselage are survivable; planes hit in the engines or cockpit are missing from the sample. Armour goes where the holes aren’t.
Back to biomass: which plants are missing from our data, and why?

If failing biomass plants shut down and disappear from the data, the remaining ones look better than average.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Counfounder bias

12:22





Older, or worse built? The fuel is not the only thing that differs. AI-generated (Gemini/Nano Banana 2)


Biomass plants might be newer than coal plants. Any efficiency difference might reflect age, not fuel.



There’s an implicit assumption here that plants only differ in their fuel type. It may not be obvious.
Summary of this section: Is your sample representative?
Any conclusion is contingent on its assumptions being correct - or violations being minor. So with any comparison, it’s helpful to explore: what are our assumptions?

title: How confident should we be?
text:
The carbon accounting rule

12:25

The standard framework: CO₂ from burning biomass is counted as zero at the point of combustion.

Why? Trees absorbed that CO₂ as they grew; new trees will absorb it again
The carbon is booked when the forest is harvested, in the land-use accounts of the country that grows it
“Zero” is an entry in a yearly inventory: not a claim about the atmosphere in any one year



Discuss as a desk:


List the assumptions this framework makes
For each: is it testable? What evidence would challenge it?
Which assumptions, if wrong, would most change the conclusion?



[12:25–12:45] This directly feeds Week 3 app (scenario analysis) and Week 4 (the briefing). Ten minutes at desks, ten collecting on the next slide.
Three clocks, which students conflate: the chimney (instant), the inventory (yearly: zero in the energy accounts the year it burns, a stock loss in the land accounts the year it is felled) and the forest (decades to regrow). The “zero” runs on the inventory clock. Whether the forest clock is fast enough is for students to find: don’t give payback times here.
Bridge from Exercise 1: which of the coal uncertainties also apply to biomass? What does biomass add (regrowth, and over what period)?
Expected assumptions: trees regrow (timescale?), supply chain emissions are negligible, land use doesn’t change, the alternative fuel would have been burned anyway.
The “if wrong, most changes the conclusion” question is the key one. It teaches students to prioritize assumptions by impact.

12:35






Type 3–4 assumptions in as students call them out. Students will need them for the application session (scenario analysis) and the Week 4 briefing.

“What assumptions are we making?”

This is the question that separates good analysis from bad.

title: What do the numbers say?
section: What are we trying to do?
text:
What are we trying to do?

11:10

Compress thousands of numbers into a few useful ones.

Three questions about any dataset:

Where is the centre?
How spread out is it?
What shape is it?



[11:10–11:30] This is bread-and-butter descriptive statistics. Keep it practical: every concept gets a geoscience example.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Centre: mean vs median

11:13



Mean
The “balance point.”
Sensitive to extremes.
Pull one value way up → mean shifts.


Median
The middle value.
Robust to extremes.
Pull one value way up → median barely moves.






The Jacobite on Glenfinnan Viaduct: Eric Kilby, CC BY-SA 4.0



Example: Scottish income tax paid. Median £4k; mean £6k. J.K. Rowling £50M income tax/yr vs 5M Scots
She and a dependent move to England: no effect on median, big effect on mean.
Picturing the effect of a solo individual can help us to think about when the shape of a dataset may invite confusion.



When do they differ? When the distribution is skewed.


A tiny number of high earners pay much more income tax than everyone else put together
Same with earthquake magnitudes — a few huge quakes pull the mean up.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Spread

11:17




Range — max minus min

Sensitive to one extreme value

IQR — middle 50 % of the data

Robust to outliers

Standard deviation — the “typical” (root mean square) distance from the mean
Median absolute deviation – the median distance from the median






Another kind of spread: Bruno, Germany; CC0

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Why spread matters

11:20



w02-spread.R



If a report only listed the means, both boreholes would appear identical.
“The borehole temperature was 15 °C” means something quite different in each case: would you stand by that statement in borehole B?

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Shape

11:23





































w02-distribution-shapes.R



Symmetric: mean ≈ median. Many natural processes.
Skewed: the mean chases the tail — income, grain size, ore grades. The long tail drags the mean away from the median. The median is the more “typical” value.
Bimodal: same mean and median but a very different distribution. Key message: a mean without a histogram can be deeply misleading.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The two-humped problem

11:27





Bactrian camels: two humps, one valley. Pixabay Content License












w02-bimodal.R




On the bimodal panel, the mean and median both land in the valley and describes almost none of the data.
One average cannot describe two populations.




Always look at the distribution, not just the mean.



The camel is the mnemonic: a bactrian has two humps, and the point between them is not where the camel is.
Real geoscience example: a sediment sample with two source areas, or a borehole set spanning two formations. The grand mean is an artefact.
Ask: “What would you report instead?” Answer: identify the groups first, then summarize each. This previews Week 5 on confounders.
We’ll talk more about visualizing the data in a mo. But first, a little break to play: IS THAT A BIG NUMBER?

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The More or Less principle

11:30




BBC Radio 4’s More or Less, presented by Tim Harford © BBC; screenshot used for instruction



A number without a comparator is meaningless.



[11:30–11:45] This is the first key refrain. It should become a running question for the rest of the course.
Named after the BBC Radio 4 programme More or Less, which interrogates statistics in the news.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Is that a big number?

11:33





Wood pellets: US Forest Service, public domain


UK bioenergy electricity: 41 TWh/year.



Is that a big number? Compared to what?



Ask: “What would be a sensible thing to compare this to?” Then throw back whichever of these fits:

Another country: the UK is the world’s 6th-largest bioenergy generator (after China, Brazil, Germany, the US, Japan). The US, which sends us ~¾ of our pellets, makes only a little more (46 TWh) with 5× our population: 1 % of its electricity, against our 14 %. France, a similar size: 10 TWh; Spain: 6 TWh.
Per person: ~580 kWh each in the UK; US 130, France 160, Germany 600, Finland 1850 (pulp and paper mills burn their waste).
Total UK generation (2025, DUKES) is ~294 TWh. So bioenergy ≈ 14 %. This is comparatively high, not top: Denmark 22 %, Luxembourg 29 %, Finland 13 %, Germany 10 %.
Other UK sources (2025): more than all UK nuclear (36 TWh); twice solar (20 TWh); half of wind (86 TWh); gas 93 TWh.
What it could power: at 2500 kWh a home, ~16 million homes: over half of the UK’s 28.6 million households (on paper).
One station: Drax alone made 15.0 TWh: over a third of it, 6 % of UK power, ~6 million homes’ worth.
Over time: 4.3 TWh in 2000; it has grown tenfold.

Sources: Ember Yearly Electricity Data (2024–25; downloaded 2026-10-12), with Our World in Data populations (2024); data/uk_electricity.csv (DUKES 2026 Table 5.6.B); data/pellet_imports.csv (US 74 % of 2024 imports); ONS Families and households in the UK: 2024; Drax Full year results 2025 (26 February 2026).

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Is that a big number?

11:36





Drax power station: © Drax

Drax power station emits 14 Mt CO₂/year.

Is that a big number? Compared to what?



UK CO₂ emissions: ~285 Mt in 2025; 367 MtCO₂e of greenhouse gases . Drax (a single station) is ~5 % of that – though not included (!) in the 285 Mt figure.
Per person: UK CO₂ is ~4.1 t per person (284.8 Mt ÷ 69 million). Drax emits as much as 3.4 million Britons.
Another country: about the whole fossil CO₂ of Slovenia or Lithuania (12.5–12.8 Mt in 2024); 40 % of Ireland’s (33 Mt).
Per unit of electricity: 14.09 Mt ÷ 15.0 TWh ≈ 940 kg CO₂ per  MWh: a touch above coal (910), 2.6× gas (360; data/emission_factors.csv). The same electricity from gas would emit ~5.4 Mt.
60 000 long haul flights = 20M passenger journeys
3M dairy cows: or almost half the UK’s cattle (dairy & beef)
Sources: Global Carbon Project via Our World in Data, CO₂ and greenhouse gas emissions (2024); Drax Full year results 2025.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Is that a big number?

11:39





United Downs well pad, 2019, before the plant was built: Jonathan Wilkins / Geograph, CC BY-SA 2.0

The UK’s geothermal power station: 3 MW.

Is that a big number? Compared to what?



United Downs, near Redruth, Cornwall: switched on February 2026. Water from a 5 km well, the deepest and hottest in the UK, at over 185 °C. Run flat out, 3 MW for a year is ~25 GWh.
Comparators to throw back:

All UK electricity (294 TWh): about 0.01 %, or 1 part in 12 000. Too small a percentage to be a sensible comparator: that is the point.
All UK geothermal electricity Deep geothermal heat is a few more MW (Eden Project 1.4 MW, Gateshead 6 MW). Shallow ground-source heat pumps are the big one: ~55 000 of them, 847 MW, ~1430 GWh of heat a year (2023), roughly 60× United Downs. Ask: is the ground’s heat a few metres down geothermal, or stored sunshine?
Homes: ~10 000 homes’ electricity (the developer’s own figure; 25 GWh ÷ 2500 kWh agrees).
Per person: split across the UK, ~0.4 kWh each a year: about four kettles (3 kW for 2 min ≈ 0.1 kWh).
Drax: Drax’s biomass makes in about 15 hours what United Downs makes in a year (15.0 TWh ÷ 8760 h ≈ 1.7 GWh an hour).
A data centre: one building of the planned QTS campus at Cambois, Northumberland, is rated at 72 MW: 24 United Downs. The whole campus (1.1 GW) would need ~370.
A swimming pool: Penzance’s Jubilee Pool lido has been heated from a 410 m geothermal well since 2020; the pool says ~80 % of its heat is geothermal. Its heat pumps are rated ~480 kW (the installer’s figure): a sixth of United Downs’ 3 MW, and heat, not electricity. Flat out all year that is ≤4.2 GWh of heat; at a more likely third to half of that, ~1.4–2.1 GWh, the gas heating of ~150–220 homes (9500 kWh each).
Closer to home (heat): Gateshead’s mine-water heat network, 6 MW of heat from flooded coal workings, is the UK’s largest. Seaham Garden Village is building one from Dawdon mine water for 750 homes. Under Weardale, the Eastgate borehole (2004) hit brine at 46 °C at 995 m in granite.
Other countries: geothermal is 29 % of Iceland’s electricity (5.6 TWh, ~220 United Downs) and 45 % of Kenya’s (6.0 TWh).

Sources: Envirotec, “Geothermal electricity generation commences at United Downs” (2 March 2026); Drax Full year results 2025; DatacenterDynamics, “QTS files to build 1.1 GW data center campus in Northumberland”; Jubilee Pool, “Geothermal pool” (jubileepool.co.uk); Thermal Earth (installer), “Jubilee Pools, Cornwall”; IEA Geothermal 2023 UK country report (BGS/DESNZ, October 2024: Table 1 and §1); Ofgem medium gas TDCV (9500 kWh, from July 2026); Mining Remediation Authority (Seaham); Manning et al. (2007), J. Geol. Soc. 164: 371–382 (Eastgate); Ember Yearly Electricity Data 2024 (“other renewables”, nearly all geothermal there).

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The habit

11:42

Every time you see a number in this module, ask:


“Is that a big number?”

And its companion: “Compared to what?”



Bookmark this moment. Return to these phrases in every subsequent week. By Week 10, students should be asking this unprompted.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Why distributions matter

11:45

A histogram shows you what the mean and SD cannot:

Is the data symmetric or skewed?
Are there outliers?
Is there more than one cluster?



[11:45–12:05] Deeper dive into distributions. Connect to geoscience.
Open with: to know “is this a big number”, we need to know how our data are distributed. 1, 2, 3 SDs from the mean = 68 %, 95 %, 99.7 %

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The normal distribution

11:49





The original bell curves: Pexels License

Ring a bell? Arises when many small, independent effects combine.

Central Limit Theorem (informally): averages of large samples tend toward normal, even if the underlying data aren’t.


Allows many statistical tests to assume normality, and carry on working even when raw data are messy.


Don’t go deep into CLT. The intuition is enough: “averages smooth things out.”

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Log-normal distributions in geoscience

11:53





Shap Granite: jtweedie1976 / Flickr, CC BY 2.0

Many geological measurements are log-normal: a long tail of large values.

Grain size
Permeability
Ore grades
Trace-element concentrations


When data are log-normal, the mean can be very different from the typical value.


The next slide is this claim as a picture: most of the rock in single figures of mD (millidarcy - unit of permeability), a tail into the thousands, and a mean well above almost every sample.
Connection to “Is that a big number?”: if the data are log-normal, the mean is a poor summary. The median or geometric mean is better.
Why ore grades are log-normal: geochemical enrichment works multiplicatively — each hydrothermal pulse or fractionation event multiplies the existing concentration by some factor. A chain of multiplications is equivalent to a sum of logs, and sums tend toward normal (CLT), so log(concentration) is normal → concentration is log-normal. Grain size gets there the same way: each breakage event leaves a random fraction of the grain, a chain of multiplications (Kolmogorov 1941). Permeability scales with pore-throat size squared, times other factors that multiply, so it inherits the skew.
Earthquake magnitudes are skewed too but are not log-normal: the magnitude is already a logarithm, and it falls off exponentially (Gutenberg–Richter). Don’t list them here if asked.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
What that looks like

11:57



w02-log-normal.R



The mean is larger than 85 % of the samples. It is not a typical permeability — it is not close to any of the rock. That is what “represents nobody” means.
The left panel is cut at the 99th percentile, and says so in the caption. Worth naming aloud: the honest way to crop a chart is to tell the reader you did.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
When to log-transform

12:01

If your data:

Are positive (no zeros or negatives)
Span several orders of magnitude
Are right-skewed

Then log() often makes them more symmetric and easier to analyse.

Reach for log if you find yourself asking “how many times more”.
Leave it on the shelf when absolute (contra relative) differences are interesting.


This comes back in Week 6 (t-test on log-transformed data) and Week 8 (regression diagnostics).

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
What a good figure does

12:05


Shows the data, not just a summary
Explains the data: labelling axes, units, captions
Facilitates comparison: simple shapes, consistent axes & scales



[12:05–12:25] Principles first, then live ggplot2 demo.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
How a good figure works

12:07

The CRARP principles of graphic design:

Contrast: Make the story stand out.
Repetition: Consistent style between figures.
Alignment: Same scale, same zero, no perspective.
Repetition: Consistent style between figures.
Proximity: Position your annotations; compare neighbours.



Graphic designers summarize layout as CRAP — Contrast, Repetition, Alignment, Proximity (after Robin Williams, The Non-Designer’s Design Book; framing via Andrew Heiss, Data Visualization with R, session 2, https://datavizsp26.classes.andrewheiss.com/content/02-content.html).

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Bad figures

12:09





Dodgy axes
Cherry-picked data
Missing labels or units
Tricksy perspective



[6 min for the three pairs that follow, within 12:05–12:25] Two minutes each at most: show the bad chart, take one guess from the room, advance to the fixed version. The “Spot the lie” exercise later does the slower version with truncated axes, cherry-picked ranges and pie charts.
Each pair is the same numbers drawn twice. Say that out loud: no data was changed between the two slides.
Missing labels and units is the one rule with no pair here — it gets a before/after of its own in Week 4 and again in Week 10.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Dodgy plot #1

12:10



w02-dual-axis-bad.R


Shows the data Explains the data Facilitates comparison



Ask: “Is the wood being burnt less efficiently every year?” That is what the chart appears to say.
Then ask what each axis starts at. The left starts at 0; the right starts at 6000 kt.
How do we fix this?

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The dual axis, fixed

12:12



w02-dual-axis-good.R


Contrast Repetition Alignment Proximity



Fix (draw it out of the room before saying it): put both series on one scale. Indexed to 2015, imports and generation move together — which is what you would expect if the pellets are being burnt at a roughly constant efficiency.
TWh and kt cannot share an axis, so index them: divide by the first year and multiply by 100. Now both axes are “percent of 2015”.
The divergence in the first chart was manufactured entirely by the choice of axis ranges.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Dodgy plot #2

12:14



w02-area-encoding-bad.R


Shows the data Explains the data Facilitates comparison



Ask for the impression first: roughly how much have imports grown? The room will say “doubled”, because the ink did.
The diameter is proportional to the value, so the area goes as the square: 1.42 across becomes 2.0 in area.
This is the standard infographic sin. It shows up with circles, tree icons and stacks of little power stations.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The area encoding, fixed

12:16



w02-area-encoding-good.R


Contrast Repetition Alignment Proximity



Fix (draw it out of the room before saying it): encode with length from a common baseline. It is the one channel the eye reads accurately — and it comes with an axis to check.
If a pictogram is unavoidable, scale the area: diameter proportional to the square root of the value. Better still, don’t.
Note what the honest version gains beyond honesty: an axis, so a reader can extract a number rather than an impression.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Dodgy plot #3

12:18



w02-colour-obscures-bad.R


Shows the data Explains the data Facilitates comparison



Ask: which origin stopped supplying the UK altogether? Give them ten seconds of squinting at the legend.
Rainbow hues are not ordered and not equally distinguishable. Red and green in the same chart also defeats the commonest colour vision deficiency — about 1 in 12 men.
Every series got a colour, so no series got emphasis.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Colour that reveals

12:20



w02-colour-obscures-good.R


Contrast Repetition Alignment Proximity



Fix (draw it out of the room before saying it): colour the story, grey the context, label on the line. Colour is a scarce resource — spend it where the reader should look.
Same six series, nothing dropped. The grey lines still carry the context; they just stop competing.
Russia’s series ends after 2021, and the 2022 gap is filled from the USA and Latvia. That is visible here and invisible in the rainbow.
Direct labels beat a legend: no eye-travel, and no memory test.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Live demo: building a ggplot

12:21











Live code this. ggplot2 is already attached on this slide. Run after each step, so the plot grows one layer at a time. Anticipated code:
elec <- read.csv("data/uk_electricity.csv")
ggplot(elec, aes(x = year, y = bioenergy_twh)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Bioenergy generation (TWh)",
       caption = "Source: DUKES 2026")
Narrate the “grammar” as you go: data + aesthetics + geometries.
Don’t map colour to fuel here. elec is wide, so that needs tidyr::pivot_longer(), which isn’t loaded on this slide; the exercise page shows the clumsy way, and the application session’s walkthrough does the reshape.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The grammar of graphics

12:23

ggplot(data, aes(x = ..., y = ..., colour = ...)) +
  geom_point() +   # geometry
  labs(...)         # labels
Data + Aesthetics + Geometries = a plot.

Data: A plot is just one way of displaying the data. Analyses don’t start with “I’d like to see a bar chart”, but with “What do these data tell me?”


Aesthetics: Translation layer: Which variable controls which visual channel? Channels: x, y, colour, plotting symbol…
Establishes the rules – doesn’t plot anything itself.


Geometries: What physical mark displays the visual channels?


Everything in ggplot2 follows this pattern.


This is the mental model. Once they have this, they can build any plot by looking up the right geom_*().

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Instructions

12:25

Open Exercises → Week 2: Dodgy plots on the course site. Each box holds the code for one of the next three plots.

For each one: what simple fix will present the data honestly?

Make the fix in the code, run it, then move on to the next plot.


[12:25–12:35] Hands-on. Students run each plot, find the cheat and fix the code; answers come from the front. Show each plot on the screen while they work on it, and hold the fixed slide back until most of the room has a fix.
Expected fixes: #4 adjust ylim (start the bars at zero); #5 show all the data; #6 (extension) drop the double-counted slice, then bars.
This previews Week 4’s “how to lie with statistics” in a lighter form.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Dodgy plot #4

12:26



w02-truncated-axis.R


Shows the data Explains the data Facilitates comparison



Let the chart sit for a moment. First reaction: “Generation is collapsing!” Then ask: what does the y-axis start at?
Don’t answer it here — advance to the fixed version.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Dodgy plot #4, fixed

12:28



w02-truncated-axis-good.R


Contrast Repetition Alignment Proximity



Fix (draw it out of the room before saying it): start the y-axis at zero for bar charts. The bar’s length encodes the ratio, so a non-zero baseline breaks the encoding.
The y-axis in the previous slide began at 270 TWh. The actual drop from 2019 to 2024 is about 13 % — noticeable, but not the catastrophe the chart implied.
Rule: bar lengths encode ratios. A non-zero baseline breaks that encoding. Line charts can sometimes justify a non-zero start, but bars never can.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Dodgy plot #5

12:29



w02-cherry-picked-range.R


Shows the data Explains the data Facilitates comparison



Three points, three years, a confident downward line. Ask what a reader would need to see to check it.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Dodgy plot #5, fixed

12:30



w02-cherry-picked-range-good.R


Contrast Repetition Alignment Proximity



Fix (draw it out of the room before saying it): show the full time range. Bioenergy grew from 4 TWh (2000) to 41 TWh (2025) — a nearly tenfold increase hidden by that window.
The dip is real: 2021–2023 genuinely falls. Cherry-picking does not require fake data, only a well-chosen window.
Shading the window rather than deleting it makes the point stick — the lie is visible inside the truth.
Ask: how would you decide, honestly, where a series should start? Best answer: at the start of the data, unless you can say why not.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Dodgy plot #6

12:31



w02-double-counted-pie.R


Shows the data Explains the data Facilitates comparison



Ask: “How many slices include wind energy?” Answer: two (Wind and Low carbon). Same for nuclear, solar, and bioenergy.
The total shown is ~448 TWh; actual UK generation is 286 TWh.
General rule: pie chart slices must be mutually exclusive and sum to a meaningful 100 %. If they don’t, use a bar chart.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Dodgy plot #6, fixed

12:33



w02-double-counted-pie-good.R


Contrast Repetition Alignment Proximity



Fix (draw it out of the room before saying it): “Low carbon” double-counted Wind + Nuclear + Solar + Bioenergy, so the slices summed to 157 %. An overlapping category is a shading, not a slice — and bars are sortable, labelable, and they add up.
“Other” is total generation minus the named fuels — computed, not asserted, so every TWh in the table is accounted for.
Note what the bar chart gains: you can read gas against wind directly, which is nearly impossible on a pie.
Pies are defensible for two or three parts of a genuine whole. Past that, bars.

title: What do the numbers say?

Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026

Exit ticket

12:40

UK bioenergy electricity output was 41 TWh in 2025. A classmate says: “That’s a lot — it must be making a real difference.”
What’s the most important question to ask first?











PollEv.com/geol

41 TWh sounds large, but it is about 14 % of UK electricity (294 TWh in 2025; DUKES 2026). Significant, but not dominant.
Students who answer A are thinking about trends — not wrong, but it’s a secondary question. The comparator comes first.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Who am I?

11:05

I’m Martin Smith, and I’m a palaeontologist.





Hallucigenia sparsa, Burgess Shale, ~508 million years old. Fossil: NMNH 198658, Smithsonian; photo Martin Smith. Reconstruction: Danielle Dufault





Youti yuanshi: internal organs reconstructed from X-ray scans. Model: Emma Long





[11:05–11:06] Who I am. Cambrian animals: Hallucigenia (famously reconstructed upside down and back to front) and Youti, whose internal organs we could trace in 3D from X-ray scans.
The point of these slides: the skills in this module travel. They matter whether you stay in research or not.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Testing hypotheses needs statistics

11:06

I test hypotheses, and I have to communicate the results to convince others. So I write R packages:


New methods for research


Mapping tree space with TreeDist.Smith 2022, Systematic Biology, CC BY 4.0



Data visualization


Contoured ternary plot: Ternary





[11:06–11:07] Being a scientist means testing ideas against data and showing your working. That needs statistics and clear figures.
Tree space: how different are the trees that an analysis produces? Are they in clusters? TreeDist maps them so you can see.
Ternary: three-part data (e.g. sand/silt/clay) plotted on a triangle. Written because nothing else did what I needed.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Skills for all of life

11:07




My spin-out, StratoBayes:
Our subcontractors use the same tool suite you will learn this term.




© StratoBayes; illustration by Kilian Eichenseer





[11:07–11:08]
StratoBayes correlates rock layers between boreholes, with quantified uncertainty. The developers we hired work in the same toolkit: R, version control, reproducible reports.
And my PhD student was hoovered by by Atom Bank because of their R skills - and they only worked with fossils!
Project management, understanding data, statistical thinking and clear writing are what employers look for.
Across life - understand fitness, health, supplements, sleep…




In demand in industry

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Research Skills for Geoscientists

11:08

This module is about learning to design experiments, and to communicate what their results really mean. This, in a word, is: Science!


[11:08–11:13] Welcome. Set the tone: warm, rigorous, honest.
This module isn’t about memorizing tests — it’s about developing habits of thought. By Week 10 you’ll have a toolkit of reflexive questions (“Is that a big number?”, “What assumptions are we making?”) that will serve you in dissertations and careers.



Two strands:

Statistics — how to test claims with data
Communication — how to present evidence so it can be trusted



This term: Quantitative data
Next term: Spatial data

title: What makes a good question?
text:
How to succeed

11:09

20 credits = 200 hours = 10 hours per week.

Each week: Content session (2 h) + Application session (2 h)


Content: I’ll break it up with exercises. We work best when we learn with others. Work with others on your bench; we’ll feed back to the class.
Application: Work through the exercises; engage with the extensions. Different working speeds - but always room to be pushing yourself (and having fun?)





Do. Per ardua ad astra!



My mantras: Writing is thinking; thinking is understanding. Good work takes time: it’s in struggle that we learn.






No. 50 Squadron Lancasters, 1943: RAF official photographer / IWM TR 1158, public domain




Read (and listen)



Show students how to find the reading list, More or Less and log into The Economist





Ask



For course questions: Point out the QR code - we’ll come back to that later
For technical questions (code & data): Allude to (don’t show yet) the GitHub discussion board





Use AI intelligently (if at all)



My AI conclusion: Half of the skill of using AI is knowing how to ask the right question. The other half is knowing when to trust the answer. That’s exactly what this module will teach you.
AI output looks convincing - until you really look at it.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Two phases

11:11



Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4)
Scaffolded mini-project:
“Does UK biomass power help reach net zero, and should we keep paying for it?”
Real data & ambiguity.
Culminates in a peer-reviewed policy briefing.


Phase 2 (Weeks 5–10)
Your investigation:
Choose a sustainable energy question. Design the study. Analyse the data. Write a 2000-word policy report.
This is your summative assessment (30 %).




Phase 1 is formative: low stakes, high learning. Everyone works with the same data so you can compare notes.
Phase 2 is summative: apply the same skills to a question of your choice. Groups of 3–4 for analysis; individual write-up.

Why? R is built for statistics. It uses the same ideas and concepts, but with a different syntax. Pre-term preparation has helped you to make the jump.


Reassure: if you’ve done the pre-term preparation, you’re ready. If you haven’t, the application session is your safety net.
R and Python have similar philosophies - they are distinct tools, best for different tasks. Knowing a little of both gives you the freedom to choose the best tool for a task.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
What is science?

11:13





“All science is either physics or stamp collecting” (attrib. Rutherford): Penarc, CC BY 3.0



Not a body of facts



A process for reducing uncertainty
Nothing is ever “proven”

Instead, we accumulate and evaluate evidence




[11:13–11:30] This is the intellectual foundation for the course.
Start here: science isn’t what you know, it’s how you decide what to believe. Every claim in this module will be held to this standard.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
The cycle

11:17













w01-ppdac-ring.R



Problem → Plan → Data → Analysis → Conclusion




Drax power station. © Drax







PPDAC. This is the scientific method as practised with data, and it is the spine of the whole module.
Each stage is itself iterative - its own mini-cycle
Walk through each stage with the biomass question, our running case. Drax first started biomass conversion in 2013.

Problem: is “biomass is carbon-neutral” a testable claim?
Plan: (Hypothesis + prediction) what would we measure, and what result would disprove it? What could confound us?
Data: DUKES generation, pellet imports, emission factors.
Analysis: summarize, plot, compare scenarios (Weeks 2–3).
Conclusion: a policy briefing that someone can act on (Week 4).

The cycle isn’t finished until the analysis becomes a decision: that is the communication strand.
Phase 2 runs the same cycle again on your own question.
Perhaps this is your mapping dissertation. What’d it look like?
Perhaps it’s your non-mapping diss. Supervisor provides one box - then what?

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Two directions of reasoning

11:22



Deductive
General → Specific
If plate tectonics is correct, then we predict matching fossils on separated continents.
We test the prediction.


Inductive
Specific → General
We observe matching fossils on separated continents. We infer the continents were once joined.
We build toward a theory.




USGS, public domain





Both are legitimate but different. Deduction is stronger logically (if the premise is true, the conclusion must follow). Induction is how we actually discover most things.
In practice, science uses both — we inductively form hypotheses, then deductively test them.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Wegener’s continental drift

11:26




1912: Wegener induces that continents move, from fossils, rock belts and glacial deposits that match across oceans
He also proposes a mechanism: forces from Earth’s spin and tides
Physicists deduce those forces are far too weak: mechanism refuted
Most geologists throw out the drift along with the mechanism


The lesson: test each claim against its own evidence.





USGS, public domain





The drift hypothesis came from induction (matching fossils and rocks). The mechanism was tested by deduction: forces not strong enough to move continents → hypothesis failed.
Two hypotheses here. Mechanism was easy to test & dismiss. The drift hypothesis made predictions - and evidence kept piling up. Rejecting both hypotheses together was the error.
Why did it happen? Wegener was a meteorologist, an outsider, and his mechanism made no physical sense. The establishment was blinded by the implausible cause and stopped looking at the evidence. The source of an idea doesn’t settle its validity.
The mechanism arrived in the 1960s: seafloor spreading (Hess), magnetic stripes (Vine & Matthews), plates (Wilson; McKenzie & Parker). Roughly fifty years after Wegener.
PPDAC link: a Conclusion can bundle several claims; each spins out its own subsequent cycle(s).

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Instructions

11:30

I’ll show you some statements.

For each one, decide: Is this a testable hypothesis?


What predictions does the hypothesis make?
What observations would / would not be consistent with the hypothesis?
What data / evidence could be collected to test it?

Think for 30 seconds, then discuss as a desk.


[11:30–11:40] Think, discuss as a desk, share. Show each statement, pause, then take a few responses.
The biomass statement should produce disagreement — that’s the hook for the rest of the module.

title: What makes a good question?
section: “The Earth is approximately 4.5 billion years old”
text:
“The Earth is approximately 4.5 billion years old”

11:32


Testable, and extensively tested (radiometric dating, meteorite & Lunar ages, astronomical evidence).

title: What makes a good question?
text:
“Earthquakes are caused by divine punishment”

11:34


Not testable as stated — no observable prediction that distinguishes this from natural causes.

title: What makes a good question?
section: “Wind turbines cause headaches in nearby residents”
text:
“Wind turbines cause headaches in nearby residents”

11:36


Testable — but tricky. How do you control for the nocebo effect? Awareness bias? The design of the study matters enormously.


This foreshadows Week 5 (experimental design, confounding).
Don’t resolve it — just flag the complexity.
Introduce the “Dawkins Zone”: Dawkins would like every hypothesis to be scientifically testable. But some might be testable in principle, but not in practice - need impossibly large sample size to detect small effects; or effect may be swamped by confounders.

title: What makes a good question?
section: “CO₂ emissions from burning biomass should be counted as zero”
text:
“CO₂ emissions from burning biomass should be counted as zero”

11:38


Testable? It depends.

What timescale?
What system boundary?




“Carbon-neutral” is partly a scientific claim and partly a policy choice.




This question underpins our first four weeks.



This statement should generate genuine disagreement. Some students will say “it depends on the trees regrowing” — good. Others may say “it’s a policy definition, not a scientific hypothesis” — also good.
Don’t resolve it. Leave it open. Curiosity is the goal.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Popper’s perspective

11:40




We can never prove a theory.
We can only fail to disprove it.


Every test that could have disproven our hypothesis but didn’t makes us a little more confident — but never certain.






Mute swan, Windermere: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0



[11:40–11:45] This is the philosophical core.
Karl Popper (1934): the demarcation problem. What separates science from non-science? Falsifiability.
You don’t need to go deep into philosophy of science. The practical lesson: seek evidence that could prove you wrong.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
The Wason selection task

11:45



Each card has a letter on one side and a number on the other.
Rule: “If a card shows a vowel, then the other side has an even number.”


A


K


4


7


Which cards must you turn over to test the rule?




Vote at PollEv.com/geol
or text geol to 07480 781235





[11:45–12:00] Let students think for 60 seconds, discuss as a desk, then poll via Poll Everywhere.
Most students pick A and 4 (confirmation). The correct answer is A and 7 (seeking disconfirmation).
Close the poll in Poll Everywhere before advancing to next slide (which shows the results).

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Poll results

11:45

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Wason selection task

11:50

Each card has a letter on one side and a number on the other.
Rule: “If a card shows a vowel, then the other side has an even number.”


A ✓


K ✗


4 ✗


7 ✓



A (vowel): if the other side is odd, the rule is broken


K (consonant): the rule says nothing about consonants


4 (even): Neither consonant-even nor vowel-even would disprove the rule


7 (odd): if the other side is a vowel, the rule is broken



The key: 4 feels relevant because it confirms the rule. But confirmation doesn’t test anything. Only disconfirmation does.
Link forward: “Hypothesis testing in statistics is a formalized version of this — we ask: if the null hypothesis were true, would we see data this extreme? We’re seeking disconfirmation.”

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Confirmation bias

11:55





Bank holidays… always a washout? Sea haar at Saltburn-by-the-Sea: Colin Park / Geograph, CC BY-SA 2.0


Humans are wired to confirm, not disconfirm: we seek evidence for what we already believe.



Give an everyday example: you think it always rains on bank holidays. You remember the rainy ones, forget the sunny ones. That’s confirmation bias.
In data analysis: if you only look for patterns that support your hypothesis, you will always find them.



Useful hypothesis tests push back against this tendency.


In this module, you’ll learn to:

Ask “what evidence would change my mind?”
Seek comparisons, not just supporting cases
Treat uncertainty as information, not failure



This connects to every subsequent week. Week 3: “what assumptions are we making?” Week 6: “how plausible was this before we tested?” Week 8: “what is the model not capturing?”
The habits are the real learning outcome. The specific tests and methods are tools in service of these habits.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Why R?

12:00



You know Python (NumPy, Jupyter, pandas)
Same ideas. Different syntax.


R is built for statistics

t.test(), lm(), aov() — one line each
ggplot2 — the grammar of graphics
Built-in data manipulation




You’ll see why this matters starting in Week 2.


[12:00–12:15] This is NOT an R lesson. That was pre-work.
The goal: show that R is working, connect it to what they know, and move on. Keep it to ≤10 minutes of live coding.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
R demo

12:05











elec <- read.csv("data/uk_electricity.csv") head(elec)
Then build: elec$bioenergy_twh, bio <- elec$bioenergy_twh, summary(bio), plot(elec$year, bio).
Narrate: “You already know how to do this. head() is like df.head() in pandas. plot() is like plt.plot(). The syntax is different but the logic is identical.”
Make sure something goes wrong, to normalize errors: “This happens to everyone. R’s error messages are actually quite helpful once you learn to read them.” Typing elec$bio is a good one — R partial-matches, so it works, which is its own lesson.
The editor swallows arrow keys and space, so slide navigation needs a click outside the cell first.
≤10 minutes. Then back to slides.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Context

12:10

The UK burns millions of tonnes of imported wood pellets for electricity.

Most come from forests in the southeastern United States.










w01-pellet-origins.R



Little aside: I’m going to try to hold myself to the same standards of data presentation to which you should aspire. It’s your job to call out when I make a claim that’s not supported by the evidence I am presenting.
Here’s a first (pedantic?) example: The chart records country of origin, not region: “southeastern” is from the sourcing literature, not from this data. The claim on the slide is finer-grained than the evidence behind it.
“Millions of tonnes” is now a number they can read off. Plant the seed: is 9.3 Mt a big number? That question is next week’s.




Under international carbon accounting rules, the CO₂ released at the chimney is counted as zero.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Is that reasonable?

12:15


Discuss as a desk. You have 10 minutes.


Write one testable hypothesis about biomass energy
What data would you need to test it?
What evidence would disprove your hypothesis?



[12:15–12:35] Circulate and listen. Collect a few examples on the board / shared doc.
Good hypotheses might be: “Biomass electricity produces less CO₂ per kWh than coal” (testable, but depends on system boundary). “Transporting pellets from the US adds significant emissions” (testable with import data + transport factors).
The disprove question is the hard one — and the most valuable. It forces students to think like Popper.

text:
Attendance

12:15


Show the QR from https://attendance.durham.ac.uk/mytimetable, then ← back to the task.

What you came up with

Type 3–4 hypotheses in as students call them out. The box is plain scratch space — nothing is saved, so screenshot it if you want it.
In speaker view (press S), click into the box on the current-slide preview and type: it appears on the projected slide as you go. Esc or a click outside the box lets the arrow keys advance slides again.

If anyone says “it depends on the timescale” or “it depends on what you include” — celebrate this. That’s exactly right, and it’s what Week 3 is about.
End the session with the question feeling genuinely open. Resist giving the punchline.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Key points

12:25


Science is a process for reducing uncertainty, not a collection of facts
We test hypotheses by seeking disconfirmation, not confirmation
The biomass question — does it help reach net zero? — is genuinely open, and the answer depends on choices you’ll learn to identify

title: Week 9: Checking Your Work
text:
Your projects are nearly finished. Before you write up, check the work with fresh eyes — because a reviewer will, and so will whoever tries to reproduce it.
Today has four exercises. Two are about your own code being trustworthy. Two are about catching an error in someone else’s, where “someone else” is a language model that will be confident, fluent, and wrong.
Goals:

Make a broken script run from a cold start, and know why it broke
Report a result in a form a policy reader can use
Catch a confident wrong answer produced by plausible-looking code
Ask “how plausible was this before we tested?” one last time







NoteHow these exercises work





The code boxes start empty, except for comments to guide you through the code that’s expected.
Work one comment at a time. If you get stuck:

Hint 1 restates what you are trying to do.
Hint 2 sketches the shape the code might take.
Hint 3 gives you the code with the key pieces blanked out.
Solution gives you the lot.

Take a real attempt before opening a hint: you will learn by doing, not by reading. The demonstrators are here to help.
Three things worth knowing:

The boxes share one R session, exactly like a script. Anything you create in Exercise 1 is still there in Exercise 2.
Variable names are up to you. The last thing your block prints is what gets checked, so end each block with the answer.
Exercises have extensions underneath them. If you finish early, give them a stab. These are designed to equip you to tackle real coding problems you might face, using the documentation. We can help – but check the manuals first!










TipStuck?



Ask a new question on the Code Q&A discussion board. The discussion board allows anyone else who is stuck on the same thing to learn from (or provide!) the answer. We are notified of new posts, and will reply when we’re next available.
The board is private to this class, so sign in to GitHub first.

title: Week 9: Checking Your Work
section: Exercise 1: Make it run from cold
text:
Exercise 1: Make it run from cold
Below is a script that worked perfectly on the machine it was written on, and fails for everyone else. It has four faults, and each is one of the four commonest reasons a shared analysis will not run.
Fix all four so the block runs start to finish and ends by printing a reproducible bootstrap confidence interval.
Use set.seed(2847) so everyone in the room gets the same answer — which is itself the point of the fourth fault.


















NoteHint 1





Run it and read the first error. Fix that, run again, read the next. Do not try to spot all four by eye — working through errors one at a time is the actual skill, and it is faster.
The four faults, in the order R will meet them:

A path that exists on one computer in the world.
Two variables defined in a comment, which is to say not defined.
A test that uses those variables and cannot say why it failed.
Randomness with no seed — the one that produces no error at all.

The fourth is the dangerous one, because nothing tells you about it. The script runs, gives an answer, and gives a different answer to the next person.











NoteHint 2





The shape of the fixes:

Paths should be relative to the project, so "data/file.csv" works for anyone who has the repo. Absolute paths are a promise about someone else’s hard disk.
Uncomment the two definitions. They belong in the script because everything after them depends on them.
set.seed(2847) goes immediately before replicate(). Once, not inside the loop — a seed inside would make all thousand resamples identical.












TipSolution





wind_data <- read.csv("data/uk_electricity.csv")

early <- wind_data$wind_twh[wind_data$year < 2015]
late <- wind_data$wind_twh[wind_data$year >= 2015]

result <- t.test(late, early)
result

set.seed(2847)
boot_means <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(late, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
The bootstrap interval is 55.2 to 75.1 TWh, and now it is the same interval every time anyone runs it.
Three of the four faults announce themselves with an error. The fourth does not: unseeded randomness produces a working script whose numbers change quietly between runs. If you quote a bootstrap interval in your report and then rerun your analysis after a reviewer’s comment, the numbers will not match the ones you wrote, and you will not know why.
A fifth fault is not in this script and will be in yours: a library() call you never wrote down, because you loaded the package once, months ago, and your session has had it ever since. The only way to catch it is to restart R and run the script top to bottom, which is worth doing once a week and mandatory before you submit.
set.seed() is not about getting the “right” answer. It is about getting a checkable one — and everything in this module that separates evidence from assertion works the same way.





Exercise 1 continued: see the shape, not just the range
Run Exercise 1 first: this builds on its boot_means.
quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975)) threw away everything except two numbers. Plot boot_means itself and look at the shape those two numbers were cut from.















NoteHint 1





One column, mean_twh, on the x-axis. Which geom_*() shows the distribution of a single numeric column as bars?











NoteHint 2





ggplot(boot_df, aes(x = mean_twh)) +
  geom_histogram(______)











TipSolution





boot_df <- data.frame(mean_twh = boot_means)

ggplot(boot_df, aes(x = mean_twh)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)
That histogram is what “55.2 to 75.1 TWh” is a summary of: the middle 95 % of 1000 resampled means. The two quantiles are two vertical slices through this shape, and the shape itself — where it’s tall, where it tapers — is information the two-number interval throws away.
One more thing to try: comment out set.seed(2847) in Exercise 1 above, rerun that block, then rerun this plot. The histogram shifts slightly and the interval changes with it — the shape is exactly as random as the two numbers were. Put the seed back before you move on; everything downstream in this page expects the seeded answer.






Extension: break your own script
Optional, and the highest-value hour of the week.

Restart R — properly, so the workspace is empty — and run your own project script from the first line. Write down every error. That list is your reproducibility debt, and today is much cheaper than the night before the deadline.
Put sessionInfo() at the end of your script and read what it prints. Which of those package versions would you need to record for someone to reproduce your numbers in three years?
Find a number in your draft report and trace it back to the exact line of code that produced it. If you cannot, that number is not evidence yet. Do this for three numbers.
Delete a variable your script depends on — rm(something) — and run again. Does the script fail loudly, or carry on and produce a plausible wrong answer? The second is the outcome to fear, and Exercise 3 is entirely about it.











Quick check
When you report a t-test result to a policy audience, what does the sentence need?


The p-value


The p-value and an effect size


“The result was statistically significant”


The effect size, a confidence interval, and a plain-language reading of what it means — with the p-value alongside


Set answer to "a", "b", "c" or "d".

title: Week 9: Checking Your Work
section: Exercise 2: Say it in one sentence
text:
Exercise 2: Say it in one sentence
You have the test from Exercise 1. Now produce the number a reader actually needs — the difference in mean annual wind generation between 2015–2025 and 2000–2014 — and then write the sentence.


















NoteHint 1





The number is a subtraction between two means you can compute from elec — or read out of the t-test object you already have, whose estimate component holds both.
For the sentence: a reader who is numerate but not statistical needs to know which way, how much, how sure, and why it happened. In that order, and in one sentence.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
mean(late) - mean(early)
or, from the test object,
diff(rev(result$estimate))
For the confidence interval, result$conf.int gives 43.4 to 68.8. Round for the reader: nobody needs 43.40985.











TipSolution





mean(late) - mean(early)
56.13 TWh. A model sentence:

UK wind generation averaged about 56 TWh a year more in 2015–2025 than in 2000–2014 (95 % CI 43 to 69 TWh; Welch t = 9.42, p < 0.001) — roughly six times the earlier average, and equivalent to about a fifth of all UK electricity in 2025 — reflecting the large-scale deployment of onshore and offshore capacity over the period.

Take it apart:

Direction and size in real units. “56 TWh a year more”, not “significantly higher”.
Uncertainty, rounded. 43 to 69. The reader learns the estimate is good to within about ±23 %, which is the honest precision.
A comparator. “Six times” and “a fifth of UK electricity” are what make 54 a big number rather than just a number. This is the refrain the whole module has been drilling: compared to what?
A mechanism. The last clause says why, which is what stops the sentence reading as a coincidence.

And one thing it does not do: claim that wind deployment caused the rise in a sense any test here established. It is an observed difference between two periods, and everything else about Britain changed too.
Common failure modes: a sentence that reports only p; a sentence that says “proves”; a sentence with the CI on a transformed scale a reader cannot picture.





Extension: the same result, three audiences
Optional.

Rewrite your sentence for a journal reviewer — who wants the test, its assumptions, and the exact numbers — and then for a local councillor, who wants to know whether to approve a wind farm. Same evidence, and almost no words in common.
Write the version a campaigner would publish. Keep every number true. Then mark which choices you made to get the effect — that list is what to look for when you read someone else’s.
Find a results sentence in your own draft report and check it against the four ingredients. Most drafts are missing the comparator, because the author has looked at the number so long that it feels large on its own.











Quick check
AI tools are useful in research, and not uniformly. Which of these is AI most reliable at?


Judging whether your sample size is adequate


Finding a syntax error in your R code


Deciding which statistical test fits your question


Judging whether your effect size is large enough to matter


Set answer to "a", "b", "c" or "d".

title: Week 9: Checking Your Work
text:
Exercise 3: The confident wrong answer
You asked a language model: “Using the factors and elec data frames, how much CO₂ did UK biomass electricity emit in 2025 under the full supply chain scenario, in Mt?”
It replied with this code and the conclusion “0 Mt — biomass electricity is carbon neutral under this scenario.”
bio_factor <- sum(factors$co2_kg_per_mwh[
  factors$fuel == "Biomass" & factors$scenario == "with_supply_chain"
])

bio_2025 <- elec$bioenergy_twh[elec$year == 2025] * 1e6 * bio_factor / 1e9
bio_2025
The code runs. It produces no warning. The answer is wrong.
Find the fault, and print the correct figure.


















NoteHint 1





Do not read the code looking for the mistake. Run it, then print every intermediate value and ask whether each is what you expected.
Start with bio_factor. It should be one number, around 1060. Print length(bio_factor) as well as its value — the length is the tell.











NoteHint 2





unique(factors$fuel) shows what is actually in that column.
When a subsetting condition matches nothing, R does not object: it returns a zero-length vector. Most functions then carry on. sum() of nothing is 0, length() of it is 0, and mean() of it is NaN — which at least looks wrong, whereas 0 looks like an answer.
This is why the fault survives: every step behaves exactly as documented.











TipSolution





unique(factors$fuel)

bio_factor <- factors$co2_kg_per_mwh[
  factors$fuel == "biomass" & factors$scenario == "with_supply_chain"
]
bio_factor

elec$bioenergy_twh[elec$year == 2025] * 1e6 * bio_factor / 1e9
43.5 Mt, not zero.
The fault is a capital letter. factors$fuel contains "biomass"; the AI wrote "Biomass". The condition matched no rows, the subset was a zero-length vector, and sum() of a zero-length vector is 0 — not an error, but the documented identity element. Every step did exactly what it promised.
Three things make this the worst kind of bug:

It is silent. No error, no warning, nothing to grep for in a log.
The sum() hid it. Without it the multiplication would have produced numeric(0) and printed nothing, which at least looks wrong. Wrapping a subset in sum() converts “no data” into “zero”, and those are very different claims.
The answer was plausible. Zero is exactly what UK carbon accounting records for biomass. A reader who already believes the conclusion will not check the code, and the model’s fluent explanation makes the check feel unnecessary.

This is what to take into your report. The risk from a language model is not that it writes code that fails — you would notice. It is that it writes code that runs and quietly answers a slightly different question. The defence is the same as for your own work: print the intermediate values, check each against what you expected, and be most suspicious when the answer is one you wanted.





Extension: make no-match loud
Optional. ?stopifnot, ?match.arg, ?identical, ?all.equal.

Rewrite the lookup so a no-match stops the script instead of returning zero. stopifnot(length(bio_factor) == 1) is one line and would have caught this. Add that check to your own project wherever you pull a single value out of a table.
Find two other ways R turns “nothing” into a number that looks like an answer. sum() and prod() are the obvious pair; max() is the interesting one, because it warns and returns something absurd.
Ask a language model the same question about this dataset and read its code before its answer. Did it check that its subset matched anything? Almost none do, and it is not because they cannot — it is because nobody in the training data bothered either.
factors$fuel == "Biomass" is the case-sensitivity trap. Find the equivalent trap in your own data: a trailing space, an inconsistent capital, a name spelled two ways across two files.

text:
Exercise 4: How plausible was it before you tested?
One last look at HolmesCo. Their gold assay is 95 % accurate in both directions, and it returned 50 positives from 10 000 samples. Their press release calls these “50 confirmed gold-bearing sites”.
Suppose only 5 samples in 10 000 genuinely bear gold.
Print the positive predictive value: of the samples that test positive, what percentage really are gold-bearing?


















NoteHint 1





Do not reach for Bayes’ theorem. Count people — or in this case, samples.
Imagine all 10 000 laid out. Five are gold-bearing; 9995 are not. Send every one through the test and count the positives that come out of each pile. Then ask what fraction of the total positive pile came from the gold pile.
That reframing — natural frequencies rather than probabilities — makes this problem easy, and it is the reason the fallacy persists: the same arithmetic in probability notation defeats most people, including most doctors, most lawyers and most geologists.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
true_pos <- 5 * 0.95
false_pos <- (10000 - 5) * 0.05
100 * true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos)
Look at the two numbers before you divide. One is under 5, the other is about 500. The answer is decided by the sizes of the two piles, not by the accuracy of the test.











TipSolution





true_pos <- 5 * 0.95
false_pos <- (10000 - 5) * 0.05

100 * true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos)
0.94 %. About 4.75 real hits are hidden among roughly 500 false ones, so fewer than one positive in a hundred means anything. HolmesCo’s “50 confirmed sites” is a number their own test cannot support — and in fact 50 positives is fewer than the ~500 this test would throw up by chance alone, which is its own interesting question.
The general shape: when what you are looking for is rare, a good test still produces mostly false alarms, because the 5 % error rate is applied to a vastly larger pile than the 95 % success rate is.
This is the p-value problem in different clothing. A “significant” result for an implausible hypothesis is most likely a false positive, for exactly this arithmetic — which is why “how plausible was this before we tested?” has been a refrain since Week 1. It is not scepticism for its own sake. It is the denominator.
And it is the judgement an AI tool is least likely to volunteer. Ask one to analyse HolmesCo’s assay and it will usually compute what you asked for, fluently and correctly, without pointing out that the base rate makes the conclusion worthless. Noticing that the question was the wrong question remains your job.





Extension: what would make the test worth running?
Optional.

How accurate would the test have to be for half the positives to be real, at this base rate? Solve it, and then say whether such a test could exist.
Hold the test at 95 % and raise the base rate instead. At what prevalence do half the positives become real? This is why screening is done on targeted populations rather than everybody, in medicine and in mineral exploration alike.
HolmesCo found 50 positives where chance alone predicts about 500. Give two explanations, one innocent and one not. What would you ask to see in order to tell them apart?
Write the sentence HolmesCo’s press release should have contained. Then ask why no consultancy writes it.
