title: Summative Project Topics
section: 1. Did cutting wastewater injection stop Oklahoma’s earthquakes?
text:
1. Did cutting wastewater injection stop Oklahoma’s earthquakes?
Oklahoma went from a couple of felt earthquakes a year to several hundred, as the oil industry pumped its wastewater into deep wells. In 2016 the state regulator ordered injection cut. Did that work? The answer shapes how the UK will regulate the next things we pump underground: CO₂ storage, hydrogen storage and geothermal fluids. Who’s listening: the Oklahoma Corporation Commission; in the UK, the North Sea Transition Authority and the Environment Agency, which permit CO₂ storage.
Ways in:

Did the earthquake rate fall after the 2016 directives?
Does the earthquake count follow injected volume better with a lag?
Does injection depth (close to crystalline basement) matter as well as volume?

Data: USGS earthquake catalogue (ComCat), CSV for any box and period, e.g. Oklahoma, 2005–2025, magnitude 2.5+. Injection volumes per well: Oklahoma Corporation Commission, Oil & Gas Data (Excel, one file per year; formats change between years).
Watch out for: the oil price drove both injection and its fall, so “the directive worked” is confounded with “the market collapsed”. Aftershocks are not independent events. More seismometers after 2010 means more small earthquakes detected.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 2. How shaky is Britain, and was the fracking “red light” sensible?
text:
2. How shaky is Britain, and was the fracking “red light” sensible?
Fracking at Preston New Road, Lancashire, was halted in 2019 after a magnitude 2.9 earthquake, under a “traffic light” rule that paused work at magnitude 0.5. Critics said quarrying and natural earthquakes routinely exceed that. Were they right? The moratorium was reaffirmed in 2024, and the same rules could govern geothermal and gas storage. Who’s listening: the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), the North Sea Transition Authority.
Ways in:

How often does Britain have natural earthquakes above 0.5, 1.5 and 2.9? Fit the Gutenberg–Richter relation (log count against magnitude) and compare the Preston New Road sequence with it.
Did small earthquakes in the coalfields change after deep mining ended (Durham 1993, Kellingley 2015) and mine water rose?
Are induced earthquakes shallower than natural ones?

Data: BGS earthquake catalogue (search form with CSV output; 1970 onwards, plus a historical catalogue). One row per event: date, time, location, depth, magnitude.
Watch out for: the smallest magnitude the network reliably detects changed over time and differs by place (Blackpool was densely instrumented in 2018–19; rural Wales is not). Quarry blasts. Base rates.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 3. Do earthquakes kill because of magnitude or because of poverty?
text:
3. Do earthquakes kill because of magnitude or because of poverty?
Aid budgets can pay for response after a disaster, or for prevention before it: retrofitting schools, enforcing building codes. If a country’s wealth explains as much about the death toll as an earthquake’s size, prevention is the better buy. Who’s listening: the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, the World Bank, national governments.
Ways in:

After allowing for magnitude and depth, do earthquakes kill fewer people in richer countries?
Has the death toll for a given magnitude fallen over the decades?
Do tsunami deaths follow a different pattern?

Data: NOAA NCEI Significant Earthquake Database (download from the search page; one row per event: date, location, depth, magnitude, deaths, damage). GDP per capita: World Bank (CSV).
Watch out for: an earthquake gets into this database because it did damage or killed people, so the sample is selected on the outcome. Population near the epicentre. Reporting has improved over time.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 4. Which volcanoes most deserve monitoring money?
text:
4. Which volcanoes most deserve monitoring money?
Volcano observatories cannot watch everything. The 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption closed European airspace for days; some volcanoes with millions of people nearby have no monitoring at all. Records also seem to show eruptions becoming more frequent. Are they? Who’s listening: volcano observatories and their funders, aviation ash advisory centres, the UK Natural Hazards Partnership.
Ways in:

Has the number of recorded eruptions per decade risen? Is the rise in small eruptions (VEI 0–2), large ones, or both?
Which volcanoes combine large nearby populations with frequent eruptions?
Do some tectonic settings or rock types erupt more explosively?

Data: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program: eruption search and volcano search, both with an Excel export (eruption dates, VEI; volcano type, setting, rock type, population within 5, 10, 30 and 100 km). The “Excel” export is really XML: open it in Excel and save as CSV.
Watch out for: reporting bias is the whole story of the “rising” eruption count: small eruptions in remote places went unrecorded before satellites. Old eruption dates are uncertain; one eruption can last decades.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 5. How often should the grid brace for a geomagnetic storm?
text:
5. How often should the grid brace for a geomagnetic storm?
Severe space weather is on the UK National Risk Register: storms in Earth’s magnetic field induce currents in long power lines that can destroy transformers, which take a year to replace. Preparing costs money, so how often is “severe”? Who’s listening: the National Energy System Operator, Ofgem, the Cabinet Office, the Met Office Space Weather Operations Centre.
Ways in:

Are severe storm days (Kp 8 or above) more frequent around solar maximum? Does the peak come in the declining phase of the cycle?
Is the current solar cycle producing more storms than the last, as its sunspot numbers would predict?
What return period does the record imply for a Kp 9 day, and how uncertain is it?

Data: Kp index since 1932 (GFZ Potsdam; plain text, one row per day with eight 3-hour values). Yearly sunspot numbers (SILSO, Royal Observatory of Belgium; CSV, semicolon separated).
Watch out for: days within one storm are not independent. Kp stops at 9, so the very largest storms (1859, 1921) look like ordinary Kp 9 days. Only about eight solar cycles are on record. Extrapolating a “1 in 100 year” event from 90 years of data.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 6. Is the sea rising faster at North Shields or in the south?
text:
6. Is the sea rising faster at North Shields or in the south?
Planning rules allow for different amounts of sea-level rise on different coasts, partly because the land itself is still moving: northern Britain is rebounding after the weight of the last ice sheet was removed, and the south is sinking. Are the allowances right? North Shields has one of the world’s longest tide-gauge records. Who’s listening: the Environment Agency (climate change allowances), coastal councils writing Shoreline Management Plans.
Ways in:

Do sea-level trends at UK tide gauges differ from north to south as glacial rebound would predict?
Has the rise accelerated since 1990?
Is any gauge an outlier, and why (local subsidence, harbour works)?

Data: Permanent Service for Mean Sea Level (annual and monthly means, one text file per gauge: North Shields from 1895, Newlyn from 1915, Aberdeen, Liverpool, Sheerness…). Also available as CSV from EMODnet.
Watch out for: gaps; short records exaggerate variability; an 18.6-year tidal cycle; successive years are not independent, so naive confidence intervals are too narrow. Gauges measure sea level relative to the land.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 7. Which stretches of coast are we prepared to lose?
text:
7. Which stretches of coast are we prepared to lose?
For every stretch of coast, councils choose between defending it (“hold the line”) and letting it go (“no active intervention”). Defending a slowly eroding cliff wastes money; abandoning a fast one loses homes. The Holderness coast is among the fastest-eroding in Europe; Durham’s Heritage Coast is still recovering from a century of colliery waste tipped on its beaches. Who’s listening: coastal councils, the Environment Agency.
Ways in:

Do soft cliffs (glacial till) retreat significantly faster than rock (Magnesian Limestone, sandstone)?
Is the policy choice (“hold the line” or not) explained by erosion rate, or by what’s behind the cliff?
How much does projected erosion to 2105 depend on the climate scenario?

Data: National Coastal Erosion Risk Mapping 2024 (Environment Agency; GeoJSON or GeoPackage, one feature per frontage with its management policy and projected erosion). Read the attribute table into R with sf::read_sf(), or open it in QGIS and export a CSV. Geology: BGS Geology 625k (free).
Watch out for: the projections are partly modelled, not measured. Defended frontages erode less because they are defended.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 8. Are landslide deaths rising, or are we just hearing about more of them?
text:
8. Are landslide deaths rising, or are we just hearing about more of them?
Rainfall-triggered landslides kill thousands of people a year, and early-warning systems are being built on the claim that the toll is rising with heavier rainfall. Is it? Who’s listening: national disaster agencies, development banks funding warning systems.
Ways in:

Has the number of recorded fatal landslides per year risen?
Do recorded landslides track rainfall seasons (monsoon, hurricane season)?
Which countries suffer most deaths per landslide, and why?

Data: NASA Cooperative Open Online Landslide Repository (Global Landslide Catalog; CSV in a zip, one row per event: date, location, trigger, size, fatalities, news source).
Watch out for: the catalogue was compiled from English-language news reports, so it records where journalists look. Large events are over-represented. Reporting changes over time.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 9. Are abandoned metal mines still poisoning North Pennine rivers?
text:
9. Are abandoned metal mines still poisoning North Pennine rivers?
Lead and zinc mines in Weardale, Allendale and the Nent valley closed a century ago, yet their drainage still supplies a large share of the cadmium, lead and zinc in England’s rivers, and makes many northern rivers fail their water-quality standards. Treatment schemes cost millions each, so they must be prioritized and shown to work. Who’s listening: the Water and Abandoned Metal Mines programme (Environment Agency, Mining Remediation Authority, Defra).
Ways in:

How much higher is dissolved zinc downstream of old mines than upstream, or than in similar unmined rivers?
Did zinc in the River Nent fall after its treatment scheme opened?
Does concentration fall at high flow (dilution) or rise (flushing)?

Data: Environment Agency Water Quality Archive (every sample since 2000; CSV download or API; one row per measurement: site, location, date, determinand, result).
Watch out for: values below the detection limit are reported as “< 5”, not zero. Sampling is not random (more samples during incidents). Wet years dilute, so a wet “after” period can fake a treatment success. Concentrations are skewed: work on a log scale.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 10. Is sewage spilling because it rained, or because of the pipes?
text:
10. Is sewage spilling because it rained, or because of the pipes?
Storm overflows release untreated sewage into rivers when sewers are full. Water companies blame rainfall, and groundwater seeping into pipes; campaigners blame under-investment. Geology is part of the answer: where sewers sit in Chalk, high groundwater can fill them for months. Who’s listening: Ofwat, the Environment Agency, water companies.
Ways in:

After allowing for rainfall, do some companies spill much more than others?
Do overflows over permeable bedrock spill for longer?
Has spilling really increased, or has monitoring?

Data: Event Duration Monitoring annual returns (Environment Agency; Excel, one row per overflow per year, 2020–2025, plus a 2016–2025 summary). Rainfall: Met Office station data. Bedrock: BGS Geology 625k.
Watch out for: monitors were installed progressively, so early years undercount. A few overflows dominate the totals.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 11. Are floods on North East rivers getting bigger?
text:
11. Are floods on North East rivers getting bigger?
The “1 in 100 year” flood that decides where houses may be built, and how high defences go, is estimated from past peak flows on the assumption that the climate isn’t changing. If peaks are rising, the design floods are too small. Who’s listening: the Environment Agency, planning authorities, the Flood Re insurance scheme.
Ways in:

Do annual peak flows on the Wear, Tees and Tyne show an upward trend?
Are trends steeper in impermeable upland catchments than permeable ones?
How much does one extreme winter (2015–16) change the estimated “1 in 100 year” flood?

Data: National River Flow Archive annual maximum flows, with catchment descriptors (area, rainfall, urban extent, permeability). Easiest via the R package UKFE: UKFE::GetDataNRFA(24001, Type = "AMAX") (24001 is the Wear at Sunderland Bridge).
Watch out for: gauges measure high flows least accurately. Urbanization. Choose your gauges before looking at their trends, or you will find the trend you went looking for.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 12. Mine-water heat: is County Durham’s coalfield unusually warm?
text:
12. Mine-water heat: is County Durham’s coalfield unusually warm?
The flooded coal mines beneath County Durham hold warm water that could heat homes: the Dawdon scheme near Seaham is being connected to a heat network planned to serve 750 affordable homes (construction began in 2025). Is the North East’s mine water unusually warm, and is that a big number? Who’s listening: the Mining Remediation Authority, Durham County Council, heat-network developers.
Ways in:

Does mine water warm faster with depth (a steeper geothermal gradient) in the North East than in South Wales or Nottinghamshire?
In blocks with both, is pumped water warmer than undisturbed water at the same depth?
How many homes could the North East’s warm blocks heat?

Data: Temperature Maps of the British Coalfields (Coal Authority and BGS), one row per Mine Water Block with temperatures every 100 m from 100 to 1000 m depth. No download button: read the query URL into R with jsonlite::fromJSON() and take $features$properties (swap Equilibrium for Pumped for pumped shafts). The Mining Remediation Authority Map Viewer shows each treatment scheme’s pumping rate and heat potential (Mine Water Heat → Waste Heat From Treatment). Method: Farr et al. (2021), The temperature of Britain’s coalfields.
Watch out for: temperatures at most depths are interpolated from a handful of readings, so a “temperature at 800 m” may be an extrapolation; keep only blocks marked “Measured”. Some readings date from working mines before 1925. Pumping draws deeper water up the shaft.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 13. Where would deep geothermal heat pay off?
text:
13. Where would deep geothermal heat pay off?
Deep geothermal wells cost millions, and pay off only where the Earth gives up its heat generously. The UK has drilled in Cornwall (granite), Newcastle (the Science Central borehole) and Weardale (Eastgate). Where should the next one go? Who’s listening: DESNZ, the Geothermal Energy Advisory Panel, city heat-network planners.
Ways in:

Is heat flow higher over radiogenic granites than over sedimentary basins?
How does UK heat flow compare with countries that already use deep geothermal heat (Iceland, Germany, the Netherlands)?
Do older measurements, or poorer-quality ones, differ systematically?

Data: Global Heat Flow Database, Release 2024 (International Heat Flow Commission / GFZ; about 91 000 measurements, one row each: location, heat flow in mW/m², depth, method, quality).
Watch out for: measurements cluster where people drilled for oil or minerals, not at random. Shallow boreholes are disturbed by past climate. Quality codes vary.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 14. Who controls the minerals the energy transition needs?
text:
14. Who controls the minerals the energy transition needs?
Wind turbines, batteries and electricity grids need lithium, cobalt, rare earths and copper. The UK Critical Minerals Strategy judges a mineral “critical” partly by how few countries supply it. If supply is concentrating, stockpiling, recycling or mining at home (Cornish lithium, Weardale fluorspar) look more attractive. Who’s listening: the Department for Business and Trade, the UK Critical Minerals Intelligence Centre at BGS.
Ways in:

Has the top producer’s share (or a concentration index) risen for the minerals on the UK critical list?
Are critical minerals more concentrated than non-critical ones, or is that circular?
Do reserves sit in the same countries as production?

Data: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 data release (CSV; production, reserves and prices by commodity and country; earlier editions give a longer series). Longer history: BGS World Mineral Statistics (Excel export, one commodity at a time).
Watch out for: “critical” is defined partly by concentration. Some countries’ figures are estimates. By-product metals (cobalt from copper mines) depend on another market.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 15. Does the rock beneath your home decide your radon risk?
text:
15. Does the rock beneath your home decide your radon risk?
Radon, a radioactive gas from uranium in rocks, is the second biggest cause of lung cancer in the UK after smoking. New homes need a radon barrier only in mapped “affected areas”, and free testing is targeted there. Do the maps, which follow geology, catch the homes at risk? Who’s listening: the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), building regulations (Approved Document C), local councils.
Ways in:

Do indoor radon levels differ between areas on granite, limestone, mudstone and sandstone?
How many homes above the action level lie outside areas classed as high risk?
Is the North Pennines’ radon (Carboniferous limestone, Weardale granite) as high as Cornwall’s?

Data: UKHSA’s Radon in homes in England: 2016 data report (spreadsheet of results from over half a million homes, by local authority and postcode area: number tested, mean, maximum, number above the action level; Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own reports). The Indicative Atlas of Radon (BGS/UKHSA, Open Government Licence, via the OS Data Hub) gives the radon class of each 1 km square. The detailed radon potential map is licensed and not free.
Watch out for: homes are tested because they are in suspected areas, so measurements are not a random sample. A district contains several rock types. Building type and ventilation matter. The Indicative Atlas gives each square its highest class.

title: Summative Project Topics
text:
16. Will the Chalk run dry?
Hosepipe bans and drought permits are triggered when groundwater at index boreholes falls below set levels. After the 2022 drought, did aquifers recover within a winter, and do some recover more slowly? Who’s listening: water companies (drought plans), the Environment Agency.
Ways in:

Did levels in the Chalk, the Sherwood Sandstone and the Magnesian Limestone recover at different rates after 2022 (or 2012, or 1976)?
How much does winter rainfall explain next summer’s groundwater level?
Are levels in the long-term records falling?

Data: Environment Agency Hydrology Data Explorer (groundwater levels at boreholes, CSV; filter stations by groundwater level). Rainfall: Met Office station data.
Watch out for: pumping near a borehole. Record lengths differ. Recovery depends on the following winter’s rain.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 17. Is nitrate in our groundwater still rising?
text:
17. Is nitrate in our groundwater still rising?
Nitrate Vulnerable Zones restrict how farmers spread fertilizer over much of England, at real cost to farming. If groundwater nitrate hasn’t fallen, is that because the rules don’t work, or because water takes decades to soak down to the aquifer? Who’s listening: Defra (which designates the zones), water companies (who must treat or blend the water), the Environment Agency.
Ways in:

Are nitrate trends in Chalk or Magnesian Limestone boreholes still upward?
Are trends different inside and outside the zones?
Do boreholes with a thick unsaturated zone lag behind shallow ones?

Data: Environment Agency Water Quality Archive (groundwater sampling points, determinand “nitrate as N”). Context: Ascott et al. (2017), Global patterns of nitrate storage in the vadose zone.
Watch out for: today’s groundwater may record 1980s farming. The zones were drawn where nitrate was already high. Borehole depth.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 18. Are glaciers shrinking fastest where people depend on them most?
text:
18. Are glaciers shrinking fastest where people depend on them most?
In the Andes and Central Asia, glacier melt keeps rivers flowing through the dry season, supplying drinking water and irrigation to millions. Adaptation funding should go where loss is fastest relative to dependence. Who’s listening: development agencies, national water ministries.
Ways in:

Does the rate of glacier mass loss differ between regions?
Do small or low glaciers lose mass faster?
Has loss accelerated since 2000?

Data: World Glacier Monitoring Service, Fluctuations of Glaciers (mass balance and length change per glacier per year, CSV in a large zip).
Watch out for: monitored glaciers aren’t a random sample: they’re accessible, often small, and mostly in the Alps. Different measurement methods.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 19. Does land use change how much carbon our soils hold?
text:
19. Does land use change how much carbon our soils hold?
The government now pays farmers to protect soil carbon. That makes sense only if land use measurably changes how much carbon topsoils hold. Who’s listening: Defra (Environmental Land Management), Natural England, the Climate Change Committee.
Ways in:

Do arable soils hold less carbon than grassland once soil pH is allowed for?
Did topsoil carbon change between the 1978, 1998 and 2007 surveys in the same squares?
How much of the land-use difference is really altitude and rainfall?

Data: Countryside Survey 2007 topsoil properties (UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology; up to 591 1 km squares; one row per soil core: habitat, pH, carbon concentration, bulk density). You may need to accept a licence or register (free).
Watch out for: land use goes with altitude, rainfall and rock type: peat is upland and wet, arable land lowland and dry. Carbon concentration is not carbon stock. Several cores per square are not independent.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 20. The gas price shock: did households really cut back?
text:
20. The gas price shock: did households really cut back?
Gas prices spiked in 2022 and the government capped them with the Energy Price Guarantee. Did households use less gas, and has use bounced back? Who’s listening: DESNZ, Ofgem (the price cap).
Ways in:

Did gas use per meter fall after 2022? Has it recovered?
Did the response differ between richer and poorer areas?

Data: Sub-national gas consumption statistics (DESNZ; by local authority, 2005 onward). Prices: quarterly energy prices.
Watch out for: a mild winter cuts gas use too. Insulation and boiler upgrades.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 21. What’s behind the fall in UK electricity generation?
text:
21. What’s behind the fall in UK electricity generation?
DUKES statistics show a sustained fall in UK electricity production over the past few years, despite economic growth, the adoption of electric vehicles, and a push to shift from gas to electricity for heating. What is behind this fall?

Are other electricity sources missing from this picture (overseas generation; rooftop solar that never reaches the grid)?
Has the decline in UK manufacturing reduced demand?
Have energy efficiency measures reduced domestic demand?

Data: DUKES Chapter 5 (generation, imports through interconnectors, consumption by sector). Energy Trends (quarterly). Manufacturing output: ONS Index of Production.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 22. Has the fall in household electricity use ended?
text:
22. Has the fall in household electricity use ended?
Household electricity use fell for twenty years as lighting and appliances became more efficient. Heat pumps and electric cars will push it back up. Network operators must forecast when, and where first. Who’s listening: distribution network operators, the National Energy System Operator.
Ways in:

Has use per meter stopped falling? In which regions first?
Do areas with more heat pumps or EVs show it first?

Data: Sub-national electricity consumption statistics (DESNZ; by local authority, 2005 onward).
Watch out for: weather, prices, housing stock, population change, deprivation.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 23. Do countries that build renewables have cleaner electricity?
text:
23. Do countries that build renewables have cleaner electricity?
Across countries, is more renewable capacity associated with less CO₂ per kWh? Who’s listening: international climate negotiators, aid programmes funding renewables.
Ways in:

Does the relationship survive allowing for GDP?
What happens to countries that rely on nuclear or hydro?

Data: IRENA renewable capacity statistics; Ember global electricity data (carbon intensity, generation mix).
Watch out for: nuclear (low carbon, not renewable); geography (Norway’s hydro); the ecological fallacy.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 24. Offshore wind: are newer farms more productive?
text:
24. Offshore wind: are newer farms more productive?
Contracts for Difference auctions set the price offshore wind is paid, and bids assume a load factor. Are newer farms, with bigger turbines further offshore, delivering more? Who’s listening: DESNZ (auction design), the Crown Estate (seabed leasing).
Ways in:

Does load factor rise with commissioning year?
Is that the turbines, or the wind further offshore?

Data: Renewable Energy Planning Database (capacity, location, dates per project); generation from DUKES or Energy Trends.
Watch out for: distance from shore, water depth, curtailment. Linking the two datasets takes care.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 25. Can old reactors bridge the gap to Hinkley Point C?
text:
25. Can old reactors bridge the gap to Hinkley Point C?
The UK’s ageing nuclear stations are closing faster than new ones open. Life extensions are keeping some running. Has output per GW held up as stations age? Who’s listening: DESNZ, EDF, the Office for Nuclear Regulation.
Ways in:

Has nuclear generation fallen in proportion to capacity?
Do load factors decline as stations age?

Data: DUKES Chapter 5 (generation by fuel; plant capacities).
Watch out for: planned outages, graphite cracking, demand.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 26. Is Scottish wind worth the cost of getting it south?
text:
26. Is Scottish wind worth the cost of getting it south?
Scotland is windier, but generators there pay more to use the grid, because most demand is in the south. Does higher output outweigh the charge? Who’s listening: Ofgem, the National Energy System Operator.
Ways in:

Do onshore load factors differ between UK nations or regions?
Is the difference big enough to matter, compared with grid charges?

Data: Regional Renewable Statistics (DESNZ; capacity and generation by local authority).
Watch out for: turbine age, altitude, curtailment, weather year.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 27. Is rooftop solar in the North worth the same as in the South?
text:
27. Is rooftop solar in the North worth the same as in the South?
Solar export payments are set nationally. If panels in Durham produce much less than panels in Devon, are northern households being short-changed, or the South over-rewarded? Who’s listening: Ofgem, DESNZ.
Ways in:

How much does solar output per MW fall with latitude?
Does latitude explain most of the variation, or does something else?

Data: Regional Renewable Statistics (DESNZ), with local authority latitudes.
Watch out for: orientation, shading, cloud, roof vs ground mounting, unreliable reporting from small installations.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 28. How fast is the UK installing heat pumps, and where can the ground do the work?
text:
28. How fast is the UK installing heat pumps, and where can the ground do the work?
Heat pumps are central to decarbonizing heating. Ground-source pumps are more efficient but need suitable geology and space. Who’s listening: DESNZ (Boiler Upgrade Scheme), local councils.
Ways in:

Is installation accelerating? Does it differ by region?
Where do ground-source installations cluster, and why?

Data: MCS data dashboard (installations by technology and area); Boiler Upgrade Scheme statistics.
Watch out for: changing subsidies; housing type; gas grid connection; income.

title: Summative Project Topics
text:
29. Does burning waste reduce landfill?
Councils with energy-from-waste plants should landfill less. Do they, or does burning only replace recycling? Who’s listening: Defra, councils’ waste strategies.
Ways in:

Has landfill fallen faster in councils with EfW plants?
Do EfW councils recycle less?

Data: Local authority collected waste statistics (Defra; tonnes by destination per council per year).
Watch out for: waste crosses council boundaries, so define “has EfW” carefully.

title: Summative Project Topics
section: 30. Is EV charging infrastructure keeping up?
text:
30. Is EV charging infrastructure keeping up?
Is the number of public charge points growing as fast as the number of electric vehicles? Who’s listening: the Department for Transport, local councils.
Ways in:

Is the ratio of vehicles to charge points worsening?
Does it differ between urban and rural areas, or with driveway access?

Data: EV charging device statistics and vehicle licensing statistics (DfT; by local authority, quarterly).
Watch out for: most EVs charge at home; company fleets.

PRESS RELEASE — FOR IMMEDIATE DISTRIBUTION
Date: March 2026

title: HolmesCo: Gold Assay Results
section: Major Gold Discovery in County Durham
text:
Major Gold Discovery in County Durham
HolmesCo is pleased to announce the results of a landmark geochemical survey across County Durham and the Northern Pennines.

Survey methodology
Our field teams collected soil and shallow rock samples from 1000 locations across the survey area. Each sample was tested using HolmesCo’s proprietary AuDetect™ geochemical assay, which identifies gold-bearing rock with 95 % accuracy:

If gold is present, the assay correctly identifies it 95 % of the time (sensitivity)
If gold is absent, the assay correctly rules it out 95 % of the time (specificity)



Results
Of the 1000 samples tested, 54 returned positive results for gold mineralization.
The positive samples are concentrated in the western part of the survey area, consistent with known geological structures in the Alston Block.


Interpretation

“Fifty-four confirmed gold hits across County Durham represents a highly significant discovery. Our AuDetect™ assay is 95 % accurate — these results give us great confidence that there is genuine gold mineralization in the region. We recommend immediate follow-up drilling at the most promising sites.”
— Dr G. Holmes, Chief Scientific Officer, HolmesCo

HolmesCo has applied for three exploration licences and is seeking investment partners to fund a Phase 2 drilling programme.
Investors interested in this opportunity should contact HolmesCo’s Business Development team.


This press release has been prepared by HolmesCo and has not been independently reviewed. AuDetect™ accuracy figures are based on laboratory validation against known reference samples. Field performance may vary. HolmesCo accepts no liability for investment decisions made on the basis of this announcement.

text:
This is a fictional document for teaching purposes.
QUARTERLY TECHNICAL SUMMARY — Q1 2026
HolmesCo is pleased to present three key findings from our recent project portfolio. All results have been subjected to rigorous statistical testing.

title: HolmesCo: Quarterly Report Card
text:
Your task
For each result, as a desk:

Name the problem: which idea from today does HolmesCo’s claim ignore?
Rewrite HolmesCo’s claim as one honest sentence that a planner could act on. Use the numbers on this page; don’t invent new ones.

This is the sentence you will write about your own results: say what you found, how big it is, and how sure you are.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
text:
Artificial intelligence is often accused of being an environmental disaster, and headlines warn that a single ChatGPT query uses “ten times more energy than a Google search.” This briefing asks how large that cost really is: it compares the energy and water used by one query with other everyday actions on a like-for-like basis, and sets the sector’s total demand against global electricity supply. We find that a typical query uses about 0.3 Wh — comparable to a Google search, and roughly 170 times less than boiling a cup of water — and that generative AI as a whole accounts for around 0.05 % of world electricity use today. The credible concern is not the individual query but the rate of growth: demand could rise more than twenty-fold by 2030, though that projection rests on efficiency gains that are hard to forecast. We therefore recommend that policy act on the supply side — low-carbon electricity for data centres, model efficiency standards, mandatory energy and water reporting, and siting rules where water is scarce — rather than on discouraging individual use, which would save very little.
The briefing also asks a question the headlines do not: under what conditions does using AI save more energy than it costs? That break-even is set out below.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
text:
Artificial intelligence is often accused of being an environmental disaster, and headlines warn that a single ChatGPT query uses “ten times more energy than a Google search.” This briefing asks how large that cost really is: it compares the energy and water used by one query with other everyday actions on a like-for-like basis, and sets the sector’s total demand against global electricity supply. We find that a typical query uses about 0.3 Wh — comparable to a Google search, and roughly 170 times less than boiling a cup of water — and that generative AI as a whole accounts for around 0.05 % of world electricity use today. The credible concern is not the individual query but the rate of growth: demand could rise more than twenty-fold by 2030, though that projection rests on efficiency gains that are hard to forecast. We therefore recommend that policy act on the supply side — low-carbon electricity for data centres, model efficiency standards, mandatory energy and water reporting, and siting rules where water is scarce — rather than on discouraging individual use, which would save very little.
The briefing also asks a question the headlines do not: under what conditions does using AI save more energy than it costs? That break-even is set out below.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
section: What does a single AI query cost?
text:
What does a single AI query cost?
Estimates of the energy consumed by one AI text query have converged around 0.3 Wh for a standard interaction with a model like GPT-4o. This figure is supported by independent analysis from the research institute Epoch AI (Epoch AI, 2025) and is consistent with a figure of 0.34 Wh disclosed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in a 2025 blog post (Altman, 2025).
Not all queries are equal. Academic estimates for more complex “reasoning” models range from 3 Wh to 20 Wh per query, depending on model size and output length (IEEE Spectrum, 2025; Jegham et al., 2025). A reasonable range for typical use is 0.3–3 Wh per query.
For reference, a single Google search uses approximately 0.3 Wh (Google, via Epoch AI, 2025).
These figures are marginal costs — the energy consumed by each additional query once a model already exists. They do not include the fixed cost of training the model in the first place. Training GPT-4 required an estimated 50 GWh (de Vries, 2023) — equivalent to roughly 170 million typical queries. But training energy is sunk: it is spent once regardless of whether the model serves one query or one billion. For individual decision-making, the marginal cost per query is what matters. For policy, the two costs require different levers: efficiency standards and renewable procurement for training; demand-side signals for inference.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
text:
Comparing like with like
To put 0.3 Wh in context, we should compare it to other brief, discrete actions — things that, like an AI query, take seconds or minutes rather than hours.

library("ggplot2")

discrete <- data.frame(
  action = c(
    "Google search",
    "AI query (typical)",
    "AI query (complex)",
    "Charging a phone\nfor 10 minutes",
    "Boiling a kettle\n(one cup, ~0.5 L)"
  ),
  wh = c(0.3, 0.3, 10, 5, 53),
  source = c(
    "Google via Epoch AI 2025",
    "Epoch AI 2025; Altman 2025",
    "IEEE Spectrum 2025",
    "~30 W charger × 10 min",
    "4.2 kJ/kg·°C × 0.5 kg × 90 °C ÷ 3.6"
  )
)

discrete$action <- factor(discrete$action, levels = discrete$action[order(discrete$wh)])

ggplot(discrete, aes(x = wh, y = action)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Energy (watt-hours)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Energy cost of brief everyday actions, compared to an AI query. Sources: Epoch AI (2025); DECC conversion factors; manufacturer data.





A typical AI query uses roughly the same energy as a Google search, and about 170 times less than boiling half a litre of water for a cup of tea.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
section: How does AI compare to what it replaces?
text:
How does AI compare to what it replaces?
The comparison above tells us what an AI query costs in isolation, but the more useful question is: what would you be doing instead? If AI replaces time spent working at a computer, we should compare energy rates — how much energy is consumed per minute of each activity.

rates <- data.frame(
  activity = c(
    "AI queries\n(~2 per minute)",
    "Laptop\n(in use)",
    "Laptop + AI\n(combined)",
    "Streaming video",
    "Gas central heating\n(running)"
  ),
  wh_per_min = c(
    0.6,
    0.45,
    1.05,
    1.3,
    150
  ),
  source = c(
    "0.3 Wh × 2 queries/min",
    "~27 Wh/hr; Arcadia 2022",
    "Sum of laptop + AI",
    "~77 Wh/hr; IEA / various",
    "~9 kW boiler at ~100 % duty"
  )
)

rates$activity <- factor(rates$activity, levels = rates$activity[order(rates$wh_per_min)])

ggplot(rates, aes(x = wh_per_min, y = activity)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Energy consumption (Wh per minute)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 2: Energy consumption rates for sustained activities. An AI session adds a small increment to the laptop baseline. Sources: Arcadia (2022); various; DECC (2012).





A person actively using AI at a rate of two queries per minute adds about 0.6 Wh/min to their energy consumption — roughly doubling their laptop’s draw. But both figures are dwarfed by background household energy use: running gas central heating consumes energy at roughly 150 Wh per minute (DECC, 2012), about 250 times the rate of active AI use.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
section: The break-even: when does AI save energy?
text:
The break-even: when does AI save energy?
If an AI query (0.3 Wh) saves even one minute of laptop time (0.45 Wh), the energy arithmetic is already favourable: the net saving is 0.15 Wh per query. In practice, a useful AI interaction might save 5–10 minutes of research, writing, or debugging — yielding a net saving of 2–4 Wh.
This does not mean all AI use is beneficial. Queries that produce no useful output — casual chatting, generating content that goes unread, or replacing tasks that didn’t need a computer at all — carry cost without benefit. The break-even depends entirely on whether the AI query genuinely displaces energy-consuming activity.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
text:
What about water?
Data centres also consume freshwater, primarily for evaporative cooling. Researchers at the University of California, Riverside estimate that a session of approximately 20 AI queries consumes roughly 500 ml of water (UC Riverside, cited in EESI, 2025). This is a lifecycle estimate that includes “indirect” water use — water consumed in generating the electricity the data centre draws from the grid — not just water evaporated on site (de Vries-Gao, 2025). The split between direct and indirect water use varies enormously by location: a data centre powered by hydroelectric or thermal generation in a humid climate has a very different water footprint from one running on the same grid as coal-fired plants in an arid region.
How big is this number? At face value, 500 ml per 20 queries sounds alarming. But a single cup of coffee requires approximately 140 litres of water to grow, process, and transport the beans (Water Footprint Network, 2025) — roughly 5600 times more water than one AI query. A single flush of a UK toilet uses about 6 litres (Waterwise, 2012). The water cost of AI is real, but it is small compared to agriculture, household use, and many industrial processes.
The aggregate picture is more nuanced. Morgan Stanley projects that global AI data centre water consumption could reach 1068 billion litres per year by 2028 (Morgan Stanley, via MindfulSlowLife, 2026). For context, UK public water supply alone is approximately 5300 billion litres per year (Ofwat, 2023). The concern is not that AI will drain the world’s water supply, but that large data centres can create localized pressure on water systems — particularly where they are sited in water-stressed regions. Policy responses should focus on siting decisions and cooling technology standards rather than on per-query consumption.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
text:
The bigger picture: aggregate demand
At individual scale, AI’s energy cost is small. At global scale, it adds up.
ChatGPT serves approximately 2.5 billion queries per day (OpenAI, via IEEE Spectrum, 2025). At 0.3 Wh per query, that is roughly 750 MWh/day, or 274 GWh/year. The entire generative AI sector consumed an estimated 15 TWh in 2025 (Schneider Electric, via IEEE Spectrum, 2025).
For context, global electricity consumption is approximately 30 000 TWh/year (IEA, 2024), so current AI use represents about 0.05 % of the total. However, projections suggest AI data centre demand could reach 347 TWh by 2030 — a 23-fold increase (Schneider Electric, 2025). Whether this materializes depends on efficiency gains in both hardware and model design.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
text:
Conclusions

A single AI query has a negligible energy footprint — comparable to a Google search and far smaller than routine household actions like boiling a kettle (Epoch AI, 2025).
On a per-minute basis, AI adds modestly to the energy cost of computer use, and both are dwarfed by household heating.
AI can be net energy-positive when it saves more human–computer time than it consumes, but this depends on whether the query is genuinely useful.
The real concern is aggregate growth: rapid increases in query volumes and model complexity could make AI a significant fraction of global electricity demand by 2030 (Schneider Electric, 2025).
Policy should focus on the supply side — low-carbon electricity for data centres, model efficiency standards, and transparent energy reporting — rather than discouraging individual use.

title: How bad is AI for the environment?
text:
Sources

Altman, S. (2025). “Three observations.” Blog post, OpenAI. CEO of OpenAI. First public disclosure of per-query energy figures.
Epoch AI (2025). “How much energy does ChatGPT use?” Gradient Updates. Independent estimate of ~0.3 Wh per GPT-4o query.
IEEE Spectrum (2025). “AI Energy Use: The Hidden Cost of ChatGPT Queries.” Synthesis of Schneider Electric projections and OpenAI data.
Jegham, N. et al. (2025). Academic estimates of per-query energy for GPT-4.1 nano, o3, and GPT-4.5. (Cited in Towards Data Science, 2025.)
Arcadia (2022). “The hidden energy costs of working from home.” Laptop energy consumption: ~53 kWh/year.
de Vries, A. (2023). “The growing energy footprint of artificial intelligence.” Joule, 7(10), 2191–2194. Training cost estimate for GPT-4.
de Vries-Gao, A. (2025). “The carbon and water footprints of data centers and what this could mean for artificial intelligence.” Cell Reports Sustainability. Lifecycle vs direct water use distinction.
DECC (2012). “How much energy could be saved by making small changes to everyday household behaviours?” Thermostat and heating energy data.
Energy Saving Trust (2021). Thermostat reduction: ~300 kg CO₂/year for a three-bedroom semi-detached home.
IEA (2024). World Energy Outlook. Global electricity consumption data.
EESI (2025). “Data Centers and Water Consumption.” Environmental and Energy Study Institute. UC Riverside estimates and WUE data.
MindfulSlowLife (2026). “How Much Water Does ChatGPT Use Per Day?” Citing Morgan Stanley water consumption projections.
Ofwat (2023). Water company performance data. UK public water supply: ~14 500 Ml/day (~5300 billion litres/year).
Schneider Electric (2025). AI energy consumption projections: 15 TWh

to 347 TWh (2030).

Water Footprint Network (2025). Product water footprints. Coffee: ~140 litres per cup.
Waterwise (2012). Toilet flush volumes in UK homes: ~6 litres per flush.

title: Week 10: Common Pitfalls
text:
You are about to write your final report, and then to review someone else’s. This page is the checklist for both.
It has two halves. The first is an audit: a paragraph of results that reads perfectly well and contains a number that is wrong. The second is a gallery of six ways a competent analysis turns into a bad report, with the refrains that catch each one.
Ten weeks of this module have been about one habit: checking the thing that looks fine.






NoteHow these exercises work

title: Week 10: Common Pitfalls
text:
Exercise 1: Audit the paragraph
A classmate sends you this paragraph from their biomass briefing. It is well written, it cites its sources, and every number in it is the right kind of number.

“UK bioenergy generated 41.0 TWh of electricity in 2025, about 14 % of total supply. Counted under the full supply-chain scenario rather than the official zero, that generation represents 43.5 Mt CO₂ — more than the 40.6 Mt the same electricity would have produced from coal, supply chain included. Shipping the 2024 pellets across the Atlantic adds a further 2.5 Mt, bringing the total to over 45 Mt.”

Three of those four figures are right. One is not, and it is out by enough to matter.
Find it and print the correct value.


















NoteHint 1





Four claims, four short calculations. Do them in the order the paragraph makes them and stop when one disagrees.
Every one of the four is something you computed in Weeks 1 to 3. If a recomputation feels like more work than it should, you are probably about to find the error in it.











NoteHint 2





The four, in order:

14 %: bioenergy over total generation for 2025, times 100.
43.5 Mt: 41.0 TWh, converted to MWh, times the biomass with_supply_chain factor, converted from kg to Mt.
40.6 Mt: the same, with coal’s with_supply_chain factor.
2.5 Mt: the 2024 rows of imports, tonnes times kilometres times 0.005, converted from kg to Mt.

The last one is Week 3 Exercise 1 exactly. If your answer disagrees with the paragraph, check your own units before you accuse anyone — then check theirs.











TipSolution





# Claim 1: 14% of supply
100 * elec$bioenergy_twh[elec$year == 2025] / elec$total_twh[elec$year == 2025]

# Claim 2: 43.5 Mt under the supply-chain scenario
sc <- factors$co2_kg_per_mwh[factors$fuel == "biomass" &
                             factors$scenario == "with_supply_chain"]
elec$bioenergy_twh[elec$year == 2025] * 1e6 * sc / 1e9

# Claim 3: 40.6 Mt as coal, same boundary
coal <- factors$co2_kg_per_mwh[factors$fuel == "coal" &
                               factors$scenario == "with_supply_chain"]
elec$bioenergy_twh[elec$year == 2025] * 1e6 * coal / 1e9

# Claim 4: shipping
i24 <- imports[imports$year == 2024, ]
sum(i24$import_kt * 1000 * i24$transport_km * shipping_co2_per_tkm) / 1e9
The first three check out: 14.0 %, 43.5 Mt, 40.6 Mt.
The fourth is 0.25 Mt, not 2.5. A factor of ten, almost certainly a missed conversion between kilotonnes and tonnes or between kg and Mt.
Three things about this error are worth more than the arithmetic.
It points the author’s way. 2.5 Mt makes transport look like a serious contributor and gives the last sentence something to say. 0.25 Mt makes it a rounding error next to combustion. Errors that weaken your argument get caught; errors that strengthen it get published.
Nothing about the paragraph looks wrong. The units are stated, the sources are real, the arithmetic in “bringing the total to over 45 Mt” is correct given the faulty input. Prose fluency is not evidence, and this paragraph is more convincing than a sloppier one that happens to be right.
Only recomputation caught it. Reading harder would not have. When you review a classmate’s briefing this week, recompute at least one number rather than reading all of them — that is the review that finds something.





Extension: audit the rest of your own report
Optional, and the most useful thing you can do with the time.

Take three numbers from your own draft and recompute each from the raw data, deliberately not looking at how you did it the first time. Independent recomputation is the only check that catches a repeated mistake.
For each number, ask which direction an error would push your conclusion. Anywhere the answer is “in the direction I am arguing”, check twice.
Write the factor-of-ten test into your own workflow: for every quantity, state the unit at every step in a comment. Almost every error in this course has been a unit, and units are the one class of mistake you can design out entirely.

title: Week 10: Common Pitfalls
section: Six ways a good analysis becomes a bad report
text:
Six ways a good analysis becomes a bad report
Each excerpt below is something a competent student could write on the way to a perfectly reasonable conclusion. For each, decide what is wrong before opening the reveal, and name the refrain that catches it.
Discuss as a desk, two minutes per pitfall. Keep notes in the box at the end — you will want them when you review someone’s briefing.

Pitfall 1: The conclusion the data cannot reach

“Our data shows that wind farm output varies by season, with lower generation in summer months. Therefore, wind energy is unreliable and should not receive government subsidies.”







NoteStuck? Start here





Cover the word “Therefore” and read the two halves separately. Is the first half in dispute? Is the second half about the same subject?









TipWhat is wrong





The observation is uncontroversial and well known. The conclusion is about subsidy policy, and nothing between the two supports the journey.
“Varies by season” is not “unreliable” — that word smuggles in a standard nobody has stated. And a subsidy recommendation needs costs, alternatives, storage, and demand patterns, none of which are in the data. The analysis could be flawless and the paragraph would still be indefensible.
Watch for “therefore” and “which proves” in your own draft. They are where an argument most often steps off the evidence, and they are easy to grep for.





Pitfall 2: The figure that explains nothing

“As shown below, there is a clear trend in the data.”
[A scatter plot with no title, no axis labels, no units, no caption and no number. It is not mentioned anywhere else.]







NoteStuck? Start here





Imagine the figure on its own, on a slide, with the text gone. What could a reader work out from it?









TipWhat is wrong





Missing: axis labels with units, a caption saying what the figure shows, a number so it can be cited, a reference in the text that is not “below” — page layout moves — and a statement of what the trend actually is.
The test is that a figure should survive being separated from the text. Yours will be: a reader flicks to the figures first, an examiner reads the caption before the paragraph.
“Clear trend” also does no work. Clear to whom, and how large? That is Pitfall 3 arriving early.





Pitfall 3: The p-value doing a job it cannot do

“The difference in solar panel output between the two regions was highly significant (p = 0.001), confirming that location affects performance.”







NoteStuck? Start here





Suppose the difference were 0.1 W. Would the sentence still be true? Would it still be worth writing?









TipWhat is wrong





How much? The p-value says the difference is unlikely to be zero. It says nothing about size — and with a large enough sample, a difference of 0.1 W would be “highly significant” too. Week 6 built exactly that demonstration.
The sentence needs the effect size, a confidence interval, and a comparator that makes the number mean something.
“Confirming” is a second fault hiding behind the first. A significant test is evidence, not confirmation, and Week 6’s significant result evaporated when its assumptions were checked.
Refrain: is that a big number?





Pitfall 4: The word “prove”

“The results prove that biomass electricity is carbon-neutral under current accounting rules.”







NoteStuck? Start here





What would have to be true of the evidence for “prove” to be the right word? And what does a reader do next, having read it?









TipWhat is wrong





Evidence supports or undermines; it does not prove. Even a result entirely consistent with carbon neutrality cannot rule out the explanations nobody tested.
Better: “the analysis is consistent with…”, or “on these assumptions, the evidence suggests…”.
The reason this matters is not etiquette. “Proven” closes the question, and the whole of this sentence’s content lives in the clause “under current accounting rules” — which is a choice, not a measurement, and is precisely the thing Week 3 showed can be moved from 0 to 1060 kg/MWh without touching a single observation.
Refrain: what assumptions are we making?





Pitfall 5: Methods nobody could follow

“We analysed the data using statistical tests in R and found significant results.”







NoteStuck? Start here





Hand that sentence, and your data, to the person next to you. Could they produce your numbers?









TipWhat is wrong





Almost everything: which data, over what period, which variables; which test and why that one; what assumptions were checked and what happened; what was excluded, transformed or cleaned, and on what rule.
The standard is reproducibility: enough detail that someone with your data and your description gets your numbers. Week 9’s broken script was the same failure in code rather than prose.
One specific thing students omit almost universally: the checks that changed nothing. “Shapiro-Wilk did not reject normality for either group” is evidence you looked, and its absence is indistinguishable from not having looked.





Pitfall 6: The paragraph with no caveats

“Wind generation in the North East is 40 % higher than the South East (p < 0.01, Cohen’s d = 1.2). We recommend prioritizing all future wind farm development in the North East.”







NoteStuck? Start here





The statistics here are reported properly — better than most. So read the second sentence on its own and ask what it assumes that the first sentence did not establish.









TipWhat is wrong





The statistics are well reported, which is what makes this the most dangerous example on the page.
What is missing is everything the analysis could not see: confounders (turbine type, terrain, hub height, age); whether the sampled farms represent the regions; grid connection costs and planning constraints, which are not in the dataset and often decide siting; and the leap from “higher average output” to “all development”, which the word “all” cannot survive.
Week 7 is the direct precedent. Region explained 31 % of the variation in capacity factor, so 69 % was within regions — site selection inside a region mattered more than the choice of region, and an average difference does not license a blanket rule.
Refrains: what is the model not capturing? and compared to what?













Extension: find the pitfalls in the wild
Optional.

Go back to the Week 4 exemplars — the faithful briefing and the traitor’s. Find one instance of each pitfall. The traitor is easier; the interesting finds are in the faithful one.
Find a real press release from an energy company or a campaign group and mark it up. Most contain Pitfall 1 and Pitfall 3 in the first paragraph.
Swap drafts with someone now, before the review session, and mark only for these six. Give them the list rather than a verdict — a review that names the category is one the author can act on.

title: Week 10: Common Pitfalls
section: Exercise 2: Match the refrain to the pitfall
text:
Exercise 2: Match the refrain to the pitfall
Five questions have recurred since Week 2. They are the whole module compressed into things you can ask out loud:




Refrain




1
“Is that a big number?”


2
“Compared to what?”


3
“What assumptions are we making?”


4
“How plausible was this before we tested?”


5
“What is the model not capturing?”



Print a vector of three numbers giving the refrain that most directly catches Pitfalls 3, 4 and 6, in that order.


















TipSolution





c(1, 3, 5)

Pitfall 3 → “Is that a big number?” A p-value with no effect size. The refrain demands a magnitude, an interval and a comparator.
Pitfall 4 → “What assumptions are we making?” Everything the sentence claims rests on “under current accounting rules”, and that rule is a choice worth 1060 kg CO₂ per MWh.
Pitfall 6 → “What is the model not capturing?” The statistics are fine. The recommendation covers terrain, grid costs and planning, none of which the analysis contained.

The refrains overlap on purpose. “Compared to what?” also catches Pitfall 3, and Pitfall 6 needs it too. Five questions asked reflexively will catch more than any checklist you try to memorize — which is the point of them being short enough to say out loud.





Extension: which refrain do you skip?
Optional, and honest self-assessment is the exercise.








Then find, in your own draft, one place where your lowest-scoring refrain would change what you wrote. Change it. That single edit is worth more than another pass of proofreading.

Three things, in this order:

title: Week 2: Your First ggplot
text:
In the content session, you learned about summarizing data (mean, median, spread), honest data visualization, and the grammar of graphics — the idea that a plot is built from layers: data, aesthetics, and geometries.
These exercises let you practise the ggplot2 syntax before the application session, where you’ll build briefing-quality figures.
Goals:

Build a histogram with geom_histogram()
Build a plot with colour mapping and a legend
Get comfortable with the ggplot(data, aes(...)) + geom_*() pattern







NoteHow these exercises work





The code boxes start empty, except for comments to guide you through the code that’s expected.
Work one comment at a time. If you get stuck:

Hint 1 restates what you are trying to do.
Hint 2 sketches the shape the code might take.
Hint 3 gives you the code with the key pieces blanked out.
Solution gives you the lot.

Take a real attempt before opening a hint: you will learn by doing, not by reading. The demonstrators are here to help.
Three things worth knowing:

The boxes share one R session, exactly like a script. Anything you create in Exercise 1 is still there in Exercise 2.
Variable names are up to you. The last thing your block prints is what gets checked, so end each block with the answer.
Exercises have extensions underneath them. If you finish early, give them a stab. These are designed to equip you to tackle real coding problems you might face, using the documentation. We can help – but check the manuals first!










TipStuck?



Ask a new question on the Code Q&A discussion board. The discussion board allows anyone else who is stuck on the same thing to learn from (or provide!) the answer. We are notified of new posts, and will reply when we’re next available.
The board is private to this class, so sign in to GitHub first. If the link shows “404 – page not found”, you’re not signed in, or you haven’t accepted the Classroom 50 invitation yet.








NoteComing back to this page?




Your code is kept in this browser. You can Import code you saved using Export all code (page footer).


























Noteggplot2 vs matplotlib — what’s different?





In GEOL1151 you built plots imperatively — one command per element:
plt.plot(year, bio, label="Bioenergy")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
ggplot2 works declaratively: you describe what the plot is, and ggplot2 figures out how to draw it.



Concept
matplotlib
ggplot2




Start a plot
plt.figure()
ggplot(data, aes(...))


Map columns to axes
plt.plot(x, y)
aes(x = year, y = value)


Choose a geometry
plt.scatter(...)
+ geom_point()


Add layers
Separate calls
+ operator


Labels
plt.xlabel(...)
+ labs(x = ...)


Legend
Manual label= args
Automatic from colour/fill mapping



The biggest shift: aes() does the mapping. You tell ggplot2 which columns mean what (x position, y position, colour), then add a geometry that knows how to draw those mappings. No quoting column names inside aes() — just bare names like aes(x = year, y = bioenergy_twh).

title: Week 2: Your First ggplot
section: Exercise 1: The shape of the data
text:
Exercise 1: The shape of the data
Last week you plotted bioenergy against time. Now throw time away and look only at the values: how are the 26 yearly figures distributed?
Build a histogram of bioenergy_twh, labelled well enough that someone else could read it.















NoteHint 1





Every ggplot has the same three parts: the data, the mapping from columns to visual properties, and at least one geometry that draws something.
A histogram is unusual in needing only an x mapping. The y axis is a count that ggplot works out from the data — which is why you never name a y column for one.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
ggplot(data, aes(x = column)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10) +
  labs(x = "...", y = "...", title = "...")
Note the + at the end of each line, not the start of the next one. R reads line by line, so a line that could be complete is treated as complete — a leading + gives you a plot with no layers and no error.











NoteHint 3





ggplot(______, aes(x = ______)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10) +
  labs(x = "Bioenergy generation (TWh)",
       y = "______",
       title = "Distribution of UK bioenergy generation (2000–2025)")











TipSolution





ggplot(elec, aes(x = bioenergy_twh)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10) +
  labs(x = "Bioenergy generation (TWh)",
       y = "Count",
       title = "Distribution of UK bioenergy generation (2000–2025)")
The distribution is lumpy and right-skewed: a cluster of low values from the early 2000s, when bioenergy was small, and a second group above 30 TWh from the years after 2015.
That shape is a warning. These 26 numbers are not 26 measurements of the same thing — they are a quantity that grew. Summarizing them with a mean describes a year that never happened. The histogram is doing something more useful than showing a distribution: it is telling you that a distribution is the wrong model.





Extension: the bins are an argument
Optional, and all in the documentation: ?geom_histogram, ?geom_density, ?geom_violin, ?geom_rug.

Redraw with 3 bins, then 30. One version says “two clusters”, one says “steady spread”, one says almost nothing. Which of these three three stories is “correct”?
bins and binwidth are two ways to say the same thing. Which would you use if you wanted charts of two different datasets to be comparable, and why?
Show the same distribution without geom_histogram(). At least three other geoms will do it. Which of them still shows the gap in the middle?
Add the individual observations along the bottom axis, so a reader can see there are only 26 of them.











Quick check
For these 26 values the mean and the median are some way apart. Print the mean minus the median.
Then look back at your histogram and work out which side the difference comes from.


















TipSolution





mean(elec$bioenergy_twh) - median(elec$bioenergy_twh)
4.88 TWh: the mean is 21.3, the median 16.4.
When the mean exceeds the median, the high values sit further from the centre than the low ones. Here that is not an outlier — it is the growth trend, showing up as skew because we threw the time axis away.

title: Week 2: Your First ggplot
text:
Exercise 2: Two fuels, one legend
Now put bioenergy and coal on the same axes, with a legend built by ggplot rather than by hand.
The trick is that elec is wide: one column per fuel. ggplot expects one column to map to one aesthetic, so with data shaped like this you need one layer per fuel. You create the legend by mapping colour to a constant string inside aes().
It is clumsy. Notice how clumsy: we’ll meet the fix in the application session.















NoteHint 1





Anything inside aes() is a mapping and gets a legend; anything outside it is a setting and does not.
So geom_point(colour = "red") makes red points and no legend, while geom_point(aes(colour = "red")) makes a legend entry labelled “red” and lets ggplot pick the colour. That looks like a bug the first time you see it. Here we are using it deliberately.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
ggplot(elec, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = first_column, colour = "First label")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = second_column, colour = "Second label")) +
  labs(x = "...", y = "...", colour = "...")
Each layer inherits x from the top-level aes() and supplies its own y. The labs(colour = ) argument sets the legend’s title, not its entries — those come from the strings you mapped.











NoteHint 3





ggplot(elec, aes(x = ______)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = bioenergy_twh, colour = "Bioenergy")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = ______, colour = "______")) +
  labs(x = "Year",
       y = "Generation (TWh)",
       colour = "Fuel",
       title = "UK electricity: bioenergy vs coal")











TipSolution





ggplot(elec, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = bioenergy_twh, colour = "Bioenergy")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = coal_twh, colour = "Coal")) +
  labs(x = "Year",
       y = "Generation (TWh)",
       colour = "Fuel",
       title = "UK electricity: bioenergy vs coal")
Bioenergy rises while coal collapses — the Week 1 picture, with a legend ggplot wrote for you.
Now count the work. Two fuels took two nearly identical layers. Six fuels would take six, and adding a seventh would mean editing the code rather than the data. That is the signal that the data are the wrong shape for the question, and reshaping them is the first thing you will do in the application session.





Extension: make the legend earn its place
Optional. ?scale_colour_manual, ?theme, ?guides, ?geom_line, ?scale_y_continuous.

Connect the dots: add a line layer for each fuel so the trends read at a glance. You will need the colour mapping on the lines too, or the legend will disagree with the chart.
ggplot picked the colours. Choose them yourself, so that coal is dark and biomass is green — then ask whether that choice is informative or persuasive.
Move the legend inside the plot area, where the empty top-right corner is. Then decide whether that is an improvement or just cleverness.
Bioenergy in 2025 is 41 TWh and coal is zero. On this axis the coal line is flat against the bottom for years. Redraw with a log y axis (ggplot will warn that it has dropped the zero) and say what it reveals — and what it hides from a reader who does not notice the axis.
