title: Week 3: Changing the Assumptions
section: Exercise 1: The CO₂ cost of transport
text:
Exercise 1: The CO₂ cost of transport


Photo: Lyle Smith, Pexels

The UK’s wood pellets travel thousands of kilometres by ship, mostly from the southeastern United States. Burning them is counted as zero. How much does shipping add?
Work out the total CO₂ released by transporting the UK’s 2024 pellet imports, in millions of tonnes (Mt).
Everything you need is in imports (columns year, origin, import_kt, transport_km) and in the constant shipping_co2_per_tkm, which is 0.005 kg CO₂ per tonne-km.
If the maths feels complicated, start by looking at the units. How would you need to multiply and divide the units of the quantities you start with in order to end up with an answer in Mt?


















NoteHint 1





Every tonne of pellets that travels a kilometre releases 0.005 kg of CO₂. So for each origin you need tonnes × kilometres × 0.005, and then you need to add those five numbers together and express the answer in megatonnes.
The hard part is not the multiplication — it is keeping track of which unit you are in at each step.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:

Subsetting rows of a data frame by a condition is the df[condition, ] pattern you used in Week 1.
You can create a new column by assigning to a name that does not exist yet: df$new_column <- .... Doing it this way — rather than making a loose vector — keeps each number attached to the origin it belongs to, which matters as soon as you want to look at the table.
sum() collapses the column to one number.
Then divide to get from kg to Mt.












NoteHint 3





imports_2024 <- imports[imports$______ == 2024, ]

imports_2024$transport_co2_kg <-
  imports_2024$import_kt * ______ *      # kilotonnes to tonnes
  imports_2024$transport_km *
  ______

sum(imports_2024$______) / ______        # kg to Mt











TipSolution





imports_2024 <- imports[imports$year == 2024, ]

imports_2024$transport_co2_kg <-
  imports_2024$import_kt * 1000 *
  imports_2024$transport_km *
  shipping_co2_per_tkm

sum(imports_2024$transport_co2_kg) / 1e9
About 0.25 Mt CO₂ — a quarter of a million tonnes. Is that a big number? Hold that question: shipping turns out to be the smallest of the things the official figure leaves out. The chimney at those same plants releases about 43 Mt (Exercise 2), so transport is under 1 % of the story. It is real, non-zero, and a useful warm-up — but if you were hunting for a big missing number, you have not found it yet.





Quick check
To make the number easier to conceptualize, let’s bring it down to a human scale. How many kilograms of CO₂ does shipping release per tonne of pellets delivered?
(A kilogram’s easy to picture: it’s the mass of a 1 kg bag of flour, or a litre of water. A tonne is the mass of people in a crowded elevator.)
Use your 2024 subset again — total shipping CO₂ divided by total tonnes imported. What sort of context does this comparison give?


















NoteHint 1





You already have the total CO₂ in kg from Exercise 1 — it is what you had just before dividing by 1e9. Divide that by the total number of tonnes the UK imported in 2024.











TipSolution





sum(imports_2024$transport_co2_kg) / sum(imports_2024$import_kt * 1000)
About 27 kg CO₂ per tonne. The pellet itself releases about 1700 kg when burned. Shipping is a rounding error next to combustion — which is exactly why arguing about shipping is a good way to avoid arguing about combustion.






Extension: would New Zealand be different?
The UK’s pellets come mostly from the American southeast. Suppose the same mix of pellets were burned in a plant in New Zealand instead. Does this big change to shipping distances shift the conclusion?
transport_km won’t help you here: you’ll need to work the distances out yourself. Look up a coordinate for each origin and destination, then compute great-circle distances.















NoteHint 1





maps::world.cities is a data frame with name, country.etc, lat, long and capital. Subsetting to capital == 1 gives roughly one row per country, and the country.etc values for our origins are spelled "USA", "Canada" and "Latvia" — convenient, and also worth being suspicious of.
geosphere::distHaversine() takes two two-column matrices of (longitude, latitude) — note the order, which is the reverse of how we usually say it — and returns metres.










ImportantWhat the extension is coaxing you to think about





The moment you compute a distance yourself, you have to decide what you are measuring. Notice the assumptions that each choice smuggles in:

A capital city is not a port. Wood pellets leave the USA from Savannah and Baton Rouge, not Washington DC. How far wrong does that put you, and in which direction?
A great-circle line is not a shipping route. No vessel sails through the isthmus of Panama or across Antarctica. Compare your computed USA–UK distance with the 6200 km in transport_km: which is larger, and why?
EU_other and Other have no coordinates at all. What did you do with them? Dropping them is a decision, not a technicality — whose emissions did you just make disappear?
A longer voyage may be a more efficient one. Emissions per tonne-km vary with vessel size and route. Holding shipping_co2_per_tkm fixed is itself an assumption.

Write down, in one sentence each, the assumptions you think most affect your answer. Those sentences are the kind of caveat your Week 4 briefing might include — and just the sort of thing a traitor might leave out.

title: Week 3: Changing the Assumptions
text:
Exercise 2: What’s counted where


Photo: guvo59, Pexels

For traditional fuels, carbon is counted where it is released.
If coal mined in Australia is burned in Germany to generate electricity used in France, then the CO₂ emissions are attributed to Germany. (One convenient route to UK Net Zero is to import all our electricity from carbon-belching plants in other people’s countries!)
Biomass is different. Its CO₂ emissions are counted where a tree is felled. That way, no-one needs to track the fate of each tree’s carbon (released through decay or burning? Locked in a building or landfill?). Counting chimney emissions separately would count the same carbon twice.
factors holds emission estimates under several accounting rules (columns fuel, scenario, co2_kg_per_mwh). Work out the CO₂ that leaves the chimneys of the UK’s biomass power stations in 2025, in Mt: the combustion_only scenario. This number adds ‘zero’ to UK emissions, because the carbon was counted when the trees were felled overseas.


















NoteHint 1





Emissions = energy generated × emissions per unit of energy. The factor is per MWh, so the generation has to be in MWh too; the factor is in kg, so the answer starts life in kg.
The fiddly bit is pulling one number out of factors: it has a row for each combination of fuel and scenario, so a single condition will not identify it.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:

To pick out one value: subset the co2_kg_per_mwh column by a condition that is TRUE for exactly one row. Two conditions joined with & will do it.
elec has one row per year, so elec$bioenergy_twh[elec$year == 2025] is the generation.
Then multiply, and divide once at the end to get Mt.

Print each piece as you go.











NoteHint 3





stack_factor <- factors$co2_kg_per_mwh[
  factors$fuel == "______" ______
  factors$scenario == "______"
]

bio_mwh <- elec$bioenergy_twh[elec$year == ______] * ______

bio_mwh * stack_factor / ______











TipSolution





stack_factor <- factors$co2_kg_per_mwh[
  factors$fuel == "biomass" &
  factors$scenario == "combustion_only"
]

bio_mwh <- elec$bioenergy_twh[elec$year == 2025] * 1e6

bio_mwh * stack_factor / 1e9
About 41.0 Mt CO₂ per year leaves UK chimneys, counted as zero under official rules. For context, the UK’s territorial CO₂ emissions in 2025 were about 285 Mt (DESNZ provisional figures): this rule accounts for roughly 14 % of that.
At the chimney, biomass (1000 kg/MWh) is higher than coal (910): wood carries less energy per unit of carbon, so a megawatt-hour from pellets releases slightly more CO₂. Adding each fuel’s supply chain gives biomass 1060, coal 990 and gas 410. For each fuel, supply chain emissions are similar in magnitude, and they mostly happen outside the UK. What makes biomass attractive is that the chimney CO₂ is booked to the exporter’s forests – and the nice thing about imported pellets is that it’s someone else’s responsibility to ensure that new growth offsets the emissions incurred by felling!





Extension: different ways to pull your data

You probably pulled one value out of factors with [ and two conditions. Get the same number without using [ at all. There are at least three other routes — subset(), with(), match(); each behaves differently when the conditions fail to match any rows. Which of them warns you, and which hands you a silent NA? This behaviour might lead which function you prefer in different settings.
Produce 2025’s emissions under all three biomass scenarios at once, as a named vector. (sapply(), or just vectorized arithmetic on the whole column.)
elec goes back to 2000. Under with_supply_chain, which was the first year that the UK emitted more CO₂ from biomass than from coal?

title: Week 3: Changing the Assumptions
section: Exercise 3: The range of defensible answers
text:
Exercise 3: The range of defensible answers


Photo: Lauri Põldre, Pexels

“Carbon payback” is the idea that a burned tree’s CO₂ comes back out of the atmosphere as a replacement tree grows in its place. How much has come back depends on how long you wait and what grows back.
To help calculate this, we’ve written a function: a recipe with a name, which takes some inputs (its arguments) and hands back an answer. You are familiar with functions built into R and its libraries (read.csv(), mean(), ggplot()); the setup block at the top of this page loaded one more, fraction_reabsorbed(), from the file data/fraction_reabsorbed.R. Run this to read the file:








The lines starting # are comments, for users; R reads the rest. (Typing a function’s name without brackets, fraction_reabsorbed, also shows its code, but without the comments.)

If you have time, compare R’s f <- function(x) {} syntax for functions with Python’s def f(x):; notice that if an R function does not encounter a return(), it will return the last thing it executes - a bit like the code blocks in this page.

The function takes three arguments:

years: how long after felling and replanting we look;
forest: what grows back. One of the forests in data/forest_growth.csv (load it with read.csv() and look);
felled_at: how old the trees were when they were cut.

It looks up how much carbon the new stand holds after years, and divides by what the old stand held when it was felled at felled_at.


Loblolly pine. Photo: Woodlot, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0


3a. Net CO₂ after 20, 40 and 90 years
About three-quarters of the UK’s pellets come from the US (look in imports). We don’t have granular data about which forests they grew in, but many south-eastern US plantations grow loblolly pine, which is usually felled at 25–35 years old.
Take a loblolly plantation felled at 25. Work out the net CO₂ cost of a megawatt-hour of biomass electricity, in kg, 20, 40 and 90 years after felling: the full supply-chain figure (1060 kg/MWh), less the share of the chimney’s 1000 kg/MWh that the new trees have taken back.


















NoteHint 1





Call a function by its name, with its arguments in brackets, in the order the recipe lists them: years, then forest, then felled_at. The forest’s name is text, so it goes in quotes.











NoteHint 2





reabsorbed <- fraction_reabsorbed(c(20, 40, 90), "______", ______)
reabsorbed

1060 - ______ * reabsorbed











TipSolution





reabsorbed <- fraction_reabsorbed(c(20, 40, 90), "loblolly_plantation", 25)
reabsorbed

net <- 1060 - 1000 * reabsorbed
net
After 20 years the new plantation has taken back 82 % of the chimney’s CO₂, leaving 236 kg/MWh: well under gas (410 kg/MWh, supply chain included). By 40 years the figure is negative. The new stand is 40 years old and holds more carbon than the 25-year-old stand we cut, because trees left alone keep growing.
Notice what you had to choose: the forest, and its age at felling. Each moves the answer a long way.






Quick check
Which assumption has the larger effect on the biomass figure: adding the supply chain to the chimney figure, or allowing 20 years of regrowth?
Set answer to 1 if the supply chain matters more, or 2 if regrowth matters more.













3b. The picture
Put every biomass answer side by side: the official zero, the chimney alone, the full supply chain, and your three regrowth figures. Draw gas’s figure (410 kg/MWh, supply chain included) as a reference line: “is that a big number” requires a “compared to what?”















NoteHint 1





data.frame() builds a table from columns of equal length: here, six labels and six numbers. If net from 3a has gone, rebuild it first.
ggplot orders a character axis alphabetically, which here is meaningless. Converting the column to a factor and setting its levels in the order you want fixes that, because ggplot respects factor level order.
For the reference line, you want a horizontal line at a fixed y value. ggplot2 has a geom for exactly this.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:

order(x) returns the positions that would sort x, so column[order(other_column)] gives you the level order you want.
geom_col() draws bars whose heights are the y values.
geom_hline(yintercept = ...) draws the reference line.
labs() sets titles and axis labels, and theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) rotates the tick labels.












NoteHint 3





answers <- data.frame(
  label = c("Official", "Chimney only", "Full supply chain",
            "Regrown 20 yr", "Regrown 40 yr", "Regrown 90 yr"),
  co2_kg_per_mwh = c(0, 1000, 1060, ______)
)

answers$label <- factor(
  answers$label,
  levels = answers$label[______(answers$co2_kg_per_mwh)]
)

ggplot(answers, aes(x = label, y = ______)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = ______, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = expression(CO[2] ~ "(kg per MWh)"),
       title = expression("Biomass" ~ CO[2] * ": the answer depends on the question")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))











TipSolution





net <- 1060 - 1000 *
  fraction_reabsorbed(c(20, 40, 90), "loblolly_plantation", 25)

answers <- data.frame(
  label = c("Official", "Chimney only", "Full supply chain",
            "Regrown 20 yr", "Regrown 40 yr", "Regrown 90 yr"),
  co2_kg_per_mwh = c(0, 1000, 1060, net)
)

answers$label <- factor(
  answers$label,
  levels = answers$label[order(answers$co2_kg_per_mwh)]
)

ggplot(answers, aes(x = label, y = co2_kg_per_mwh)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 410, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = expression(CO[2] ~ "(kg per MWh)"),
       title = expression("Biomass" ~ CO[2] * ": the answer depends on the question")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
The range runs from −56 to 1060 kg/MWh. With no regrowth, biomass is two and a half times dirtier than gas; after 20 years of regrowth it is cleaner; after 40, it is apparently drawing carbon out of the air. Which bar you quote depends on what question you’re answering and what timescale you care about, and the choice spans the whole distance from “worse than gas” to “better than nothing at all.”
The dashed line is what makes the chart argue rather than merely display: without it, 1060 is just the tallest bar.






Extension: choose your forest

Swap the plantation for "loblolly_average" felled at 35, then for "sitka_spruce" felled at 40. Which forest gives biomass its most / least flattering 20-year figure?
Felling age is a choice too. Fell the plantation at 15 instead of 25. What happens to the 20-year figure, and why? (What does the function divide by?)
Ask for 100 years. What comes back, and why is that preferable to a number?
Colour each bar by whether it sits above or below the gas line.

title: Week 3: Changing the Assumptions
text:
Exercise 4: It takes time
So far every figure has assumed a steady state. But a replanted forest takes decades to regrow: if I fell a tree to make electricity today, how long does it take before I’m back to carbon neutrality?
Let’s generate 41 TWh (about what the UK will generate from biomass this year) and follow the resultant CO₂ over the coming fifty years.

Step 1: Gas
First up, let’s generate the 41 TWh from gas. How much extra CO₂ is in the atmosphere (yes, pedant, and the oceans too) in each of years 0 to 50, in Mt? Store it as gas, and plot it.


















NoteHint 1





Nothing is added after year 0, and nothing is taken away, so the same number repeats 51 times: rep() does that. The number is year 0’s emissions, worked out as in Exercise 2, but with gas’s emission factor. Which of gas’s two rows in factors is a fair comparison with biomass’s full supply chain?











NoteHint 2





years <- 0:50
pulse_mwh <- 41 * 1e6

gas_factor <- factors$co2_kg_per_mwh[
  factors$fuel == "gas" & factors$scenario == "______"
]
gas <- rep(pulse_mwh * gas_factor / ______, length(years))

scenarios <- data.frame(year = years, gas = gas)
ggplot(scenarios, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ______, colour = "Gas"))











TipSolution





years <- 0:50
pulse_mwh <- 41 * 1e6

gas_factor <- factors$co2_kg_per_mwh[
  factors$fuel == "gas" & factors$scenario == "with_supply_chain"
]
gas <- rep(pulse_mwh * gas_factor / 1e9, length(years))

scenarios <- data.frame(year = years, gas = gas)
ggplot(scenarios, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = gas, colour = "Gas")) +
  labs(x = "Years after generation",
       y = expression("Extra" ~ CO[2] ~ "in the atmosphere (Mt)"),
       colour = NULL)
Putting colour = "Gas" inside aes() names the line, and ggplot builds a legend from the names. Each new line gets its own name.






Step 2: Biomass, no regrowth
Now make the same 41 TWh from biomass. In year 0 we fell the trees, make pellets, ship them and burn them. First assume that nothing grows back. Create the variable biomass to record the extra CO₂ that is in the atmosphere each year. Add it to scenarios, and add a line to the chart.


















NoteHint 1





This is Step 1 again with biomass’s factor. scenarios$biomass <- biomass adds a column, and each geom_line() in a chart draws one line.











TipSolution





bio_factor <- factors$co2_kg_per_mwh[
  factors$fuel == "biomass" & factors$scenario == "with_supply_chain"
]
biomass <- rep(pulse_mwh * bio_factor / 1e9, length(years))
scenarios$biomass <- biomass

ggplot(scenarios, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = gas, colour = "Gas")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = biomass, colour = "Biomass, no regrowth")) +
  labs(x = "Years after generation",
       y = expression("Extra" ~ CO[2] ~ "in the atmosphere (Mt)"),
       colour = NULL)






Step 3: Replant
Now let the forest back in. We fell and burn the trees in year 0, as before, then replant the land with loblolly pine. Each year the new trees take back a little more of the chimney’s CO₂; fraction_reabsorbed() tells you what fraction. Store the result as replanted and add its line. A horizontal line at zero will help.


















NoteHint 1





Of biomass’s 1060 kg/MWh, 1000 came out of the chimney: that is the carbon the trees held. The other 60 came from the supply chain: we’d need to plant more trees than we harvested if we wanted to soak that up too.
fraction_reabsorbed() will happily take all 51 years at once.











NoteHint 2





chimney <- pulse_mwh * 1000 / 1e9

replanted <- biomass - chimney *
  fraction_reabsorbed(______, "loblolly_plantation", ______)











TipSolution





chimney <- pulse_mwh * 1000 / 1e9

replanted <- biomass - chimney *
  fraction_reabsorbed(years, "loblolly_plantation", 25)
scenarios$replanted <- replanted

ggplot(scenarios, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(y = gas, colour = "Gas")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = biomass, colour = "Biomass, no regrowth")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = replanted, colour = "Biomass, replanted")) +
  labs(x = "Years after generation",
       y = expression("Extra" ~ CO[2] ~ "in the atmosphere (Mt)"),
       colour = NULL)





Quick check
In which year does the replanted line first drop below zero?











What should we do then? In year 29 the new plantation holds all the carbon we burned. Should we fell it and burn it again? Leave it standing? Sell its future growth as a carbon credit? The line goes on falling below zero: is biomass entitled to that? Decide with your desk before you go on.



Step 4: What would the trees have done anyway?
Our gas line assumes that, had we burned gas, the plantation would have stood frozen in time. But the 25-year-old pines would otherwise have gone on growing, drawing down carbon that they never get the chance to in the biomass scenario. That growth belongs on the gas side of the ledger.
After years more, the standing plantation is 25 + years old. fraction_reabsorbed(25 + years, "loblolly_plantation", 25) compares it with the stand at 25: anything above 1 is extra growth. Make a new vector gas_standing that subtracts this extra growth from the gas emissions, and add its line.


















NoteHint 1





At 1, the standing stand holds what it held at 25, which is all the carbon we’d have burned: chimney. Above 1, the excess is new growth. So the extra uptake is chimney times (fraction − 1).











NoteHint 2





extra_growth <- chimney *
  (fraction_reabsorbed(______ + years, "loblolly_plantation", 25) - ______)
gas_standing <- gas - extra_growth











TipSolution





extra_growth <- chimney *
  (fraction_reabsorbed(25 + years, "loblolly_plantation", 25) - 1)
gas_standing <- gas - extra_growth
scenarios$gas_standing <- gas_standing

ggplot(scenarios, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(y = gas, colour = "Gas")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = gas_standing, colour = "Gas, pines left standing")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = biomass, colour = "Biomass, no regrowth")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = replanted, colour = "Biomass, replanted")) +
  labs(x = "Years after generation",
       y = expression("Extra" ~ CO[2] ~ "in the atmosphere (Mt)"),
       colour = NULL)
Biomass drops below gas-with-standing-pines in year 19 (years[replanted < gas_standing][1]), two years later than against plain gas. For a fast plantation felled near its peak, that’s before 2050, though not by much.
Now look back at Step 3. Below zero, the replanted line was banking growth that the standing plantation also does. If biomass claims that growth, gas should claim it too; and once both do, the line to beat is gas_standing, not zero.





Quick check
Rerun Steps 3 and 4 for "loblolly_average", an ordinary stand felled at 35 (change the 25s to 35). In which year does biomass drop below gas_standing now? Enter 0 if it never does within 50 years.
(Make sure you don’t miss any 25s! Defining a well-named variable (perhaps felling_age <- 25) makes your code more readable, and means you only have to change a single line of code. Unexplained numbers are bad coding practice: when you come back to your code, will you remember where the 25 came from?)














Extension: interrogate the sketch

Try "sitka_spruce" felled at 40. Does biomass ever beat gas with the spruce left standing?
Fell the plantation young, at 15. When does biomass beat plain gas, and when gas with the pines left standing? Which comparison would an advocate for biomass quote?
Mark 2050 on the chart (24 years after a 2026 burn) without using geom_point(). (Try: ?geom_vline, ?annotate)
Mapping a line to colour alone fails the 1 in 12 men with some degree of colour-vision deficiency. Map linetype too.
A power station burns every year, not once. How would you add up 25 years of pulses, each starting a year later than the last?

title: Week 3: Changing the Assumptions
text:
Start your briefing
Drax Power Station’s subsidy contract ends in 2031, and the government has to decide what happens next. Your briefing advises a minister to do one of three things:

Biomass: keep subsidising Drax to burn biomass.
Coal: encourage Drax to return to coal.
Close: withdraw support and let Drax close.

Whichever you pick, ask whether the numbers add up: can we continue to generate enough electricity whilst maintaining our target of net-zero CO₂ by 2050? drax_generation.csv has Drax’s own output since 2009.
Maximum 800 words, written in Markdown: plain text with a few symbols for formatting, which GitHub shows as a formatted page with its figures. That is how your reviewers will read it. Deadline: noon on the Thursday of Week 4. Get everything set up today, so you are ready to write in your own time.

Your drax repo
The briefing has a repository of its own, geol-skills-drax-yourname, which already holds a template briefing.md, a figures folder and the data. Access the repo by accepting the drax assignment.
In GitHub Desktop, File → Clone repository, choose geol-skills-drax-yourname and clone it next to your biomass repo. From now on you have two repos. The Current repository button at the top left of GitHub Desktop says which one you’re working in, and switches between them. Check it before every commit.


Folders and paths
Each repo is a folder on your computer, and a folder can hold other folders:
geol-skills-drax-you/
├── briefing.md
├── data/
│   └── drax_generation.csv
└── figures/
    ├── payback-scenarios.R
    └── payback-scenarios.png
A path says how to reach a file. An absolute path starts from the top of the drive, such as C:\Users\you\Documents\GitHub\geol-skills-drax-you\figures\payback-scenarios.png, and works only on your computer. A relative path starts from where you are: from briefing.md, the figure is figures/payback-scenarios.png. That one still works when the repo is on github.com or on your reviewer’s computer, so always use relative paths, with /.
Capitals count (Figures/ is a different folder), and spaces in names cause trouble, so use -. You’ve used a relative path since Week 1: read.csv("data/uk_electricity.csv").


Step 1: Save a figure
Pick the figure from today that best makes your case. Right-click it and choose Save image as…. Save it in the figures folder of your drax repo, with a name that says what it shows: for example figures/payback-scenarios.png.
In GitHub Desktop, with Current repository set to your drax repo, commit and push the figure.


Step 2: Save the code that made it
Every figure in your briefing gets its own script, with the same name, so anyone can remake it. On github.com, open your drax repo and choose Add file → Create new file. Type the name figures/payback-scenarios.R: typing the / puts the file in the figures folder.
Paste in just the code that draws that one figure, from loading the data to the plot. If it calls fraction_reabsorbed(), include the line source("data/fraction_reabsorbed.R") near the top: your drax repo has the function in its data folder. End with a line that saves the image:
ggsave("figures/payback-scenarios.png", width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 150)
Here in the browser, ggsave() can’t reach your repo folder, which is why you saved the image by hand in Step 1. The script will make the image for real once you run R on your own computer. Click Commit changes.


Step 3: Point briefing.md at your figure
On github.com, open briefing.md in your drax repo and click the pencil to edit it. Change figures/your-figure.png to your figure’s path, then click Preview. You should see headings, bold text and your figure. If the figure is missing, check the spelling of the path (capitals matter) and that you pushed the figure in Step 1.
Click Commit changes. Then, in GitHub Desktop, click Fetch origin and Pull origin, so the copy on your computer is up to date.


Step 4: Submitting
To submit, before next week, tag your last commit final and push the tag. The repo’s README shows how, in GitHub Desktop or on github.com. Make sure you tag the right commit: once it’s pushed, the final tag can’t be moved. If you forget, the version you pushed by noon will be reviewed.


Markdown formatting overview



You type
You get




# Title
The title


## Section
A section heading


**bold**
bold


*italic*
italic


- item
A bulleted list


1. item
A numbered list


![alt text](figures/name.png)
The figure


A blank line
A new paragraph



The briefing structure guide says what goes in each section; the Markdown guide has the rest of the Markdown you’ll need, and more on folders and paths.
For a sense of what a finished briefing looks like, read two that take opposite views on a different question, the environmental cost of AI: How bad is AI for the environment? and The hidden environmental cost of AI. Both are longer than yours will be. We’ll discuss them in Week 4: note which you find more convincing, and why.

title: Week 3: Changing the Assumptions
text:
Save your work

Export all code Import code
Export all code downloads every box on this page as one R file. Each box sits under a line like # Exercise 1: … [w2_1] ----; keep those lines if you edit the file, and Import code can put it back into the boxes on any computer. Your code is also kept in this browser as you type, so reloading the page doesn’t lose it.



Put the exported week3.R in your biomass repo, then commit and push via GitHub Desktop. Write a commit message that explains what you discovered about the assumptions.

title: Week 5: Designing Your Investigation
text:
In Weeks 1–4, you learned to question, explore, analyse, and communicate, under the banner of your biomass mini-project. Now you’ll apply these skills to an investigation of your own design.
No coding today: this page contains prompts for you to discuss as a desk. Discuss as a desk, and argue before you open a reveal — they are ordered so the first gives you a way in and the last gives you the answer.
Each exercise has an extension underneath it. If your desk finishes early, that is where to go.

title: Week 5: Designing Your Investigation
text:
Exercise 1: Critique HolmesCo’s site investigation
Read the HolmesCo ground investigation report, then answer the questions as a desk.






WarningHolmesCo Ground Investigation Report



See the full report: HolmesCo Site Investigation
Summary: HolmesCo was hired to assess whether a proposed wind farm site in County Durham has suitable ground conditions. They drilled 3 boreholes and concluded that the bedrock is competent throughout the site.


Discuss as a desk:

How were the borehole sites located? Where will the turbines actually go?
Is 3 boreholes enough to characterize a whole site? Do 36 core specimens change your answer?
What kind of sampling bias is this?
What is missing that would make this a proper investigation?


Extension: What do the data really support?

HolmesCo’s conclusion is not necessarily false; but it is not supported by the data they present. Rewrite a one-sentence conclusion so that is fully supported by the three boreholes drilled. How much of the original claim survives?
You are given budget to drill two additional boreholes. Where would you drill them? Write the sentence you would include in your conclusion if the new holes yieleded (i) reassuring; and (ii) non-reassuring results.

title: Week 5: Designing Your Investigation
text:
Integrative exercise: design sketch
Browse the list of summative project topics for 5 minutes. Then, with your provisional group, pick a candidate topic and sketch answers to:

What is our question? (One sentence.)
What data would we need?
What is our control or comparison?
What confounders should we worry about?

Each group shares one sentence with the class.






NoteThe test to apply before you commit





Say your question out loud, then say what you would conclude if the result came out the opposite way to your hypothesis. If you cannot finish that second sentence — or if the honest answer is “we would go looking for a different analysis” — it is not yet a research question.

title: Week 5: Designing Your Investigation
text:
Key points

You cannot know whether something is big unless you measure something else. Controls are how you isolate what matters.
A confounder is linked to both the grouping and the outcome. Ignore it and your result may be an artefact.
Sites picked because they were extreme look better next time anyway: regression to the mean. Only a comparison group chosen the same way, and left alone, shows how much of the change is real.
Know your unit of replication. Many measurements from one place are one sample of that place.
Your sampling strategy is a decision you have to justify. “We sampled these because they were there” is honest but weak — and it is the most common design in real geoscience, so learn to state which way it biases you.
Everything HolmesCo does wrong this week, you should do right in your project — and where you cannot, say so in writing.

title: Week 6: Check Your Assumptions
text:
In the content session you learned how to run a t-test and read its output. But every statistical test rests on assumptions, and when those are violated the test can hand you a confident answer that is wrong.
Today’s data come from a HolmesCo borehole survey. HolmesCo measured temperatures at depth in two geological formations — the Whin Sill (a dolerite intrusion) and the Stainmore Formation (sedimentary) — to assess geothermal potential in County Durham.
By the end you will have produced a significant result, and then destroyed it, without touching a single number.
Goals:

Look at distributions before testing them
Run a t-test and read what it actually claims
Check normality rather than assuming it
Build the reflex: look, test, check, and be willing to go back

title: Week 6: Check Your Assumptions
text:
The HolmesCo report
HolmesCo has sent the report below to a client who wants to know where to drill for geothermal heat. Read it as the client would. Then read it again as a referee: what does it not let you check?


⚒️ HolmesCo
Geological Consultants Since 2019
“Our Results Are Never Skewed”™

Geothermal potential of County Durham: borehole temperature survey
Summary. Excellent news: the Stainmore Formation is significantly hotter than the Whin Sill. We recommend that all exploratory drilling target the Stainmore.
Methods. HolmesCo field teams logged the temperature at depth in 70 boreholes, 35 in the Whin Sill (a dolerite intrusion) and 35 in the Stainmore Formation (sedimentary). We compared the two formations using a two-sample t-test, the industry standard, run in R.
Results. Stainmore boreholes averaged 35.3 °C, against 26.9 °C in the Whin Sill (Figure 1). The error bars are small, which shows how precise our measurements were.





Figure 1. Mean borehole temperature by formation. Error bars: ±1 standard error. * p < 0.05.




Discussion. We ran a t-test and the difference was significant (p = 0.03), meaning that there is a 97 % chance that the difference is real! The Stainmore Formation is the clear target for geothermal development.

Keep these questions in mind. Each exercise below answers one of them.

A bar is one number per formation. What do the individual boreholes look like? (Exercise 1)
How big is the difference, and how sure can we be of its size? (Exercise 2)
What does a t-test assume about the data, and did HolmesCo check? (Exercises 3 and 4)
Is “a 97 % chance that the difference is real” what a p-value means? (Exercise 2)

title: Week 6: Check Your Assumptions
text:
Exercise 1: Look before you test
borehole holds HolmesCo’s data: 70 rows and two columns, formation and temperature_c. Figure 1 showed you two bars. Before running anything, find out what the two groups actually look like.
Draw one histogram per formation, then finish the block by printing the standard deviation of each group.


















NoteHint 1





facet_wrap() splits a plot into panels by the values of a column, so you do not have to filter the data twice. It takes a formula: ~ column_name.
For the second part, you want one summary per group. Doing it by hand — subsetting each formation and calling sd() — works and is worth writing once. Then find the function that does it in a single call.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
ggplot(data, aes(x = value_column)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12) +
  facet_wrap(~ group_column)

tapply(data$value_column, data$group_column, sd)
tapply(values, groups, f) splits the first argument by the second and applies f to each piece, returning a named vector — which is why the output tells you which number belongs to which formation.











NoteHint 3





ggplot(borehole, aes(x = ______)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12) +
  facet_wrap(~ ______)

tapply(borehole$temperature_c, borehole$______, ______)











TipSolution





ggplot(borehole, aes(x = temperature_c)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12) +
  facet_wrap(~ formation)

tapply(borehole$temperature_c, borehole$formation, sd)
Both distributions are right-skewed — a long tail of high temperatures — and Stainmore is much the worse, with a few very hot boreholes pulling its mean upward. That is typical of geoscience measurements like temperature at depth, permeability and grain size, which are often roughly log-normal.
The spreads are 9.1 and 20.3: the Stainmore group varies more than twice as much. Compare HolmesCo’s “small” error bars, which were standard errors of about 1.5 and 3.4. The SE says how precisely the mean is pinned down, and shrinks as you add boreholes. The SD says how much the boreholes themselves vary, and it doesn’t shrink. Plotting the SE made the spread look tidy. That is worth knowing but is not the problem. R’s t.test() uses Welch’s version by default, which handles unequal variances perfectly well.
The skew is the problem, and no default will save you from it.





Extension: four views of two groups
Optional. ?geom_violin, ?geom_density, ?scale_x_log10, ?geom_jitter.

Show the same comparison without facet_wrap() — both groups in one panel. At least three geoms will do it. Which makes the difference in spread easiest to see, and which makes the difference in centre easiest?
A violin of 35 points hides 35 points. Overlay the raw observations on it. Now count how many Stainmore boreholes are above 60 °C, and ask whether a summary of this group is meaningful at all.
Put the x axis on a log scale and redraw the histograms. The shape changes completely — and you have not altered a single value. Keep that plot; Exercise 4 explains it.
Which single chart would you put in front of a client who wanted a yes-or-no answer about geothermal potential? Which would you put in an appendix? They should not be the same chart.

title: Week 6: Check Your Assumptions
text:
Exercise 2: The significant result
Now do what HolmesCo did: run a two-sample t-test asking whether mean temperature differs between the formations.
End the block by printing the test.


















NoteHint 1





R’s formula interface lets you say “this outcome, split by that group” in one expression. The tilde ~ means “described by”.
You do not need to split the data yourself — passing data = borehole lets R find both columns by name.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
t.test(outcome_column ~ grouping_column, data = df)
Print the result of that, rather than assigning it and printing one element. The output has four things worth reading: the t statistic, the degrees of freedom, the p-value, and the confidence interval for the difference in means.
The degrees of freedom will not be a whole number. That is Welch’s correction for unequal variances, and it is R’s default.











NoteHint 3





raw_test <- t.test(______ ~ ______, data = borehole)
raw_test











TipSolution





raw_test <- t.test(temperature_c ~ formation, data = borehole)
raw_test
p = 0.030. Significant at the conventional threshold, and this is where HolmesCo stopped.
It is not “a 97 % chance that the difference is real”. The p-value is calculated in the null world, by assuming there is no difference: it is the chance of a gap this large if the formations were the same. It says nothing directly about the chance that they differ, so 1 − p is not the probability that the difference is real.
Look at the confidence interval before you do: roughly 0.9 to 16.0 °C. The data are consistent with the Stainmore Formation being 16 °C hotter on average, and equally consistent with it being one degree hotter. A result can be “significant” and still be almost uninformative about the size of the thing you care about, which is why a p-value on its own is never a finding.
And there is a worse problem. You saw the skew in Exercise 1. The t-test assumes something about these data that you have not checked.





Extension: the test has options
Optional. ?t.test is the whole exercise — it is a longer help page than you expect, and almost every argument in it changes the answer.

Run it again with var.equal = TRUE. That is Student’s original test, which pools the variances. The p-value barely moves here — construct group sizes where it would move a lot. (Hint: unequal variances hurt most when the group sizes are also unequal.)
What does alternative = "greater" do to the p-value, and why is choosing it after seeing the data indefensible?
The output reports degrees of freedom of about 47, not 68. Find out in the help page where the missing 21 went.
t.test(x, y) and t.test(y ~ g) are two ways to call the same function. Reproduce your result using the other form, and check the sign of the estimate. Which group did R subtract from which, and how would you know without being told?

title: Week 6: Check Your Assumptions
text:
Exercise 3: Check the assumption
The t-test assumes the values within each group are roughly normally distributed. You have seen that they are not. Now demonstrate it, rather than asserting it.
A QQ plot puts your data against what a normal distribution would have produced. Points on the diagonal mean normal; a curve away from the line at one end means skew.
Finish by printing a formal test of normality for the Stainmore group.


















NoteHint 1





Two of these steps you have done before. Subsetting one group’s values is the x[condition] pattern from Week 1, with a character comparison instead of a numeric one.
qqnorm() draws the plot and qqline() adds the reference line to the plot that already exists — the same “start it, then add to it” pattern as plot() and lines().
The third step is a test whose null hypothesis is the data are normal. Think about what a small p-value means when that is the null.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
group <- df$value[df$group_column == "GroupName"]

qqnorm(group)
qqline(group)

shapiro.test(group)
Careful with the name: the formation is recorded as Stainmore, and a comparison against a slightly different spelling returns no rows and no error.











NoteHint 3





stainmore <- borehole$temperature_c[borehole$formation == "______"]

qqnorm(stainmore, main = "Stainmore, raw")
qqline(______)

shapiro.test(______)











TipSolution





stainmore <- borehole$temperature_c[borehole$formation == "Stainmore"]

qqnorm(stainmore, main = "Stainmore, raw")
qqline(stainmore)

shapiro.test(stainmore)
p = 0.032. The null hypothesis of Shapiro-Wilk is that the data are normal, so a small p-value is evidence against normality — the opposite reading from the t-test you just ran, and a reliable source of confusion. Say it out loud each time: “small p, reject the null, the null was normality.”
The QQ plot shows the same thing without a threshold: the points curve away above the line at the top end, which is what a long right tail looks like.
Two cautions before you start applying this everywhere. First, the Whin Sill group passes (p = 0.28), so “the data are skewed” was really “one of the two groups is skewed”. Second, Shapiro-Wilk gets more powerful with sample size, so with 35 points it can miss real skew, and with 3500 it will reject normality over deviations too small to matter. The QQ plot does not have that problem, which is a good argument for looking at one every time.





Extension: what does non-normal cost you?
Optional.

Run Shapiro-Wilk on the Whin Sill group as well, and put its QQ plot beside Stainmore’s. ?par and its mfrow argument will get them side by side. Does the pair of plots change your view of Exercise 2?
Generate 35 values from a genuinely normal distribution with rnorm(35, mean = 35, sd = 20) and QQ-plot them. Do it five times. How wiggly does a normal sample look at this size? That is the baseline you should be comparing against, and almost nobody establishes it before judging their own plot.
Shapiro-Wilk on 3500 values will reject normality for deviations far too small to affect a t-test. Demonstrate that with rnorm() plus a tiny amount of skew, and then decide which of the two tools — the test or the plot — you would rely on in a report.

title: Week 6: Check Your Assumptions
text:
Exercise 4: Transform and re-test
Taking logs pulls in a long right tail. If the values are roughly log-normal — as temperature at depth often is — the logged values will be roughly normal, and the t-test becomes entitled to its assumption.
Redo the test on logged temperatures and see what survives.


















NoteHint 1





log() applies to a whole vector at once, so one line creates the new column. Assign it into the data frame with $ so that the formula interface can find it by name.
Then repeat Exercise 3’s check and Exercise 2’s test, with the new column in place of the old one. The only thing that changes is which column you name.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
df$log_value <- log(df$value)

shapiro.test(df$log_value[df$group == "..."])

t.test(log_value ~ group, data = df)
log() in R is the natural logarithm. Base 10 would work just as well for this purpose — the p-value is identical, because taking logs in a different base multiplies every value by a constant.











NoteHint 3





borehole$log_temp <- ______(borehole$temperature_c)

shapiro.test(borehole$log_temp[borehole$formation == "Stainmore"])

t.test(______ ~ formation, data = borehole)











TipSolution





borehole$log_temp <- log(borehole$temperature_c)

shapiro.test(borehole$log_temp[borehole$formation == "Stainmore"])

t.test(log_temp ~ formation, data = borehole)
Shapiro-Wilk on the logged Stainmore values gives p = 0.21 — normality no longer rejected. The t-test then gives p = 0.22, nowhere near significant.
So much for HolmesCo’s report: raw values gave p = 0.03 and a drilling recommendation, logged values give p = 0.22 and nothing. The finding was driven by a handful of extreme boreholes in the tail, not by a difference between formations.
One honest complication, which matters more than the headline. The logged test is not the raw test made more reliable — it is a different question. A t-test on logs compares geometric means, so you are now asking whether the typical Stainmore borehole is hotter, rather than whether the average is. For skewed data that is usually the better question. But you have to say which one you answered, and switching to it after seeing the first p-value is a decision a reader is entitled to know about.
The lesson: a p-value is worth exactly as much as the assumptions behind it. Check first, and write down what you checked — including the checks you ran that did not change anything.





Extension: three more ways to handle a skewed tail
Optional. ?wilcox.test, ?sqrt, ?boxplot.stats.

A Wilcoxon rank-sum test makes no normality assumption at all. Run it on the raw temperatures. You will get p = 0.09 — a third answer, from the same data, on the same question. Which of the three would you report, and could you defend that choice if you had chosen it before running any of them?
Try a square-root transformation instead of a log. Does it fix the Shapiro-Wilk result? Transformations are not interchangeable, and the right one depends on the shape you are trying to fix.
The alternative no one should take but everyone considers: drop the extreme values and rerun the raw t-test. Do it, note the p-value, and then write down the sentence you would have to include in your methods section to describe what you did. (That sentence is why this is not an acceptable route.)











Quick check
Across Exercises 2 and 4, did the p-value go up or down when you log-transformed?
Set answer to "increase" or "decrease".

title: Week 7: Comparing Groups
text:
Last week you compared two groups with a t-test. What if you have four?
You could run every pairwise t-test — six of them for four groups. The content session showed you what that costs: at α = 0.05 each, the chance of at least one false positive when nothing is going on is 1 − 0.95⁶, about 26 %. Run enough comparisons and you will always find something.
ANOVA asks a single question instead: does any group differ? If the answer is yes, a post-hoc test such as TukeyHSD says which pairs, with the correction for multiple looks built in.
Today’s data: wind farm capacity factors at 100 sites across four UK regions. Does geography matter for wind output?
Goals:

Visualize four groups at once, and order them usefully
Run an ANOVA and read its output
Find which pairs differ, with the correction applied
Understand what the correction does and does not buy you







NoteHow these exercises work





The code boxes start empty, except for comments to guide you through the code that’s expected.

title: Week 7: Comparing Groups
section: Exercise 1: Four groups at a glance
text:
Exercise 1: Four groups at a glance
wind has 100 rows: a region and a capacity_pct — the percentage of its theoretical maximum output that a site actually delivered.
Draw violins by region, ordered by median rather than alphabetically, and finish by printing the four group means.


















NoteHint 1





The violins are the Week 6 pattern with four groups instead of two — nothing changes.
The ordering is the new part. ggplot puts a character axis in alphabetical order, which here means “Northern England, Scotland, Southern England, Wales” — an order that hides the two clusters. You want the regions arranged by the thing being measured.
reorder(factor, values) reorders the first argument by a summary of the second. Its default summary is the mean; FUN = median orders by the middle site, which a few extreme sites can’t drag about.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
ggplot(df, aes(x = reorder(group, value, FUN = median), y = value)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(x = "...", y = "...")

tapply(df$value, df$group, mean)
Reordering inside aes() leaves the data alone and changes only the plot. That is usually what you want — the alternative, converting the column to a factor with explicit levels, affects every later use of it.











NoteHint 3





ggplot(wind, aes(x = reorder(______, capacity_pct, FUN = ______),
                 y = ______)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(x = "Region",
       y = "Capacity factor (% of maximum output)",
       title = "Wind farm capacity factor by UK region")

tapply(wind$capacity_pct, wind$______, ______)











TipSolution





ggplot(wind, aes(x = reorder(region, capacity_pct, FUN = median),
                 y = capacity_pct)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(x = "Region",
       y = "Capacity factor (% of maximum output)",
       title = "Wind farm capacity factor by UK region")

tapply(wind$capacity_pct, wind$region, mean)
Two clusters, and ordering the axis is what makes them visible:

Higher: Northern England 29.9 %, Scotland 29.6 %
Lower: Wales 24.7 %, Southern England 23.2 %

That is geographically plausible — northern and western sites are windier. But the gaps are very different in size. Six points separate the clusters; three-tenths of a point separates Northern England from Scotland. The question is not “are the four numbers identical”, because four sample means never are. The question is which of these gaps is bigger than the sampling noise.
Note also that the violins are much the same height. ANOVA assumes roughly equal variance across groups, and you have just checked it without being asked to.





Extension: show the sites
Optional. ?geom_jitter, ?geom_violin, ?stat_summary, ?geom_errorbar.

Overlay the 25 individual sites on each violin. Does any region look like it has sub-groups within it? A bimodal region would make its mean nearly meaningless, and a violin’s smoothing can blur sub-groups away (or invent them); the points can’t.
Now replace the violins themselves with means and an approximate 95 % confidence interval, but keep the jittered points from step 1 showing behind them. That combination — raw points plus mean ± CI — is what ANOVA actually reasons about, and it is noticeably less reassuring than the violins: the points overlap heavily between regions even where the CIs do not. stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, fun.args = list(mult = 1.96)) draws it in one line (mean_cl_normal() would be the exact t-based version, but it needs the Hmisc package, which isn’t available here — 1.96 standard errors is close enough at 25 sites per group).
Add a horizontal line at the overall mean of 26.8 %. ANOVA compares the spread of group means around that line with the spread of sites around their own group mean, so this one line makes the F statistic visible.
Order the regions north to south instead of by output, and decide which ordering you would publish. There is a real argument for each.









Further reading: on why we don’t use box plots — they are harder to read than they look — and what to show instead — Nick Desbarats, “I’ve Stopped Using Box Plots. Should You?”, Nightingale, and Claus Wilke, “Visualizing uncertainty”, Fundamentals of Data Visualization, ch. 9.

title: Week 7: Comparing Groups
section: Exercise 2: One test instead of six
text:
Exercise 2: One test instead of six
ANOVA compares the variation between group means with the variation within groups. If the group means are further apart than the noise inside each group would explain, F is large and p is small.
Run it, and print the summary.


















NoteHint 1





aov() takes the same formula shape as t.test(). The difference is what you do with the result: printing an aov object on its own shows you sums of squares and not much else, so wrap it in summary().
The degrees of freedom are worth a moment. One line of the table is about the regions, the other about everything left over. With four groups and 100 sites, you should be able to predict both numbers before you run it.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
fit <- aov(outcome ~ group, data = df)
summary(fit)
Save the fit to a name. TukeyHSD in the next exercise needs the aov object itself, not its summary, and re-running the fit there would work but would also invite the two to drift apart.











NoteHint 3





wind_aov <- aov(______ ~ ______, data = wind)
summary(______)











TipSolution





wind_aov <- aov(capacity_pct ~ region, data = wind)
summary(wind_aov)
F = 14.21 on 3 and 96 degrees of freedom, p = 9.8 × 10⁻⁸.
The degrees of freedom are 3 (four groups, minus one) and 96 (100 sites, minus four group means). If those numbers are not what you expected, something is wrong with the data before anything is wrong with the test — a common cause is R having read a grouping column as something other than four distinct values.
F = 14.2 means the group means are spread about fourteen times more widely than the within-region scatter would produce by chance. The p-value is tiny.
And it tells you almost nothing you can use. “At least one of four regions differs from at least one other” is not a planning recommendation. You already suspected it from the plot. What ANOVA buys is permission to go looking for the specific differences without the 26 % false-positive problem — which is the next exercise.





Extension: what ANOVA assumes
Optional. ?plot.lm, ?kruskal.test, ?oneway.test, ?bartlett.test.

plot(wind_aov) gives four diagnostic plots. The first two are the ones to read: residuals against fitted values (look for a fan shape) and a QQ plot of residuals (look for curvature). Does this ANOVA deserve to be trusted?
Run kruskal.test() on the same data — the rank-based version that assumes no normality. It gives p = 1.5 × 10⁻⁶. Both are tiny, so the conclusion survives, which is the most useful possible outcome of a robustness check and the least reportable.
oneway.test() is the ANOVA equivalent of Welch’s t-test, dropping the equal-variance assumption. Compare its answer. Then work out from the group standard deviations why it barely moves here.
ANOVA with exactly two groups is a t-test. Confirm it: run both on Scotland and Wales alone, and check that F equals t².

title: Week 7: Comparing Groups
text:
Exercise 3: Which pairs actually differ?
ANOVA said something differs. TukeyHSD says what, comparing all six pairs while holding the overall false-positive rate at 5 % rather than letting it climb to 26 %.
Run it, then finish by printing how many of the six pairs are significant at the 0.05 level.


















NoteHint 1





TukeyHSD() takes the fitted aov object — not its summary, and not the data.
What comes back is a list with one element per grouping variable, named after that variable. Inside is a matrix with a row per pair and four columns: the difference, its lower and upper bounds, and the adjusted p-value.
Counting how many entries of a vector are below a threshold is a one-liner: a comparison gives you TRUE and FALSE, and sum() treats TRUE as 1.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
tukey <- TukeyHSD(fit)
tukey

sum(tukey$grouping_variable[, "p adj"] < 0.05)
The column is called p adj, with a space, so it has to be quoted inside the brackets. The comma before it means “all rows, this column”.











NoteHint 3





tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(______)
tukey_result

sum(tukey_result$______[, "______"] < 0.05)











TipSolution





tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(wind_aov)
tukey_result

sum(tukey_result$region[, "p adj"] < 0.05)
Four of the six:



Comparison
diff
p adj





Scotland – Northern England
−0.33
0.994
no difference


Wales – Southern England
+1.43
0.673
no difference


Wales – Northern England
−5.21
0.0005
differs


Wales – Scotland
−4.88
0.0012
differs


Southern England – Scotland
−6.32
<0.001
differs


Southern England – Northern England
−6.64
<0.001
differs



Every north–south pair differs; neither within-cluster pair does. The finding is not “region matters” but something sharper and more useful: latitude matters, and the distinction between Scotland and Northern England is not supported by these data. A developer choosing between those two on capacity factor alone would be choosing on noise.
One honest footnote. Run the six comparisons uncorrected and you get the same four. The correction changed nothing here, because these p-values are not close to the threshold. That is the usual case, and it is exactly why the correction is easy to skip: it looks like it never matters, right up until the study where your best pair sits at 0.03 and the corrected value is 0.18.





Extension: the correction, and what it costs
Optional. ?p.adjust, ?pairwise.t.test, ?plot.TukeyHSD.

Plot the Tukey result. Six horizontal intervals; the two that cross the zero line are the two non-significant pairs. Then work out why this figure is more use in a report than the table is.
Run pairwise.t.test() with p.adjust.method = "none", then "bonferroni", then "holm". Four comparisons stay significant throughout. Construct — or simulate — a dataset where they do not agree, which is the only way to see what the correction is for.
Corrections are not free: holding the false-positive rate down raises the false-negative rate. With 28 pairs instead of 6, how large would a real difference have to be to survive Bonferroni? ?power.t.test with a smaller sig.level will show you.
The deeper problem the correction does not solve: it assumes you declared your six comparisons in advance. Describe, in one sentence, how someone could run this exact analysis honestly and still end up reporting a false positive.











Quick check
With four groups there are six pairwise comparisons. How many are there with eight groups? Print the number.


















TipSolution





choose(8, 2)

Doubling the groups nearly quintuples the comparisons, so the false-positive problem grows much faster than the study does:




Groups
Pairs
Chance of at least one false positive at α = 0.05




2
1
5 %


4
6
26 %


8
28
76 %


12
66
97 %



At 12 groups you are essentially guaranteed a “finding”. This is the arithmetic behind the HolmesCo mineral survey, and behind a good deal of published science.

title: Week 8: Models and Their Limits
text:
A model is a deliberate simplification: it captures some of reality and ignores the rest. The skill is not fitting one — lm() does that in eight characters — but knowing what yours has thrown away.
Today you will fit two models. One is honest about being incomplete. The other is HolmesCo’s, and it is about to be taken apart.
Goals:

Fit a linear regression and say what the slope means in words
Read residual plots for the structure the model missed
Rebuild a bad model and measure how much was being left out
See why a model that fits better can predict worse







NoteHow these exercises work





The code boxes start empty, except for comments to guide you through the code that’s expected.
Work one comment at a time. If you get stuck:

Hint 1 restates what you are trying to do.
Hint 2 sketches the shape the code might take.
Hint 3 gives you the code with the key pieces blanked out.
Solution gives you the lot.

Take a real attempt before opening a hint: you will learn by doing, not by reading. The demonstrators are here to help.
Three things worth knowing:

The boxes share one R session, exactly like a script. Anything you create in Exercise 1 is still there in Exercise 2.
Variable names are up to you. The last thing your block prints is what gets checked, so end each block with the answer.
Exercises have extensions underneath them. If you finish early, give them a stab. These are designed to equip you to tackle real coding problems you might face, using the documentation. We can help – but check the manuals first!
